(Para 11.5)
            The Committee observes that the major option for limiting imports that remains for use by policy-makers in a
QR-free regime is that of higher tariffs. The Committee recommends that QRs may be converted into tariff and non-
tariff equivalents to give an adequate protection to the domestic SSls. While this measure would be a discouraging
factor for foreign producers to export their cheap goods to India, it would also mean increasing revenue for the
Government of India.
(Para 11.6)
            The Committee therefore, recommends tariff and non-tariff barriers may be imposed in the form of higher safety
standards, and sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures as are permissible within the WTO framework.
(Para 11.7)
            The Committee further recommends that compulsory printing of manufacturing date, maximum retail price (in
Indian rupees) and composition of the products, by foreign exporters should be introduced. This would, of course, be
compatible with the national obligation under WTO, as domestic manufacturers are already required to comply with
these requirements.
(Para 11.8)
              The Committee recommends that all banks should take effective steps to help sick SSIs restructure themselves. 
The Committee observes that the abolition of Sick Industries Companies Act (SICA) so as to facilitate prompt winding
up of unviable enterprise and swift redeployment of their resources in production remains a promise. Similarly, on the
Competition Law, nothing has been done. It has reached only the stage of Parliamentary consideration. It has not
become a law. 
(Para 12.4)
              The Committee recommends that action may be taken in regard to Abolition of Sick Industries Companies
Act.  Further, Ministry should endeavour to see that Competition Law is enacted soon.
In order to revive sick industries, the Committee recommends further: -
(a)
             A special fund may be created for rehabilitation of sick SSls and the commercial banks may earmark a
portion of loans to ailing SSls.
(b)            The State Level Inter Institutional Committees (SLIICs) need to be revitalised and DICs may be used as
a forum to redress the grievances regarding delays in rehabilitation.
(c)             An Arbitration Clause may also be included in all borrower-lender arrangements in terms of Indian
Arbitration Act to avoid protracted litigation and costs. Although Entrepreneurship Development through
small enterprises is basically owner-managed, a significant number of them do employ persons for
performing managerial functions. The SSI units on the growth path should encourage their key personnel
to think and work more as entrepreneurs than as mere employees.
(Para 12.5)
In view of the above, the Committee feels that there is need for ensuring harmonisation of tax structure by
providing the following: -
(a) Rationalisation of duty may be ensured on finished goods vis-a-vis their raw materials or intermediate
goods.          
(b)
   Capital Gains Exemption may be given to sick SSI units selling off their fixed assets to repay bank loans.
(c) The coverage of Excise Duty Exemption Scheme may be made available to all the items produced by the small-
scale units.
(d)  Under MRP based assessment an additional 10% rebate may be allowed to SSI units. Rationalisation of customs
duty on raw materials/intermediate goods and finished goods for Uninterrupted Power Supplies (UPS),
components/parts of domestic electrical appliances, components/parts of auto bulbs, umbrella components,
plastic raw materials, lead ingots, electric copper wires, parts and components of RF and IF coils and reduction

file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/75threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:40]
of custom duty on low carbon Ferro chrome and linear alkyl benzene (LAB) may also be done.   
 (Para 13.3)
The Committee recommends that banks and other financial institutions provide marketing oriented financial
assistance to small scale sector, particularly for advertising, product promotion and setting up of regional marketing
offices. Factoring services by the banks may also be given greater priority.
(Para 14.3)
           The Committee further recommends that: -
(a)    Establishment of a Marketing Development Fund with a minimum corpus of Rs 500 crore should be made.
(b)   Engagement of marketing experts by State Financial Corporations and banks for appraisal of projects may be
done.
(c)    Consultancy by banks to small scale units regarding formulation of their marketing plans may be taken up.
(d)   Organisation of exhibition events for SSI products in major cities of the country and abroad may be done.
(e)    Appointment of a central level educational institution for designing of short-term courses on specific aspects of
marketing and other management aspects may be made.
(f)     A well planned strategy at the national level for developing exports from small scale industries sector, including
identification of sub-sectors with high export potential may be carried out.
(g)    Recognition of marketing companies as small scale enterprises and provision of institutional credit facilities to
them for the necessary infrastructure and purchase of goods may be done.
(Para 14.4)
(a)        For effective technological upgradation in Indian SSI units, the Committee recommends that the partnership
approach to develop linkages between large and small enterprises be strengthened.
(b) Technology Bureau for International Industrial Partnerships and Technology Bureau for Small Enterprises, Delhi
have been providing useful services for technology upgradation in the small scale units. These organisations need to be
strengthened further and their activities need to be marketed / advertised in an effective manner. The small scale
industries in India have added strength to the industrial infrastructure and have been the engine of growth for
industrialisation. However, they are known for producing poor quality products. This makes the Indian goods less
competitive in the international markets.
(c)        The Committee observes that Government has set up a number of organizations for the purpose of technological
upgradation and quality improvement in the SS1 units. However, most of these facilities are either non-functional or
grossly under-utilised. There is an urgent need to revamp the whole system and make it effective and beneficial to the
small industries.
(d)        The Committee further recommends that quality training to significantly improve quality by creating awareness
among personnel about meeting customer requirements, standardizing processes, training operatives and enforcing
technical discipline should be institutionalized. There is a need to conduct a comprehensive research study in a sample
of SSI units to determine areas of waste and non-value adding activities and develop methodology for quality
improvement and cost reduction programmes. Further 1SO 9000 certification. may be made more attractive to introduce
quality-consciousness among small entrepreneurs. BIS standards may also be upgraded from time to time in tune with
the developments in quality worldwide.
(Para 15.1)
 
            The Committee observes that the present structure of labour laws does not encourage efficient performance by
the SSls. Managements find it difficult to manage their human resources optimally because of the constrained labour
laws. As of now, the same set of labour laws is applicable to all industrial undertakings, irrespective of their size.
(Para 16.1)
 

75th Report of Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/75threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:40]
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of a plethora of labour laws, a single unified Act with
simple provisions understandable by the entrepreneurs of SSI units be legislated. SSI units employing upto 50 persons
should be kept outside the purview of the labour law. Instead of the complex Industrial Disputes Act, a simpler law to
govern the relationship between the Employer and the Employee be made applicable. The Shops and Establishments
may also be suitably modified.
(Para 16.2)
            The Committee further observes that the existing social security legislations such as Employees' Provident Fund
& Miscellaneous Provisions Act, Employees State Insurance act, Maternity Benefits Act, Workmen's Compensation
Act, and the Payment of Gratuity Act are very cumbersome for entrepreneurs of small scale units to understand and
comply with. The Committee therefore recommends that instead of so many social security legislations, a
comprehensive Social Security Scheme be formulated for providing for one insurance cover to each workman. The
small scale units should be able to devote more time to quality management rather than inspector management.
(Para 16.3)
 
            The Committee observes that at present, there are several Government agencies to deal with small scale
industries in India. These include Ministry of SSI & ARI, Office of Development Commissioner (SSI), Small Industries
Development Organisation, Small Industries Service Institutes, National Small Industries Corporation, Small Industries
development Bank of India, Product-cum-process Development Centres, Regional Testing Centres, District Industries
Centres, State Financial Corporations, State Industrial Development Corporations, State Small Industries Development
Corporations, etc.
(Para 17.1)
 
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that roles of all these organisations be re-evaluated and clearly defined.
It needs to be ensured that their activities do not overlap each other. There should also be co-ordination in the activities
of these agencies. Most importantly, all of these should be able to provide effective service to the small scale sector.
 (Para 17.2)
 
            The Committee feels that the Government should have given such a package to the affected units. This may
include timely and low cost credit, export assistance and proper infrastructure facilities. After giving the package, a time
frame may be simultaneously given to such affected units to enable them to fight for survival.  In the absence of such
package, the Committee feels the units might be hard-pressed to survive.  Moreover, effecting dereservation without any
package will bring deleterious socio economic changes as reservation directly affects employment and economic
growth.
(Para 18.4)
 
            The Committee recommends that unless state governments play a proactive role in creating infrastructure for
industries, integration and harmonization of villages with industrial development can not be achieved. Active
participation of state governments, NGOs and SSI Associations should be ensured by providing appropriate
encouragement to them. This is in keeping with the Industrial policy announced in 1991to give special thrust to the
promotion and strengthening of small tiny and village industries.
(Para 19.3)
           The Committee, therefore, recommends that stringent action should be taken against the erring large companies
which have failed to make payment to SSIs in due time.   Necessary amendment for taking punitive   action may also
be   contemplated in the Delayed Payment Act.
(Para 20.3)

75th Report of Industry

            The Committee therefore, recommends that RBI should review the guidelines issued in respect of NPA to
banks   and should prescribe that no loan asset would become NPA even if the loan installments or interest remains
overdue   for a period of one year
(Para 21.2)
            The Committee therefore, recommends that in order to protect small scale sector from multinational companies
and others, a certain % of items, say 33% should be purchased by Central and State Government Departments/agencies
specially when the items reserved for SSI sector have been withdrawn and majority of the items have been put on OGL
list.  The policy of purchase preference system as followed by USA Government for protection of indigenous industries
may be emulated.  Necessary action in this regard should be initiated by the Ministry of SSI immediately.
(Para 22.2)
            The Committee observes that proposal of Limited Partnership mooted by    the SSI Association has been a long
pending demand.  This should be looked into by the Ministry of Finance.  The Ministry of SSI should take appropriate
action in the matter.
(Para 23.2)

Shunting of Pots in Smeiter Plant:

The Committee recommends that adequate safeguards be bililt within to avoid such recurrence in
future,

Action Taken :

In the aftermath of Smelter debacle, several committees including one external finding
Committee were constituted. The Committee has broadly come to the conclusion that gradual
deterioration in the performance of pots over the years was mainly due to non-adherence to
standard operating practices, improper maintenance, poor werk culture, improper planning and
lack of team work. Based on the recommendations of the Committee. the following safeguards
were built within the system to avoid such failure in the future.

With a view to have effective utilization of manpower for a full eight hours, the gate
control system was reinforced with effect from 13.05.98 and workers in shifts are being retained
for the full eight hours, Workers are now being allotted sufficient work and more flexibility in
utilization of manpower has been enforced so that they are engaged in full shifts.

Commencing from Ist July, 1998, a system has been introduced to carry Out
inspection/surprise checking to check the attendance and physical presence of the employees
deployed in the respective shifts and mark absent those not found present in the place of work,

Instructions have been issued to implement the standard operating procedures,

The undeserved overtime has been completely stopped since 1st of July, 1998. A number
of committees headed by Dy, General Managers are inspecting different work areas to ascertain
the number of employees engaged on overtime, the reasons for such overtime, and the attendance
of the workmen during overtime hours, and, in case any of them is not found at work, spot they
are marked absent.

The incentive scheme has been revised. In the revised incentive scheme maximum
importance has been given to production and a cut off level of production has been provided
below which no incentive becomes payable to employees,

An effective strategy has been chalked out to enforce discipline, Any act of indiscipline is
being viewed seriously and action is being taken against the erring employees. Already three
workers of Smelter Plant have been shifted from Angul Sector to other Units, Employees
unauthorisedly occupying Company's accommodation at township were evacuated with the help
of the local police,

Recommendations/Observation of the committee (Para 19,1)
Import Duty

The Committee recommends that the Government may consider enhancing the import
duty on such scraps to the same level as that of primary aluminium metal,

Action Taken Report

Enhancing the import duty on aluminium scrap would lessen its utilization, specially
when use of scrap is cost effective and energy efficient. Conversion of scrap into metal uses only
about 5% of the energy required to reduce alumina into metal, Moreover, recycling is
environmentally friendly as it does not release green house gases like CO2. Aluminium is also
fully recyclable, a process which can conserve a precious non-renewable resource like Bauxite.
For these reasons, about 30% of the global aluminium metal Production is scrap based, and the
duty on scrap is generally lower than that on primary metal. Since the use of scra,) is not
widespread in India, the Report of the Working Group on Non-ferrous Metals (Ninth Plan 1997-
2002), had specifically recommended that recycling of scrap requires less energy and is also
able to meet the gap between the domestic demand and supply. This can be achieved with import
of scrap. Thus, import needs to be promoted with low duty structure to make metal production
competitive. The global data on comparative customs duties does indicate that the duty on scrap
is generally lower, although there is not much difference in the tariffs on metal and scrap, the
tariffs on both being very low, both in deyeloped countries as well as in developing countries.
Keeping in view the above reasons, the Department of Mines had recommended to the Ministry
of Finance for low duty structure on import of aluminium scrap to make metal production
competitive (Union Budget 2002-2003). However, the basic import duty on aluminium serap has
been kept by Ministry of Finance at 15%.

The Committee recommends that NALCO should explore possibilities of commercial
sale of surplus power at competitive prices. Efforts may be made to complete the project in time
as per schedule.

NALCO had taken recourse to sell surplus power to third parties, In this connection, the
company issued an advertisement in May 1999 but this was contested by Grid Corporation of

Commission (OERC) for allowing sale of power to ferro alloy industries in the state, but OERC
also rejected NALCO's petition. NALCO has now gone in appeal to the Orissa High Court,

The appeal is still pending adjudication. The Department of Mines has also taken up the
issue with the Government of Orissa.

The installation of seventh unit of Captive Power Plant of NALCO is expected to be
completed by September, 2002. The project for installation of eighth unit of CPP is in progress.

While the NALCO management should keep on apprising the Committee about

the matter with the Government of Orissa regarding commercial sale of surplus power at a

Recommendations of the Committee
 
Performance of  mineral maps
 
(Para 4.6) : The Committee is happy to note that IBM has taken up the task of  providing  the specialized and
Customized data, preparation of mineral maps and forest overlays. The Committee hopes that the IBM in tandem with
the Forest Survey of India and Ministry of Environment and Forest would continue to take up latest forest overlays
maps. Forest overlays maps used by State Government and Central Forest Department would help to cut-down delays in
obtaining forest clearance for Mining Lease ( ML ) and   prospective licence  (PL).
 
Action Taken 
: As per the decision taken by the National Advisory Committee on Environment aspects in Mining Areas
under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Mines) and Secretary (MOEF), 50 multi- mineral maps were completed by IBM
as per target of 2001-02 and sent to FSI for the forest overlays. The annual target for such maps for subsequent years has
been fixed  at 100 index maps on a scale1:50000. This activity is envisaged to cover entire mining area in the country
with the priority assigned to ecologically fragile area in the State of. Chattisgarh, Jharkhand, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh,
Karnataka  and   Rajasthan~ in line with the decision of MOEF.
 
Recommendations of the Committee
 
Division wise functions of IBM
 
Mines Control and conservation of Minerals Division (MCCM Division)
 
(Para 5.1.2): The Committee feels that MCCM division of IBM would be able to function effectively once IBM is made
a regulatory body because MCCM is entrusted with enforcement of systematic development of mineral deposits and
conservation studies.
 
Action Taken: There is a need for strict enforcement of MCDR, 1988 particularly in respect of small (B) category of
mines Special integrated studies covering 30-40 groups of mines in each region have been programmed to highlight the
issues involved in scientific mines on regional basis including  that of environmental aspects.
 
Recommendations of the Committee
 
(Para 5.1.3) :  The Committee  further recommends  that MCCM should keep on up-dating mineral maps and cover all
minerals throughout  the country .
 
Action Taken :  All efforts. will be  made to update the mineral maps; excluding  that of coal and minor minerals  all
over  the country as per the targets.

Ore Dressing Division (OD Division)
 
(Para 5.2.4) : The Committee recommends that IBM management and the Department of Mines should ensure that R&D
wings of IBM may be well equipped for mineral beneficiation. The Sub-Committee further recommends that Ore
Dressing division of IBM should undertake such research work pertaining to beneficiation of low-Ore content mineral
in cost effective manner for viable and commercial production of metals.

imparted to any  interested party engaged in mining operations and thus IBM would be able to generate more revenue to

recommends that  adequate  structural mechanism should be evolved  within the  overall structure of  IBM  for the
discharge of role  and responsibilities of a Central Regulatory Authority.  So far as recommendations of expenditure
Reforms Commission  regarding down sizing of  IBM  is concerned, the Committee  holds  the view that  downsizing of
government  Department  has also become a national policy  with the purpose of cutting  down  non-plan expenditure. 
So, the  committee doesn't     differ from the  recommendations made by the ERC.  However, the Committee hopes that
IBM management  would  take    due care while downsizing  IBM so that it IBM  should not become a stumbling  bloc
in the way of IBM  discharging  its  responsibility  as a Central Regulatory Authority.

assessing  the   actual financial requirement of IBM  and the  same alongwith  detailed  appropriation   should have

            It would have  been another  thing that the IBM  could be  granted  enhanced  budgetary  support at  RE stage of

(Para 4.3 )

Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry of Mines :
 
Recommendations     (Para 3.2 )
 
Activities of  MECL
 
The Committee understands the vital  role of MECL in carrying out  detailed systematic mineral  exploration and hopes 
that  MECL  management  would be guided  by the management by objectives (MBO) and make its  earnest efforts for
achieving the cherished goals.
 
Action Taken
 
            The  observation of the  Committee has been noted.   MECL's  management is committed to  an overall
improvement of physico financial  performance of the company, to achieve the  goals set.
 
Recommendations        (Para 5.4)
 
Co-ordination and co-operation between MECL and GSI/Merger of MECL with GSI
 
The Committee is of the view that GSI should   undertake  honest effort for  searching and identifying   new prospects
for MECL for detailed exploration. 
 
Action Taken
 
MECL is in  constant touch with  GSI for identifying new prospects for obtaining detailed exploration work for the
company.
 
Recommendations     (Para 6.5)
 
Budgetary support
 
MNCs and private parties are doing exploration only for four  to  five precious and base etals and many other minerals
of national importance are still required to be  explored, which form a part of 64 minerals as mentioned in National
Mineral  inventory  of IBM, for which MECL  is the right choice.  Government should,  therefore,  continue budget
support to MECL.
 
Action Taken
 
            For  the year 2002-03 (BE),  Rs.8.00  crores has been provided  to MECL for promotional  projects which  is to
be reimbursed against work to be executed by  MECL.  Additional  funds  requirements.  if, any could be met out of the
Mineral Exploration Fund (MEF)  under which Rs.12.00  crores is also available
 
Recommendations     (7.3)
 
Performance of  MECL
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by MECL and hopes that it  would continue to strive its best in
implementing its programme of minerals exploration and mine development.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
MECL  ensures to strive its best in implementing its programme of mineral exploration and mine development in  the 
country.  Customers satisfaction is  one of the key areas where the company needs to improve.  Under the ongoing

liberalization process, it  is the endeavour of the company to obtain more contractual work from multi-national

competitive.

Physico-financial performance of MECL
 
The Committee is constrained to note that public sector support to MECL through promotion of  projects and
contractual work has considerably eroded.  The Committee feels that, if our PSUs are to remain, inter PSU cooperation
and synergy  is  required.

            To improve the physical performance of the company efforts are being made to get more jobs from PSUs and

field.

            For the year 2002-03 work order  for Rs. 250 lakhs  for coal sampling and analysis are available.  Though  in this

Organisational Structure
 
            The Committee is of the view  that  zonal office should be made a profit making centre  and all projects assigned
to them should be in a such  a  way that each zonal office justifies is existence and each zonal office must   contribute in

Recommendation       (8.5)
 
Physical  and financial performance of MECL
 
            The Committee, while appreciating the physical performance of MECL, recommends that MECL management
should make efforts to  procure work orders from all concerned areas so that physical  performance of the  company
should have direct  positive impact on the financial performance of MECL.  The Committee hopes that once the
diversification programmes are implemented and financial restructuring proposals,  which is under the consideration of
Ministry of Finance, is approved and comes into effect, MECL would start making net profit.

MECL has been making  losses.  The gross sales  of the company has been mainly  on account of the work done for the
Government sector.  The company is dependent on equity,  loan and promotional grants.  Financial restructuring of the
company has been under the consideration of the  Government.   However, such an  exercise could be done only if the
company is able to remain viable on  a sustainable basis after such a process.  However, from the data presently
available it does not appear that financial restructuring would be viable.

SWOT analysis of MECL
 
The Committee understands that the strength of MECL is enough to be competitive in its activities and, therefore,   
recommends  that MECL  management  should take every  possible step to take advantage  of its strength and avail
opportunities to improve the financial and physical performance.  The Committee  further  recommends that MECL
management should make efforts for overcoming its weaknesses and imbibe sufficient and sustainable  resilience to
combat  threat to its existence.  MECL should also try  to  shed surplus work force under VRS.

MECL is committed to avail all opportunities in the field of Mineral Exploration and related activities with  its

Recommendation       (5.5)
 
Co-ordination and co-operation between MECL and GSI/Merger of MECL with GSI
 
            The Ministry of Mines may explore the possibility of merger of MECL with  Geological Survey of India (GSI) 
for better co-ordination and continued prospect for MECL for detailed exploration.  MECL could work as a separate
division in GSI structure.
 
Action Taken
 
            MECL had earlier   been a part of  GSI  and had been carved  out  of the  latter  in  1972 to undertake  detailed
exploration work.  Moreover, GSI as an organization, is itself in the process of revamping.
 
Further recommendation       (5.5)
 
Budgetary support
 
            The Committee is of the view that the Department of  Mines  should have furnished the details  of   GSI's
revamping  process and the extent  and  scope for co-operation and collaboration between GSI and MECL.  It is
because  of the fact that  MECL has been  covered out of GSI and  keeping in view the need to rationalise non-plan
expenditure through rightsizing manpower  and avoiding double set up  of administration, the  Committee recommended
merger of MECL with GSI.  At least MECL could be made a division of GSI while  discharging its present functions
and responsibility.   Such measures would not only lead to rationalisation of non-plan expenditure and avoidable
administrative expenditure, but would also strengthen both GSI and MECL.
 
Recommendation       (10.3)
           
Revival plan of MECL
 
Financial Restructuring
 
The Committee is of the view that implementation of the recommendations of the Revival Committee would have a
positive impact on the physical and financial performance of MECL.  The revival  committee had  recommended the 
writing off  of accumulated losses and waiver of interest on Government  loan to clean the balance sheet of  MECL.   
The Committee recommends that the request of MECL for  waiving  of the interest on loan and transfer of balance loan
amount to  equity should be considered by the Government so that MECL could make a turnaround .  The Department 
of Mines may seriously pursue the matter with the Ministry of Finance.
Action Taken
 
 
            MECL has been making  in losses.   The gross sales of the company has been mainly on account of the work 
done for the Government  sector.  The company is  dependent on equity, loan and promotional grants.  Financial
restructuring of  the  company has been under  the consideration of the Government.  However, such an exercise  could
be done only if the company is able to remain viable on a sustainable basis after such a process.  However, from the data
presently available it does not appear that financial restructuring would be viable.  The matter is presently under the
consideration of the Department of Mines.
 
Further recommendation       (10.3)

The Committee is constrained  to express  its concern over the reluctant approach of Department of Mines in regard to
future  prospects of MECL.  On the one hand   Department of Mines is indifferent  to the view of  merger  of MECL
with its parent body i.e.  GSI for injecting  a new  lease of life.  On the other hand,  the Department of Mines in not
convinced of MECL's capacity/resilience  to become viable even after implementation of financial  restructuring.  The
MECL's  proposal of financial restructuring   is gathering  dust in the Department of Mines.  This is a paradoxical state
of  affairs and speaks of inaction of the Department of Mines.  It seems that the Department  of Mines is banking on the
idea  that the things  would improve automatically  without  any efforts/measures  while  the fact of the situation is that
MECL's proposal of financial restructuring needs immediate aid from the Government to make the company sustainable
on a regular basis. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Department of Mines must come out of its slumber
and act promptly in pushing ahead the financial restructuring proposals of MECL.
 
Recommendation       (11.6)
 
Grant of PL and ML
 
            The Committee is happy to note that MECL is making efforts towards obtaining prospecting licence and mining

units should conform to  the overall cost  benefit analysis.   Government  may review the  VRS  requirement and  fulfill

separated by VRS. VRS requirement has been further reviewed and it is planned to separate 3000 employees on VRS
for which the Government proposes to make the funds available as  a grant and a restructuring proposal to that effect has

The production of metal in concentrate in MCP during 2001-02 was 24,085 tonnes. Hence, the target was achieved.

Production Cost
The  Committee notes that the progressive increase in the  production cost of   metal in concentrate  is mainly due to
increase in interest burden and administrative expenditure  on Head Quarter.  The  Committee  strongly recommends
that HCL should   take   steps in right earnest for rationalisation /reduction in administrative expenditure so that  MCP 
would be able to run without  much losses.

The company has taken various steps to reduce its interest burden and administrative expenditure on Head Quarter.
High cost term loan of Rs.150 crore taken from IDBI, bearing interest rate of 16% ,has been with issue of bonds with
interest 10.65% per annum. This has resulted in savings of Rs. 8 crores per annum.

its condition considerably.

The Committee is constrained  to express  its concern over the adverse business prospects of Hindustan copper Ltd due
to weak financial base of the company which   continued to work long   on  unviable mines .  The Company is  in deep   
troubles  and is  heading towards a  point of no return.  Its  operation might come to a standstill if  concrete steps  are not

79th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/79threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:42]
taken in right direction.    The Committee hears the  rings of  the alarming bell .  Its really a time to  work  now or never
.
Action Taken
 
The objectives of the first Capital Restructuring sanctioned in 1999 were to save the company from being referred to
Board for Industrial and Financial Restructuring (BIFR) and improvement in its overall operational performance. The
first objective of saving the company from BIFR was achieved while the other objective of improvement in financial
performance could not be achieved.
 
2.         Efforts to reduce cost of production and expenses have been narrated in the report. However, more steps have
been taken which are given below:-
Production of Metal in Concentrate from most economic mine i.e. Malanjkhand Copper Project(MCP) and loss of
production due to closure of uneconomic mines had been partly offset by increase in production from Malanjkhand
Copper Project.
Improvement in productivity i.e. Refined Copper production per man.
Despite steep increase in price of petroleum products, power tariff and substantial reduction in customs duty on the
finished copper products, the average cash loss has been continued.
Further Recommendation 
 
The Committee is constrained to express its concerns over the fact  that HCL management  could not inject a new  lease 
of life by  implementing  successfully the  First capital restructurings  sanctioned  in 1999. The cherished objective of
the first restructuring programme was to improve the company's overall operational performance.  However, the
management just managed the company form falling in the net of Board for Industrial and Financial Restructuring
(BIFR).  Efforts to reduce the cost of production    was not fruitful   due to steep increase in price of petroleum product,
power tariff  and  substantial  reduction in custom duty on the finished copper products, as a result of which, the
company continues to run in loss.
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that HCL requires a total  overhauling, which  is possible only when
management with a new  vision and structuring strategy is put in place.
 
Recommendation  (Para 3.8)
CAPITAL RESTRUCTURING
The Committee is  constrained  to note  that  efforts made for capital  restructuring could not   prove beneficial  to the
company.  Net worth of the company is dwindling and the company is almost knocking the door of BIFR.  The
Committee feels that concrete steps  towards capital restructuring must be taken for  ameliorating  the company at the
earliest not with standing the process of disinvestment. 
Action Taken :
 
In order to keep the net worth of the company positive, another restructuring proposal is under active consideration of
the Government.
Further Recommendation
 
 The Committee observes that it is due to failure in achieving  the objectives of first capital restructuring  programme 
that HCL's net worth started  to dwindle  and the financial  base of the company  continued to suffer further.  However,
the Government has  given  due hearing to the warning bell sounded by the Committee and sanctioned intermediate 
package in order to keep company operational.
            The Committee desires that the Department of Mines would furnish the details of financial assistance as
extended by the Government  along with the outcome of the package on the financial  performance of the company.
Recommendation  (Para 3.9)
CAPITAL RESTRUCTURING
The Committee feels that    factor like fluctuating  LME price    is perhaps beyond  reach  and controlling limit of HCL
management and the Department of Mines.  However, the Department of Mines  in general and HCL management   in
particular  should take steps for  harnessing  the further business prospects of HCL by working on  those  factors  viz 
identification  of viable mines/deposits , reduction in  cost  of production  , interacting  with State Governments for

providing power to the units of HCL at the viable rate, approaching Ministry of Finance  for rationalisation of  tax
structure. 
Action Taken
 
Process to close further two uneconomic mines namely Surda and Khetri has been initiated.
Increase in the recovery rate of power being supplied to the employees in residential colony of the different projects has
been implemented.
The State Governments of Jharkhand and Rajasthan have been requested to take over part of the residential colonies at
Indian Copper Complex(ICC) and Khetri Copper Complex (KCC) to reduce substantial expense being incurred by the
company on maintaining water and power supply etc. The matter is being followed  up regularly.
Higher targets for improvement in recovery and reduction in power and fuel cost have been set.
Geological Survey of India(GSI) is doing exploration work near Malanjkhand Copper Project to locate better reserves
which can be exploited more economically. However, in view of proposed disinvestment further expansion would be
unjustified.
In line with the suggestions made, Department of Mines has already taken up the matter of rationalisation of tax
structure with the Ministry of Finance on the basis of the recommendations made by a Multy- Disciplinary Committee
on Taxation Regime for the Mineral Sector in the country .
 Further Recommendation
 
While the Committee  welcomes the closure of two  uneconomic mines namely  Suda and Khetri, the
Committee,however, desires that the interest  of workers should be kept in  mind   while giving VRS to workers
working  in these two mines.
 
            The Committee desires that the Department of Mines would furnish  the details of  Jharkhand  and Rajasthan
Government’s response to the  request of Department of Mines for taking over  part of the  residential  colonies at
Indian Copper Complex (ICC) and Khetri   copper Mines (KCC) for maintaining waste and power supply etc in order to
reduce expenditure presently incurred by the company.
 
            As regards the issues of identification of viable mines /deposits the committee is of the considered opinion that 
Geological   survey of India (GSI)  should continue with its exploration work in Malanjkhand  and other areas of the 
country to locate better reserves  for their commercial   exploitation irrespective  of the proposed disinvestment of the
company.
 
            The Committee is pleased to note that the Department  of Mines  has taken up the matter of rationalisation of tax
structure with the Ministry of Finance.  The Committee desires that the Department of Mines should   apprise the
Committee of the outcome of efforts made by   it.  The Department of Mines may  also furnish  the details of the
recommendation made by a Multi-Disciplinary  Committee  for the mineral sector in the country in regard to
rationalisation of  tax structure.
 
Recommendations          (Para 4.2)
PRODUCTION CAPACITY OF  HCL MINES
The Committee,  while taking note of the Ore capacity  of  KCC, ICC and MCP  mines  of HCL,  hopes that all the units
would make full capacity utilisation  in a cost effective manner.   The Committee also recommends that  all units of 
HCL  smelter plant  would make optimum capacity  utilisation for the production of  metal.  The Sub-Committee also
hopes that Tajola copper plant would also produce   CC  Rod to the maximum capacity .
Action Taken :
 
Four underground unviable mines have been closed and it is proposed to close two more mines while augmenting the
production from open cast mine at Malanjkhand.
 
The optimum capacity utilisation for Smelter Plants located at KCC and ICC is difficult in view of the lower availability
of MIC from economic captive mines. The benefit from processing of imported concentrate has dwindled substantially
because of steep reduction in customs duty from 35% to 25% in the year 2002-03.
 Further Recommendations

            While the committee welcomes the closure of  unviable  mines and continuation of  operation at the

Recommendations  (Para 8.5)
STATUS OF   AMR SCHEMES IN HCL
The Committee recommends that workers interest should  be protected  when the company  is disinvested.  In case the
disinvestment does not take  place  within six months the Government should  come forward to  implement its 
revival/expansion plans.
Action Taken
 
The Government would try to include suitable clauses in the share Purchase Agreement to be signed with the
prospective buyer(s) of HCL to protect the interest of the workers to the best possible extent i.e. no retrenchment would
be made in the first year after taking over the charge of HCL by the buyer; and in case someone is given VRS, it should
not be less than what the Government is already giving.
 
The exercise for disinvestment, which is on, would take about three to four months for completion. In case no suitable
buyer is found, then the company would be closed, as has also been observed by the Ministry of Finance in their
comments to draft CCEA note for restructuring of HCL.
Further Recommendations
 
The Committee is pleased to note the government assurance  for incorporation of suitable clause to protect the interest
of  workers  in the share purchase agreement of be signed with the prospective buyer(s)  of HCL in the case of
protection of  disinvestment of the company.  The committee is of the considered opinion that revival/expansion
programmes of HCL   shouldn't be delayed beyond a fixed time in view of   proposed disinvestment.  As far as the
observation of the Ministry of Finance made in the  draft CCEA note far restructuring of HCL regarding the closure of
company, in case no suitable buyer is found, is  concerned, the committee  opines that government  should  reconsider
its decision.  That is so because closure of company would make even the Malanjkhand copper project defunct.  In any
case profit making operational plant should not be affected with the closure of the company, the  Committee   maintains.
PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY KHETRI UNIT OF HCL   (Para : 12.6)
The Committee is of the opinion that the problems of KCC are deep-rooted   therefore, immediate panacea   might not
be  possible.   Since  total  turn around  of  KCC involves huge investment  it may not be  possible before the
restructuring takes place.  However, the Committee is of the view that  the process of restructuring   should not be
procrastinated.  In case it is going to be  delayed for more than six months Government should come to the rescue  of  
KCC with necessary fund   for an early  solution to  its problems.
 
Action Taken
As stated earlier, a restructuring proposal for HCL which includes KCC has been submitted to CCEA to improve
chances of disinvestment.
Further Recommendations :
 
The Committee hopes that any decision in this regard  to Khetri unit of HCL should not  be delay beyond a period of
time as the same would  erode the financial base of the company further.

 The Committee is of the opinion     that HCL management should  take up  the case of  Banwas Deposits of KCC  on

SWOT ANALYSIS OF  MCP
The Committee understands that  MCP due to its  open pit mines and experience manpower, has a trend of increasing

the  operational efficiency.    The Committee  recommends that   the Department of Mines would give due consideration
to the strategic expansion and modernisation programmes of MCP at the time of capital restructuring of HCL  as a
whole.  In sufficient infrastructure  are the basic weaknesses   and need to be addressed.

EIGHTH REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman of ·the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this Eighth Report of the Committee on the Trade Marks Bill, 1993 with the Bill, 
as amended by the Committee, annexed thereto. 
2. The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 19th April, 1993. It was referred 
to the Committee for examination and report through separate paras published in Rajya 
Sabha/Lok Sabha Bulletins Part II dated the 6th August, 1993 and 13th August, 1993 
respectively. 
3. The Committee held six meetings. A verbatim record of these meetings was kept. 
4. At its first meeting the Committee decided to invite Memoranda/suggestions from 
different organisations/bodies dealing with trade marks and also issue a pres..<~ communique 
in this reeard. Accordingly a press communique inviting memoranda from various 
individual!./organisations interested in the subject matter of the bill was issued on the- 26th 
August,_ 1993 to be submitted latest by 15th September, 1993 (Appendix I). 
5. 11. Memoranda containing views, opinions comments and suggestions on ttte various 
provisions and aspects of the Bill were received by the Committee from individuals, 
organisations, Trade Marks Attorneys, Legal practitioners and organisations conne~ted with 
Tr~de Marks (list at Appendix II). 
6. The Committee decided that the Memoranda received by it be sent to the Ministries 
of Industry/Law, Justice and Company Affairs for their comments. The comments of the 
Ministry of Industry endorsed by the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs were 
received and considered by the Committee. 
7. The Committee heard the oral evidence tendered by 13 witnesses who represented 
various organisations and bodies in addition to the oral evidence of the representatives of 
the Ministries of Industry and Law, Justice and Company Affairs. (Appendix III). 
8. The Committee decided that the evidence recorded and memoranda received should 
not be laid on the Table of both the Houses and that only a set of memoranda received by 
it from organisations/bodies/individuals be placed in the Parliament Library after'" the report 
is pJesented to the Houses for reference purposes. 
9. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 
31 March, 1994. · 
10. Taking into account the documents, memoranda' and evidences in respect of the 
Trade Marks Bill, 1993 the Committee concludes as under:-
A trade marks is generally a visually perceptible sign used in relation to goods 
or services. The primary purpose of a trade mark is to identify the commercial or 
trade origins of the goods or services. As such a trade mark distinguishes a 
particular product from another product. It offers an assurance to the consumer that 
when he is buying a particular item with a trade mark he is purchasing the same 
item which he has been assured of its quality (9mposition etc. So a trade mark 
reflects the goodwill or reputation of a paJ1icular product. It is statutorily not 
compulsory for somebody to register a trade mark. If a Trade Mark is registered by 

some one in that case he has a built in right to the safety of that particular mark. To 
qualify for registration as a trade mark any mark must fulfil the criteria as undcr:-
(a) It should be distinctive. It should be something which can be separated from 
other marks .. 
(b) It must not cause any confusion or deception. 
(c) It should not contain scandalous or obscene matters. 
(d) It should not contain any matter which may hurt the religious susceptibilities of 
any class or section of the people. 
The registration of a trade mark does not confer any new right on the holder of the trade 
mark. It only ~upplements a right which is already existing. Therefore, a· trade mark is a 
cumulative and not alternative to the protection of the mark by the common law. 
As regards the replacement of the existing law on the subject namely the Trade and 
Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 by a New Bill which was under consideration of the Committee, 
the Government was of the opinion that the existing Act has served its purpose reasonably well. 
To bring a new Bill before the Parliament there were various other reasons also. One is that any 
Act relating to Trade Marks in the field of trade, "both national and inteJ:national evolves 
reflecting the changing realities of the market place. As such the existing Act having been there 
nearly for 30 and odd years started needing certain necessary amendments and changes. Similarly 
over a period of time the case law pertaining to trade marks got built up and there were a 
number of judicial pronouncements and\_gradually it was found that it would be desirable to 
incorpora~e these into the body of the Act. In some cases the increasing globalisation of trade 
also viewed some lacunae in the existing Act as.~ non tariff barrier. Accordingly the Government 
decided to bring the desired modifications in the Act as it felt that instead of bringing a number 
of modifications and amendments it would be more desirable to bring forward a new Bill. The 
present Bill according to the Government incorporates certain changes which were felt necessary 
thereby making if more comprehensive and more transparent. It provides for more specific and 
greater degree of protection against infringement and more punishment for the violators of the 
Act. 
11. The Government highlighted the following salient features of the Trade Marks Bill. 1993 
which were examined by the Committee:-
(a) Presently the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958" provides for registration 
of trade marks only of "goods". The one area which was not covered was 
"services". The present Bill seeks to cover seJYices in addition to goods under the 
trade marks protection. 
(b) The registration of trade marks which are imitations of well known trade marks is 
not to be permitted. EQlarging the grounds for refusal of registration and 
consequently provision of defensive registration of trade marks are proposed to 
be omitted from this Bill. 
(c) This Bill is taking away the system of maintaining registers of trade marks in part 
A and part B. At present part A trade Marks will inclUde those trade marks 
which are very clearly distinguishable and about which there would be no doubt 
whereas in part B trade marks the trade mark is not very distinguishable. This 
two tier system is proposed to be done away with in this Bill. 
(d) In view of doing away with Part A and Part B trade marks the Bill proposes that 
there will be oniy a single register and pot two ·registers. 
(e) The Bill proposes. to simplify the procedure of registration of registered users and 
enlarging the .scope of the use in ter;ms of a permitted use. 

(/) The Bill proposes to establish an Appellate Board for speedy disposal of appeals 
which presently go before the courts and due to pressure of work a speedy 
redressal is not forthcoming. 
(g) Tbe final authority relating to registration or certification of trade marks be 
vested in the Registrar instead of the Central Government. 
(h) The Bill proposes enhanced punishment for offences relating to tra de marks at 
par with the Copyright Act to prevent sale of spurious goods. In the Copyright 
Act offences are cognizable inviting a minimum punishment of 3 years whereas in 
the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act it is non-congnizable and punishment is 
for two year. So it is sought to be made cognizable and punishment to be 
enhanced to 3 years for infringement of trade marks. 
(i) The Bill proposes to prohibit use of someone else's trade mark like the name of a 
corporate company or a business concern. 
12. Some members of the Committee were of the opinion that the liberalisation of trade 
marks legislation may provide added advantage to the foreign multinational units. Instead, the 
policy should be to go .slow in according recognition to foreign trade marks with a view to 
encourage domestic initiatives in the same or similar lines of production. They emphasised the 
need to make efforts to encourage the use of indigenous trade marks. 
In the matter of inclusion of services in the jurisdiction of the Bill, they expressed the view 
that it should await the resolution of the current controversies that arose after the signing of 
GAIT treaty and the agreement by western countries to provide 5atisfactory trade concessions on 
a reciprocal basis. 
Also in view of the amendments required in the Indian Patents Act of 1970 consequent upon 
the GATT treaty they felt that the new legislation should await the changes in the Patents Law. 
Some members of the Committee specifically mentioned some modifications in various 
Oauses of the Bill under consideration Regarding Clause 2 of the Bill, some members were of 
the opinion that instead of "a device, shape of goods and packaging", there should be 
"description of device, shape of goods or packaging" because items having functional use should 
be dealt by Patents Law. 
Members were of the opinion that defensive registration may be c~ntinued as stipulated in 
the existing Act which is in force. Members while considering Clause 15 of the Bill pointed out 
that no mechanism for part cancellation of registration has been mentioned in the Bill. Members 
questioned the fate of the registration made in series if some of the marks in that series is 
subjected to non use Members of the Committee put forth a suggestion that Associated trade 
marks may be named as other individual trade mark. Commenting on Clause 18 of the Bill some 
Members expressed apprehension that provision of single application for multiple class could lead 
to blockage of trade mark for others. With regard to Clauses 37, 39 and 43 of the Bill, some 
Members of the Committee wanted that a limit should be imposed on consideration against 
assignment. Members were also of the opinion that instead of consent of the Registrar, 
assignment certificate should be provided for the validity of assignment. 
13. 'The changes suggested by the Committee in the Bill and the reasons therefc;»re are set out 
in the succeeding paras of this report:-
13.1 CLAUSE 2. - (i) The Committee observes that almost all the organisationslbodies/ 
individuals have desire<\ to retain the defjnition of "goods" jn the present Bill also because it is 
there in the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 and there are no obvious reasons for 
omission of this definition. The clause. has been amended accordingly. (ii) Cause 2(l)(g) of the 

Bill has been amended to excluse members of partnership from the scope of Association of 
persons. This will certainly help in removing any ambiguity since individual partners of a 
partnership will not be entitiled to use a registered trade mark separately and the mark can be 
used" only by the partnership. 1be amendment has been made in the clause. (iii) In Oause 2(/)(x) 
the words "construction and repair" "transport and storage" and "material treatment" at 
appropriate places have been incorporated in the Bill which will conform to the international 
classification of goods and services. 
13.2 CLAUSE 8. - In aause 8 of the Bill the word "shall" bas been substituted with the 
work word "may" which wiD give more flexibility to the law in its implementation. The language 
of rule 26(2) which was added to the rules framed under the existing Act bas been inserted as 
sulKlause (2) of clause 8. The Government has informed that this was added in 1992 to 
overcome the judgment of Madras High Court which held that the Registrar has no jurisdiction to 
register trade mark for goods which are not specifically enumerated in the classification of goods. 
This amendment will enable the Registrar to properly classify the goods as and when new kind of 
goods emerge into market. The amendment has been incorporated in the Bill. 
13.3 CLAUSE 9. - In sub-clause (1) of clause 9 the words "or is a wen known trade mark" 
have been added at the end of the proviso to extend registration to well known trade marks. The 
amendment has been incorporated in the Bill. 
(ii) The following Explimation has been adde.d to clause 9 of the Bill which reads as 
under:-
" Explanation: The nature of goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is used 
or proposed to be used shell not be a ground for refusal of registration". 
(iii) The Committee is of the opinion that any symbol relating to religion, gods, godesses, 
places of worship should not ordinarily be registered as a trade mark. However the Committee 
do not want to disturb the existing trade marks by prohibiting their registration as it will result in 
a chaos in the market. At the same time the Committee trusts that Oovernment will initiate 
appropriate action if someone complaints that a particular trade mark is hurting his religious 
susceptibilities. 
13.4 CLAUSE 11. - The words "has a reputation" have been substituted with the words 
"well-known" in clause 11 (2)(b) of the Bill. 
The Committee is of the opinion that the words "For the purposes of this Act" be added in 
the beginning in the Explanation II and accordingly the addition has been incorporated. 
13.5 CLAUSE 15. - In sulKlause (3) of clause 15 the words "same goods" the words 
"same or similar goods" have been substituted. The amendment has been incorporated. 
13.6 CLAUSE lS. -The following proviso has also been added after the Sub-clause (3) of 
clause to remove the present lacunae:-
"Provided that the Registrar shall not remove the mark from the register if an application 
i$ made in the prescribed form and prescribed fee and surcharge is paid within six months 
from the expiration of the last registration of the trade mark and shall renew the 
registration of the trade mark for a period of ten years under sub-section (2)." 
13.7 CLAUSE 29. --. In sub clause (5) of aause 29 the words "dealing in goods cr; services 
in respect of which the trade mark is registered" have been incorporated in the Bill. 
13.8 CLAUSE 12. - The Committee propose to omit the words "the English or" in para 
(a) of sulKlause (2) of 82 as aU over the world metric system is used and it would be illegal to 
use the word .. Enalith system" ~der the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986. The amendment 
bas been incorpcnted in the Bill. 

• 
13.9 CLAUSE 85. - This clause of the Bill deals with the composition of Appellate Board. 
The C.ommittee suggests that a Bench shall as far as may be of 2 members one of whom shall be 
judicial member ar.d other shall be a technical member having specialised knowledge and 
experience in the law of trade marks. The amendment has been incorporated in the Bill. 
13.10 CLAUSE 86. - This clause prescribes the qualifications for appointment as Chairman 
and Members of Appellate Board. The Committee considered certain clause related suggestions! 
amendments for incorporation in Clause 85. The Committee has not found such suggestions 
practicable and instead recommends deletion of para (b), (e) and (f) sub-clause (2) of Clause 86 
without making further changes in Clause 85 of the Bill. The deletion has been incorporated in 
the Bill. 
14. At this stage of deliberation, the Committee would like to have recommended some 
more amendments in the Bill on the basis of certain suggestions put forth before it but is not 
doing so because they can· be incorporated in the rules. The Committee, would, however, not 
miss to highlight its observations with regard to sub-clause (1) of Oause 92 which provides that 
any person aggrieved by an order or decision of the Registrar· under the Act, or the rules made 
thereunder, may, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date on 
which the order or decision sought to be appealed against is communicated to such person 
preferring the appeal. Thus an aggrieved person can file an appeal as of right. The appeal 
provisions to the appellate Board as to be provided a new. The Committee has been informed 
that Forty-Second Amendment to the Constitution in 1976 inserted a new Part XIV A of the 
Constitution with a view to establishment of tribunals for reducing litigation. Decisions of such 
tribunals can only be challenged under Article 136 of the Constitution before the Supreme Court. 
The Committee, therefore, without persisting for an urgent addition of a special clause 
recommends that Government should include provision for the establishment of an Appellate 
Board envisaged under Part XIV A of the Constitution for the said purpose. The Committee is of 
the opinion that if required, Government should bringforth an amendment to the relevant 
provisions of the constitution for implementing the recommendation of the Committee in letter 
and spirit. The Committee trusts that Government would take a positive action in this regard in 
due course. 
15. All other modifications not enumerated in the foregoing paragraphs ar~ either of 
consequential or of drafting nature. 
16. The Committee recommends that the Bill as amended, be passed.

PRESS COMMUNIQUE 
The Trade Marks Bill, 1993 which was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 19th April, 1993 
and published in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary Part II, Section 2, dated the 19th April , 
1993 has been referred to the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry for examination and report. The Committee consists of 42 Members of both the Houses 
of Parliament is headed by Shri Moturu Hanumantha Rao, M.P. 
l11e Bill inter-alia propose to amend an consolidate a law relating to Trade Marks to provide 
for registration and better protection of Trade Marks for goods and services and for the 
prevention of the use of fraudulent marks. 
The Committee has decided to invite suggestions/comments from concerned individuals , 
organisations and bodies on the various clauses of the Bill. Interested parties are, accordingly, 
requested through this Press Communique to send their views in the form of memorandum for 
the consideration of the Committee latest by 15th September, 1993. Copies of the memorandum 
may be sent to Shri Tapas Das Gupta, Under Secretary, Department Related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry , Rajya Sabha Secretariat, Parliament House, New Delhi 
(preferably with 75 copies both in English and Hindi of the Memorandum). 
Copies of the Bill for reference purposes are available in Parliament Library , New Delhi and 
Libraries of all the State Legislatures in different States. Copies may 3lso be obtained on specific 
request from Committee Officer, Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry , Rajya Sabha Secretariat, Room No. 123A, Third Floor, Parliament House , New Delhi .

REPORT
 
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Mines (Ministry of coal and Mines) on
the Recommendations contained in its 66
th   Report (of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry) on Performance Review of Jawaharlal Nehru  Aluminium Research Development and Design and Centre
(JNARDDC) which was presented /laid to  on the Table of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha on  8th March,  2002.
 
 Action Taken Notes have been received from the Department  of Mines in respect of the recommendations contained in
the Report.   These have been categorized as follows:

Recommendation       (Para    2.3)
 
Objectives of JNARDDC
 
The Committee while appreciating the objectives for setting up the Research Centre for Aluminium Industries has
noticed during its visit that the Centre is well equipped with modern analytical facilities and process development
monitoring and control facilities in order to carry out research work in the areas of bauxite, alumina and aluminium
smelting. The Committee recommends that the Centre should strive its best to achieve its cherished goal and make all
efforts towards removing the problems being faced by the Indian aluminium industry. 
 
Action Taken
 
JNARDDC has  assured that it will continue to strive its best to achieve its cherished goals. In consultation with the
Indian aluminium industry it will continue all efforts towards solving the problems being faced and referred to it by the
industry. 
 
Recommendation          (Para   4.2)
 
On-going projects of  JNARDDC
 
The Committee notes the projects undertaken by JNARDDC and hopes that the efforts made by the Centre would be
utilized as the store house of all aluminium related “experiments and observations” and the knowledge and experience
derived of the efforts would be helpful in removing the problems of aluminium industry. The Committee also hope that
each project under study by JNARDDC must involve the highest degree of intellectual honesty as far as the relevance
and the purpose of the projects are concerned.
 
Action Taken
 
JNARDDC has always stood by the need for showing exemplary intellectual honesty in choosing and executing projects
for the aluminium industry. The Centre will continue to act in the most responsible manner and enforce the highest
standards of discipline and honesty in its dealings with the Indian aluminium industry. Protecting intellectual property
rights as well as ensuring the highest level of confidentiality of the results of the work done for individual customers are
the very pillars of the Centre’s functioning. These will be maintained at all costs.
 
Recommendation          (Para   5.2)
 
Thrust areas for R&D
 
The Committee understands the significance of adopting the practice of process monitoring and modeling to carry out
the research work in a result -oriented manner. The Committee, while noting the steps taken by JNARDDC regarding
the process development and product development, recommends that JNARDDC should carry on such research work
which may help aluminium industry in developing new designs of products with the help of product mix. The research

80th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/80threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:43]
work should lead to the evolution of process development for cost reduction. JNARDDC should make a survey of the
market demand and engage itself in such research work which might lead to development of products in accordance
with market demands. The new initiatives being envisaged may be taken up at the earliest.
 
Action Taken
An entire new Division with the name “Process and Product Development” has been created for this purpose. The
Centre is well aware of its responsibility to come up with new processes and products for the benefit of the aluminium
industry and will continue to strive to achieve this goal to the best of its ability. Towards this end, the Centre will be
bringing out several technology capsules for transfer to the Aluminium industry both big and small.
 
Recommendation    (Para : 5.4)
           
The Committee desires that JNARDDC should involve itself in such research work which would provide better quality,
speed up design engineering and lead to cost  effective production for the ultimate survival and growth of indigenous
Aluminium industry in the changing scenario caused by globalisation and liberalization. The globally emerging trends
that need to be implemented in aluminium industry may be addressed on a emergency basis in collaboration with
aluminium industry.
 
Action Taken
 
The Centre is in continuous touch not only with the major aluminium producers but also a number of small industries
particularly in the Vidarbha region (through the Vidarbha Industries Association) to promote the use of aluminium in
the country in the form of new products and better quality of existing ones. The Centre is very conscious of the need to
bring to India globally emerging trends in the aluminium industry, particularly newer technologies such as inert anode
and wettable cathode.  Almost the entire R & D work taken up by the centre for the Aluminium Industry is concerned
with improving the efficiency and speed of processes, quality of the product,   material and energy conservation,
minimizing environmental hazards reduction in overall cost of production and related issues.  It  thus addresses all the
concerns  expressed by the Committee.

Recommendation   (Para  : 6.4   )
 
Diversification programmes of JNARDDC
 
The Committee feels that JNARDDC should chalk out its diversification programme in such a way as to benefit the
aluminium industry in the short as well as long term. Since technology for setting of such plants is not available in India,
JNARDDC can play a vital role in developing such technologies. The Committee recommends that research may be
undertaken to develop and adapt new technology which may help setting up of small and medium capacity alumina and
aluminium plants.
 
Action Taken
 
This is a major thrust area that the Centre is keen on developing. It has already initiated steps to find the factors

remove the bottlenecks that stand in the way of establishment of mini-aluminium plants in the country that would help
in improving the availability of aluminium in the country.
 
Further Recommendation
 
The Committee   is pleased to note that JNARDDC is keen on developing diversification programme in  such a way as
to benefit the aluminium industry in the   short as well as long  term.  JNARDDC has made its diversification

steps taken to remove the bottlenecks that stand   in the  way of establishment of mini-aluminium plants  in the country.
 
Recommendation          (Para: 7.3  )
 
Seminar/Conferences
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by JNARDDC in conducting seminars and conferences and recommends
that JNARDDC should conduct such conferences and seminars more frequently. The Committee also recommends that
JNARDDC should make some nominal entry fee from all the participants in order to raise funds to meet its financial
requirements.
 
Action Taken
 
The Centre has already initiated steps for increasing the number of seminars and conferences that it proposes to hold
during the year 2002. The calendar of events planned includes short course / workshops and international conferences
practically every month of the year starting from April 2002. Adequate participation of industry in such courses is being
ensured and the registration fee collected is added to the fund generated by the Centre. The Centre gives the widest
possible publicity to these programmes by way of mailing circulars to over 250 industrial establishments, academic and
R&D institutes as well as through personal contacts and electronic means such as e-mail.
 
Recommendation (Para: 8.2  )
 
Training programmes and workshops
 
Conducting of training programmes and workshops provides a platform to scientists for productive interaction and
encourage them to gather knowledge and share experience. JNARDDC should charge a  nominal fee from the
participants for the training programme to generate revenue to meet JNARDDC’s non-plan financial requirements. The
Committee also recommends that JNARDDC should give wide publicity to its training programmes.
 
Action Taken
 
The Action Taken Notes  in respect of  Para 7.3  at  Sl. No. 7 may  please be seen

the  year 2002-03 and the likely outcome of  these workshop and conferences .  The Committee would  like  also to
know the amount of   fee collected as  registration amount upto  the date of such workshop and conference held.

Recommendation  (Para : 13.4  )
 
Annual Budgetary requirement of JNARDDC
 
The Committee is constrained to express its concerns over the languishing and pathetic condition of Centre like
JNARDDC due to lack of sufficient fund flow from the Government where all research work pertaining to aluminium
industry might be carried on successfully. The situation emerging out of the development is really pathetic and requires
immediate attention. JNARDDC has an excellent layout with required equipment and technology for research work in
aluminium industry, therefore, the Sub-Committee is of the view that such an extra-ordinary Research Centre should not
languish because of financial crunch. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Mines should take stock of
actual financial requirement of JNARDDC to meet its plan and non-plan expenditure. The Committee further
recommends that since JNARDDC is a research centre and does not generate substantial revenue of its own except from
consultancy and services, JNARDDC should be allowed budgetary support to meet at least its non-plan expenditure so
that the scientist should  remain in peace while doing research work and have not to bother for their future survival. The
Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Mines should explore the possibility to generate/appropriate funds
out of Aluminium Development Fund and also from Indian Aluminium companies to meet the plan-expenditure of
JNARDDC. At the same time, JNARDDC management and the Ministry of Mines should propagate the utility of
JNARDDC for aluminium industries. The aluminium industries can refer to the Centre for all of their R&D problems as
their involvement would definitely help in the development of technology packages for future expansion programmes. If
the Central agency like Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research Development & Design Centre is involved in importing
technology for green field as well as brown field expansions there is a possibility of saving a lot of foreign exchange by
avoiding duplicate transfer of technology.
 
Action Taken
 
The Government has agreed to release 80% of the salary requirement of JNARDDC out of non-plan funds.  In addition,
the annual interest accrued on AMDF will also be passed on to the centre together with grants under S & T components
for projects.  However, JNARDDC has to establish its utility to the aluminium industry and generate resources for
continuing the R & D work.

                                                                                    REPORT
CEMENT INDUSTRY — AN INTRODUCTION
1.1       There was a wide gap between the demand and supply of cement during the Seventies. During that time the
major cement units were not motivated either to produce to their full capacity or to expand as cement production was
under both price and distribution control i.e., their entire production was under levy obligation on the rate fixed by the
government from time to time.
1.2       The then Central Government had been considering various measures for achieving rapid increase in the
production of cement by establishing a large number of mini cement units, as in the case of China, where it was found
that the working of mini cement units are highly successful.
1.3       In the existing situation, a perception grew that establishment of mini cement plants would usher in an era
resulting in exploitation of smaller limestone deposits, dispersal of cement production capacity all over the country,
reduction of burden on the railway, lower capital cost and quicker installation and higher employment especially in
rural, hilly and other inaccessible areas. The then Government accordingly constituted two working groups to make
suitable recommendations regarding the choice of technology, and provision for fiscal incentives to attract large number
of entrepreneurs to this field.
Criteria for Mini Cement Plants
2.1       The Government considered the reports of both the working groups and announced the following decisions in
their press release No. 9-98/78 Cem dated 4.1.1979 :-
                 1.  The capacity for the mini cement plant will be limited to 200 tonnes per day on 66000 tonnes per annum.
                 2.  The choice of technology to be utilised should be left to the entrepreneurs.
                 3.  In addition to the units which may be set up by the entrepreneurs in the private sector or by the State
Government in the joint sector, the Cement Corporation of India would also enter the field to set up mini
cement plants as a promotional effort.
                 4.  The ex-works price of cement produced by the mini cement plants would be the same as the price
admissible to new large sized plants, viz. Rs. 296 per tonne. This price was assured for a period of five
years from the date of going into commercial production.
                 5.  Mini cement plants will be allowed a rebate in the payment for a period of five years.
                 6.  While the mini cement plants will be subject to price control under the Cement Control Order, they will be
exempted from distribution control under the same order.
                 7.  Mini cement plants set up in hilly and remote areas will be eligible for additional excise duty relief and
cash subsidy on merit.
                 8.  Mini cement plants will also be eligible for all other existing incentives and facilities available under the
Income Tax Act or under other schemes offered by the State Government.
                 9.  Large houses and foreign majority companies will not be allowed to set up mini cement plants.

2.2       Taking a cue from the above Government notification and announcement made by the Central Government in
the 8th Five Year Plan about building of infrastructure in the country, 126 mini cement plants were set up in the State of
Uttar Pradesh to supply the much needed cement for the various projects. But due to variety of reasons, these units
became sick and unviable.
Study made by the Sub-Committee for the Ministry of Small Scale Industries
            The Sub-Committee for the Ministry of Small Scale Industries of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry decided to study the problem faced by the mini cement plants in UP. The Sub-Committee
consisted of the following Members :
                 1.  Dr. Bolla Bulli Ramaiah — Convenor
                      RAJYA SABHA
                 2.  Shri P.K. Maheshwari
                 3.  Shri Rama Muni Reddy Sirigireddy
                 4.  Shri S. Sivasubramanian
                 5.  Shrimati Saroj Dubey
                      LOK SABHA

                 8.  Shri Deepak Kumar
                 9.  Shri Thomas Hansda
