               12.  Shri Manjay Lal
               13.  Dr. K. Malaisamy
               14.  Shri A. Narendra
               15.  Shri Uttamrao Deorao Patil
Meeting with the Mini Cement Plants Association
            The sub-committee had a meeting with the U.P. Mini Cement Plants Association on 4th June 2002. The
morandum submitted by the Association is reproduced below: -
                 (i)  Almost all mini cement units in the State have been closed because the guarantee given to provide
government protection to these units has not been fulfilled either by the State government or by the so call
Industries friend "Udyog Bandhu". This fact is known to one and all that no such decision has been taken
by UP Finance Corporation, Industrial Directorate and the "Udyog Bandhu" during the last four years after
much deliberations which could help the said units to revive while on the other hand, Rajasthan Finance
Corporation by making into account the seriousness of the situation, had taken a quick decision not only to
waive the interest completely but waived 20 per cent principal amount also so that mini cement units
situated in Rajasthan may be revived.
                (ii)  The Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation which on the one hand had the survey conducted by the ICRA for
the small cement industries falling on the verge of closure and sought suggestions for the revival thereof,
turned down the proposals made by the ICRA completely to be implemented. The letter of the MD,
Finance Corporation, in this regard is enclosed (Annexure–I).
               (iii)  Whereas the said issue was approved to be decided by the High Power Committee headed by the Chief
Minister (Annexure II) on the one hand, the Udyog Bandhu did not feel it pertinent to include the same in
the meeting of the High Power Committee, on the other hand. The letter forwarded by the Association in

this regard is enclosed (Annexure–III).
               (iv)  On the one hand, Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation has accepted in its report that out of 48 units, 46 are
sick while on the other hand it has started the process of harassment against these units instead of reviving
them. As a result thereof, remaining units are also closing (Report of Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation
Annexure–IV).
                (v)  Taking inspiration from press release No. 9-98/78 cement dated January 4, 1979 
(Annexure–V) by Central Government and Eighth Five Year Plan, State Government had invited
entrepreneurs for setting up small cement units. The aim of Central Government behind this was that with
the setting up of these industries, small deposits of limestone will be utilised where it is not possible to set
up big units. On the other hand, on the basis of resolution adopted by the Central Government during the
said Five Year Plan that for construction of 20000 km double express highway, two million houses, target
to generate 1 lakh megawatt power and construction of 12000 km highway and urgent requirement of
cement, it was decided that the said target can be met only when small units of cement are set up under the
protection of Government and supply of cement is taken from the said small units of cements because it
would have taken 5 to 6 years for getting cement as per production capacity of big units.
               (vi)  Central Government had also kept it in mind that small producers of cement requires less capital as
compared to big producer of cement and setting up expenditure per ton will also be less, employment
opportunities will increase and the main thing was that small scale industries will develop and the country
will be prosperous.
                      Review statement regarding causes of Small Scale Industries getting sick :-
                         (i)  The interest rate was fixed at 13.5 per cent per annum at the time of sanctioning financial assistance
by the Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation to these small units but after investing margin money and
complying with all the formalities such as NOC from Pollution Control Board and letter of sanction
regarding power from the Power Corporation by these industries, it has been fixed @ 19.75 per cent
at the time of getting loan and before taking such step no consideration has been made with regard to
the future of these units and ultimately all the units have come under the burden of credit and became
almost closed.
                        (ii)  In 1996-97, Hon'ble Supreme Court banned the mining of limestone. As a result thereof supply of
major raw material i.e. limestone had stopped and self-producing capacity of units of making clinker
vanished.
                       (iii)  126 small cement units in which 50 per cent have the capacity to produce clinker, have completely
vanished due to further enhancement in production vis-a-vis its demand and decrease in purchase of
cement by the Government and no increase in the price of cement since last eight years in the State
and remaining units are doing only grinding by purchasing clinker from big units.
                       (iv)  Large scale units have been exempted from sales tax for 12 years for establishing industry in Uttar
Pradesh and consequently, large scale cement manufacturing units like Satna, ACC, have established
and still establishing their new grinding units in Uttar Pradesh. These units manufacture cement after
grinding the clinker and they get clinker from their parent unit which is situated in other States.
Therefore, they get exemption from sales tax from one State owing to the manufacture of clinker and
on the other hand after showing the transfer of clinker stock to other State they get exemption from
sales tax owing to the manufacture of cement. Due to this double relaxation, the sale price of their
cement is less because of low production cost and no burden of sales tax, whereas small scale
industries have been exempted from sales tax only for two years and because of this injustice, the
small scale industries of cement are adversely affected in the State.
                        (v)  It is clear from the above-mentioned explanation that small scale industries which are on the verge of
closure, and are doing only grinding work, pay the sales tax to the State at the rate of 12.5 per cent for
manufacturing cement by taking clinker from these large scale industries. Thus these small-scale
industries pay total 12.5 + 4 = 16.5 per cent sales tax whereas large scale industries sell their cement

after getting the clinker stock transferred and also by getting the benefit of exemption for 12 years
and without paying any tax. Thus the production cost of small-scale cement manufacturing units is
16.5 per cent more comparing to large-scale industries. In this situation, these units cannot survive in
the market.
                       (vi)  When the said units were on the verge of closure, the State Government for their revival, passed an
ordinance that preference in purchasing from small scale industries and 15 per cent of price
preference will be provided by all the departments of the state but no department considered the need
to comply with this.
                      (vii)  More purchase preference is given to the small cement units of the state as compared to the large
scale cement units outside the state, the small cement units will have the opportunity to work upto
their full capacity and employment opportunity will be generated.
                      (viii)  Big companies are able to increase their production capacity by getting easy loans from IDBI
whereas small units always face the scarcity of capital and the financial institutions also avoid to
provide finance to these units due to which the production capacity of these units is affected.
                       (ix)  A comparative statement of investment, employment generation, revenue losses of exemptions etc.
of large scale cement units and small scale cement units established in the state is given at Annexure-
VIII.
                        (x)  Out of the 126 small cement units established in the state, 48 units were established with the help of
UP Finance Corporation. Out of these, 46 units are those units which have been declared defaulter by
the Finance Corporation in its report, 6 units are those units whose promoters after repeated requests
hand handed over every thing to the Finance Corporation and have migrated from the state. 8 units
are those whose promoters could get relief from the Finance Corporation by paying under lump sum
scheme in pressure of penalty action by the Finance Corporation despite the fact that these units are
closed. 13 units are those units which are on the verge of being closed (Annexure VI and VII).
                       (xi)  In view of the above mentioned problems and adverse circumstances, a study was got done by Uttar
Pradesh Finance Corporation through ICRA to find out the reasons of failure of small scale industrial
units and measures for their revival. They have categorically made by the following suggestions in
their report for the revival of the said industrial units :
                              "...complete waiver of interest coupled with full
                              exemption of sales tax and imposition of 15% price
                              preference results in positive profit for the eastern
                              UP units and a breakeven scenario for the western
                              UP units...."
PRAYER
            If the Government is interested in running these industries in the state in order to provide employment and
assistance to the Government in manufacturing work in the national interest, and thereby making the State self-
dependent, the following measures must be considered:
                 (i)  If compliance of suggestions made by ICRA with respect of 13 units as mentioned in Annexure-VII is
ensured and the interest due on the said units is waived, Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation would not only
receive Rs. 15,02,59,415/- but also the said 13 units would also get revived.
                (ii)  Small scale cement units would not be able to compete with big units unless they are fully exempted from
sales tax, as suggested by ICRA since larger units are enjoying exemption from sales tax for the last 12
years.
               (iii)  Public Sector Undertakings should ensure purchase preference and imposition of 15% price preference.
Besides all Government Departments should be directed to meet their entire cement requirement first from

81st Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/81streport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:43]
small scale cement units and should go for procurement from big industries only if it is not possible to
procure it from small units.
            Parliamentary Committee is, therefore, requested that if aforesaid suggestions are implemented, the sick small
cement units of the state could be revived otherwise the chapter of small-scale industries in the state would close.
5.         Committee's findings, observations and recommendations
5.1       Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation made a study regarding mini cement plants financed by the Corporation. The
study report inter-alia  mentioned that the performance of the cement industry is closely linked with the industrial
growth of the country. In the period from 1993-94 to 1995-96, when the industrial growth was higher, the scenario in
the segment was bright. In 1995-96 with 11.7% industrial growth, the cement production grew at 10.6%. As the industry
slowed down in 1996-97, so did the cement segment. The same downward trend continued in 1998-99. According to the
industry sources, the current take-off position is inadequate to generate more profits, as the low price realisation is still
not matching the production cost. The recession in construction activity, low investment in major infrastructure projects,
rise in the cost of power cost etc. coupled with high borrowing cost has marked down the industry's earnings.
5.2       Another major constraint in this segment is excess capacity. During the growth phase of the industry, almost all
major players in this sector had gone for huge capacity addition. As a result, the installed capacity of cement industry
doubled in the last four years. In 1996-97 the installed capacity was 96.25 million tonnes, going up to 105.25 million
tonnes in 1997-98. Some additional capacity is still expected to be installed in the coming years. Due to the huge
capacity available with major plants, they have encroached upon the segment of the mini cement plants by entering the
remotest areas. Mini cement plants, which traditionally used to cater to the local markets of remote areas, were
therefore, badly affected.
5.3       The study report further mentioned that the immediate future is not very encouraging. However, once the
Government starts the revival of the economy through investment in infrastructure and construction activity picks up,
the demand for cement will grow.
5.4       The Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation also entrusted ICRA with the job of preparing a report on the cement
sector. The ICRA had cited high interest rate charged by Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation as one of the problems
faced by the SSI units in cement sectors.
5.5       The Committee observes that the State Government had revised the rate of interest from 13.5% to 19.75% in
1991-92. The reasons for charging high rate of interest by Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation was due to the fact that it
got loans from SIDBI/IDBI at a higher rate. The Committee, however, feels that revising the rate of interest was not in
the interest of mini cement plants. The Government should have calculated the viability of those projects before revising
the rate of interest as it proved a disincentive for SSIs in the cement sector. As regards giving loans by SIDBI/IDBI on
higher rate of interest to Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, the Committee observes that the U.P. Administration with
SIDBI/IDBI should have sorted out the matter.
5.6       The Committee notes that SSIs engaged in this business took loans from the financial institutions/banks, but due
to industrial slow down and stiff competition from giant plants they have to dispose of their products through distress
sale, which contributed to accumulation of interest against the principal amount of loan. Rising of interest by
Government under such circumstances proved to be the death knell for the SSIs in the cement sector. The Committee
further notes that Rajasthan Financial Corporation, under a one-time settlement, not only waived the interest completely
but also waived 20% principal amount so that the mini cement units situated in Rajasthan may survive.
5.7       In comparison, the units of Uttar Pradesh are working in a climate of apathy. Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation,
in a letter dated 4.10.2000 addressed to "Udyog Bandhu" (A Forum of Industrial Associations), mentioned that the
members of the mini cement plants association desired that whatever repayment (by way of interest or repayment) they
have made till date to the corporation may be adjusted towards principal and balance may be recovered from them in
easy instalments. The Board had already rejected this proposal earlier. However, if there is any demand of the
association for waiver of total or part of interest, the same is to be taken to the Board again for its approval.
5.8       The Committee fails to understand as to why Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation is not able to bail out the units
in UP taking a cue from the RFC when the units in UP are struggling for survival.

81st Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/81streport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:43]
5.9       From the memorandum submitted by the Association, the Committee notes that problems of the units were to be
deliberated by a High Power Committee under the chairmanship of the Chief Minister. In this regard, the Directorate of
Industries, UP, in their letter dated 1.8.2000 requested Secretary, UP Administration, to place the matter before the said
High Power Committee. It appears that such a sensitive matter was not brought before that Committee. It reflects lack of
coordination between the departments of the Government. Similar situations also prevail at the central level also. On
various occasions, the Committee observed that various ministries did not have on integrated approach to solve the
problems of the industry. The Committee observes that if SSI units are to be given a boost, the different departments of
the State Government and Central Government are to work in a coordinated manner.
5.10     Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation portfolio has, at present, 48 cement-manufacturing units. Out of 48 units only
2 units are regular in payment whereas 1 unit has recently gone in production. As per the study conducted by the Uttar
Pradesh Finance Corporation, these units are facing problems relating to market recession like in transportation cost,
wage cost ban on mining, unimplemented units, temporary default, etc. The Committee notes the plethora of problems
being faced by the cement units. In the circumstances, the Committee observes that the reported harassment of these
units, instead of reviving them by the Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, as mentioned by the Association, needs to be
looked into.
5.11     The Central Government had announced in the 8th Five Year Plan about construction of double express
highway, houses for millions, generation of power to take the electricity to the rural areas. Had such activities relating to
infrastructure building arisen, the present state of low intake of Cement would not have arisen. In fact, market demand
of cement was not in line with the Government's projection. In subsequent budgets of the Central Government the above
schemes did not find place, resulting in decline of demand of Cement.
5.12     The giant units which take 5-6 years to produce cement started production on in 1996 in UP after taking
financial assistance from IDBI on easy terms and flooded the market with cement at a cheaper rate and ousted smaller
units by waging an unfair and unequal competition. Had the development work regarding building up infrastructure
started before 1992 or during 1992-96 the smaller units would have survived and established themselves.
5.13     The Central Government had facilitated in establishing the mini cement plants to meet the demand of cement in
the emerging scenario of building up of infrastructure facilities in the country by enabling the SSI sector to get loans
from the IDBI. In all, 126 units were set up, of which 50% were in the category of integrated units (which produced
cement out of its own manufactured clinkers) and 50% were in the category of grinding units (which ground clinkers to
produce cement after purchasing clinkers from the big units). This method of producing cement by the SSI sector
received a setback when the Supreme Court banned mining of limestone and as a consequence, limestone mines were
closed in Dehradun. As a result, the supply of major raw material i.e. limestone, had stopped and self-producing
capacity of units for making clinker vanished. The remaining units are doing only grinding by purchasing clinker from
the big units. The woes of SSI sector did not end here. The capacity to produce clinker and producing cement out of
clinker has not only been taken away by the big units from the SSI sector, the price of clinker sold by them to small
units has been raised to such an extent that either the small units are unable to purchase it from big units or if they
purchase and grind them, they would not be able to sell that cement in the market because of high cost of production,
resulting in closure of mini cement plants.
5.14     Recently, the UP Government had offered 100% concession of Sales Tax for 12 years to those industries whose
investment is over PSUs crore. Under this scheme, the giant cement industries like ACC and Satna Cement have
established their grinding unit of total 8.6 lakh tonnes per annum capacity in Rai Bareily District of UP and are availing
of this concession. The State Government would lose a huge amount of revenue by granting this concession to the giant
units. The cement so produced after grinding by the giant units is much cheaper and their selling price is much lower
than that of mini plants. All the more, the giant units are availing double concessions: -
                (a)  Firstly, as a manufacturer of intermediate product i.e. clinker, they are availing sales tax exemption in
their parent state; and
                (b)  they are availing sales tax concession in UP as a manufacturer of cement.
5.15     During the course of oral evidence before the Sub-Committee, the SSI association expressed the apprehension

81st Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/81streport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:43]
that those giant industries would leave UP after 12 years and establish their units in other states to avail sales tax
concession. The Committee was informed that small units are given only two years sales tax free concession as against
12 years to the giant units.
5.16     Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation's letter dated 4th October, 2000 addressed to "Udyog Bandhu" corroborates
the above fact. The study made by ICRA had concluded that integrated mini cement units were not viable. The report
further concluded that in case the unit took up grinding function alone, the operation could become viable with some
incentives. The study had further concluded that the units could be marginally viable if they were granted total sales tax
exemption. It has been further mentioned that Government of UP had granted 12 years sales tax exemption to big units.
The revenue loss to Government from these two units along would be Rs. 345 crores. It had been reported that there was
a third new large unit coming up in the State. Revenue loss from this unit alone would be Rs. 691 crores.
5.17     The above communication is the testimony of the fact how small units are discriminated against and have been
forced to wage a battle against stronger competitors.
            When the small units were gasping for oxygen, UP government issued a circular in 1998 asking its cement
consuming departments to send their demands to small-scale industries only. In spite of this, Government departments
are not complying with the order. As a result, the order remained on paper only without any visible results. The
Committee feels that a mechanism to monitor the compliance of the Purchase Preference Policy should have been
evolved if the Government really wanted to help the SSI sector. The Committee observes that an early action to monitor
the compliance of the order even now may save the situation for the dying SSI units.
5.18     Another factor, which has crippled the mini cement plants, is the lack of credit flow to the sector. While the giant
units had no difficulty in securing loans from banks and FIs, the small units are still struggling to get loans from banks
even after the announcement made to the effect that loan would be given without any collateral security. In addition,
restriction on load carrying capacity of trucks proved to be a strangulatory provision for the mini cement plants.
6.1       In nutshell, a vision was created during the successive Five Year Plans and notifications issued in 1979 that huge
infrastructure would be created nationwide but large cement plants would not be in a position to supply the required
quantum of cement. SSI sector was encouraged to set up mini cement plants to meet the demand of additional quantum
of cement in view of its lower capital cost, quicker installation and higher employment potential coupled with the
exploitation of smaller limestone deposits by it in rural and hilly areas. The banks gave these units loan assistance and
FIs and they started setting up units when the cement industry was hailed as the harbinger of overall development of the
state. The good days for the SSI sector did not last long due to economic recession when construction activities come to
low ebb.
6.2       SSI's cup of sorrow was full when the Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation increased the rate of interest from
13.5% to 19.75% and the giant units flooded the market with their brand of cement at a much lower price than that of
mini cement plants which in turn were forced them to sell cement at a price lower than their cost of production. They
failed to pay interest on the principal amount and the banks and FIs shut their doors to these sick units.
6.3       Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation made a study about problems and possible revival scheme of mini cement
plants through ICRA, which suggested complete waiver of interest coupled with full exemption of sales tax and
imposition of 15% price preference for the revival of mini cement plants. But so far, no positive step has been taken to
save the industry.
6.4       The Committee observes that in the recent past, there has been an overall increase in the rate of growth in the
cement industry. This is an indication that construction activity has again picked up. But these activities are confined to
certain places in the country and, by and large, large industries are able to reap the benefit of such a situation. The
renewed demand for cement has not percolated to the lower level of the industry. The Committee feels a lending hand
should be given to those sick units. Ways and means should be explored to bail out them from then pathetic situation.
6.5       The Committee also notes that as per norms specified by the Reserve Bank of India, a sick unit is considered as
potentially viable, if it would be in a position, after implementing a relief package spread over a period not exceeding
five years from the commencement of the package from banks, financial institutions, Government (Central/State) and
other concerned agencies, as may be necessary, to continue to service its repayment obligations as agreed upon
including those forming part of the package, without the help of the concessions after the aforesaid period. The

6.6       In view of the RBI guidelines, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Small Scale Industries, in
consultation with the RBI, Lead Bank Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, and UP Administration should make an
attempt to revive these units keeping in view the ICRA report as well as action initiated by the Rajasthan Financial
Corporation so that these units, which are more or less victims of circumstances, can survive.

I.          Introduction

II.         BACKGROUND OF MOU SYSTEM
 
2.1       The Department of Public Enterprises in their Background Note on the MoU system have stated that as a major
policy initiative, the MoU system was introduced by the Central Government as an important tool to improve the
performance of the Central Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs).  The New Industrial Policy of 1991 laid greater emphasis
on the MoU system requiring all PSEs to be brought under the ambit of the MoU system.  Beginning with 4 PSEs in
1987-88, the MoU system has now been extended to a large number of PSEs during the course of time and during the
year 2000-2001, 108 PSEs have signed the MoUs.
 
2.2       It was stated that the main objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of the PSEs by
imparting increased autonomy and accountability and to provide a method of evaluation of the performance of the
managements of the PSEs in an objective and transparent manner.  Further, the objective of providing clarity of goals to

82nd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/82ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:16:44]
be achieved by PSEs is another dimension of the MoU system.
 
2.3       The Committee has noted that there is a High Power Committee (HPC) at the apex level, headed by the Cabinet
Secretary which is basically a policy making body for the MoUs.  This HPC consists of Secretaries of all nodal
Departments of Government such as Finance, Expenditure, Planning Commission and Programme Implementation, etc. 
The HPC undertakes the evaluation of the performance of the PSEs and in addition the HPC also provides a forum to
resolve inter-ministerial issues.
 
2.4       To assist HPC in this task and also to provide the technical inputs and to finalise the MoUs, there is an Advisory
Body called Adhoc Task Force (ATF), it was stated.  The members of the ATF are drawn from various fields having
vast experience in their areas and include retired Secretaries, Chief Secretaries, top experts in different disciplines like
finance, management, science and technology, and prominent academicians.  This body provides the neutrality and
objectivity to the MoU system.
 
2.5       The Department have also informed that under the present set up there is a small MoU Division under the
Department of Public Enterprises, Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, which co-ordinates the entire
exercise of finalizing the MoUs in respect of all the PSEs numbering 108. In addition to finalizing the MoUs, the MoU
Division is also responsible for the evaluation of performance of PSEs, both on the basis of the provisional results as
well as the audited results.
 
2.6       Explaining about the process of preparing MoUs, the Department have stated that the MoU process starts with
the issuing of guidelines by the DPE to the PSEs/Administrative Ministries for drafting the MoUs.  The PSEs prepare
their MoUs on the basis of these guidelines and these draft MoUs are then discussed with the Administrative Ministries
and in the Boards of the PSEs and are then submitted to the DPE.  DPE prepares background papers and its comments
on each draft MoU keeping in view the past performance of the PSE, its future potential, the industry scenario and the
economic environment of the PSE, it was added.  It was further stated that these draft MoUs are discussed in the MoU
negotiation meetings where the ATF members, managements of the PSE, officials from the Administrative Ministries
and the representatives from nodal Government Agencies like Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Statistics and
Programme Implementation and Planning Commission are also present.  The MoUs and the targets are finalised in these
meetings through mutual discussions.
           
III.       PERFORMANCE OF MOU SYSTEM IN THE STRATEGIC SECTOR

succeeding pages.
 
IV.       BHARAT EARTH MOVERS LIMITED, BANGALORE
 
4.1       Bharat Earth Movers Limited (BEML) came into being in May 1964 as a Public Sector Undertaking, with the
transfer of its present Bangalore Complex (formerly known as Rail Coach Division) from the Hindustan Aircraft
Limited, Bangalore. BEML is a company under the administrative control of the Department of Defence Production &
Supplies, Ministry of Defence. The Registered Office of the Company, including Marketing Headquarters, is located at
Bangalore. BEML commenced its operations from January, 1965 with the production of rail coaches and assembly of
spare parts at the Bangalore complex.
 
4.2       Since March, 1992, the company status has changed to a “Partly Owned Government Company” from “Wholly
Owned Government Company”. Presently, the  Government owns 61.2 percent of the total equity.
 
4.3       BEML is managed by a Board comprising Directors and headed by a Chairman and  Managing Director.
 
4.4       PRODUCTION UNITS
 
            The company has manufacturing units established at Kolar Gold Fields (KGF) Mysore and Bangalore – all in the
State of Karnataka.

            Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL) is a public sector enterprise under the Department of Atomic
Energy (DAE), Government of India. It was registered on 17 September 1987 with the objective of operating the atomic
power stations and implementing the atomic power projects for generation of electricity in pursuance with the schemes
and programmes of the GOI under atomic energy act 1962.

6.4       Development Phase of Nuclear Power in India
 
6.4.1    The basic research in the nuclear field commenced about four decades ago in units of DAE. The initial R&D and
the experience in setting up and operations of  research reactors provided the core competence for the nuclear power
programme.  DAE, the Administrative Ministry, has  established over the years  comprehensive .capability in the entire
spectrum of nuclear fuel cycle in terms of fuel, special materials for nuclear power plants and nuclear waste
management facilities etc.
 
6.4.2    NPCIL has acquired comprehensive capability for designing, constructing, commissioning and operating nuclear
power plants. PHWRs of 220 MWe -unit size developed indigenously have reached a significant level of maturity.
Development of 540 MWe PIIWR has also been carried out indigenously and the  first  two  units are being set up at
Tarapur (TAPP-3&4). The 540 MWe unit rating of PHWR.s is also being updated to about 680 MWe with minimal
design changes and partial , boiling in the coolant channels for setting up PHWRs beyond TAPP-3&4.
 
6.4.3    The path of self- reliance has been chosen from the very beginning of the programme. Cost of generation from
nuclear power plants is comparable to contemporary coal thermal power plants located away from coal-mines. Nuclear
power is also associated with the advantage of being devoid of carbon-dioxide releases. The indigenous industries have
gained intense experience and are now in a position to take up the manufacture of critical nuclear components with high
precision.
 
With this background, nuclear power programme is now poised for rapid growth.

6.6     Safety & Environmental Protection
 
6.6.1    NPCIL accords the highest priority on Quality Assurance (QA) and safety and environmental protection at all
stages of the nuclear power programme. The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) which is an independent and
statutory body in terms of the Atomic Energy Act 1962, monitors, prescribes and enforces safety review at NPCIL.
Well-known design safety principles like defence-in-depth, multiple barriers, release of radioactivity and fail safe
designs are adopted in the engineering of the plants so that  releases from the plants will be well within the prescribed
limits stipulated by AERB.
 
 
During safety review at operational stage, release from the plants are monitored and regulated to be within the stipulated
limits. Environment Survey Laboratories are set up at each operating nuclear power station, which monitor a number of
samples of air, water, road and other products in the environment around the power station for radioactivity and the
reports of these laboratories are reviewed by AERB. Nuclear power is one of the environmentally clean sources for bulk
generation of electricity. It is very relevant in protection of the environment from greenhouse gases, acid rain and smog.

programmes like in-plant induction training, qualification of operation staff to different positions as per requirements of
AERB, on the job training and training in specific specialised in the human resource development in NPCIL.

6.11     HISTORY OF MOU SYSTEM IN NPCL
 
6.11.1    The company, after its formation in September, 1987 studied the MOU system which a few Public Sector
Enterprises (PSEs) had adopted them,.  Seeing the advantages of the system for performance  improvement of the
company, NPCIL   for the first time entered into MOU with the Administrative Ministry i.e. Department of Atomic
Energy for the year 1991-92.  Since then, every year, MOU has been  signed between NPCIL and DAE.   The
performance evaluation is carried out based   on the stated commitments in the MOU.
 
6.11.2     The process of arriving at MOU is as follows:
 
(i)         Compiling comprehensive set of criteria for company’s performance evaluation.  These criteria broadly cover
the Generating Performance, profitability, Project milestones, quality assurance, Human Resource Development,
Research & Development, Environment Protection & Public Awareness, etc.  This   fulfills one of the objectives of the
industrial policy resolution of  1956 that the performance of all PSE’s should be judged by their over-all results.
 
(ii)        NPCIL assigns weightages to different criteria of the MOU based on the relative importance of the indicators
and priorities between different objectives of the company.The aspects stated above are evolved through a process of
participation by respective functional Directorates. The target values for, each parameter are fixed, based on the
commitment of executing agencies. The process of involvement is complemented by other documents like performance
budget, annual plan or capital budget and revenue budget generated by the company. After in-house deliberations and
finalisation, the details are reviewed at DAE, before the MOU is proposed for consideration of DPE. The institutional
arrangement for MOU facilitates the third party vetting by Department of Public Enterprises (DPE). The industry
specific Adhoc Task Force (ATF) of DPE vigorously examines the MOU and gives clearance for entering into
performance contract of MOU of NPCIL and DAE.

6.12     DISCUSSIONS WITH THE MANAGEMENT OF NPCIL
 
6.12.1    Shri V.K. Sharma, the acting CMD of NPCIL, made a presentation on the history of the corporation since its
incorporation in 1987 till today, including its ongoing projects and thereafter, the Committee deliberated with officers of
the NPCIL and the following points emanated from the discussions.
 
6.12.2   Since 1987 additional capacity of 1760 MWE has been created through commencement of commercial
operation at NAPS-1&2, KAPS and kaiga
 
6.12.3    The present Nuclear power capacity in the country is 2720 Mwe and projection for enhancement of this
capacity is 6680 Mwe by 2008 in the light of additional capacity enhancement of 3960 Mwe through completion of
ongoing projects at TAPP, KAIga and Rapp and Kudankulam. Overall contribution of Nuclear energy in the total
energy component of the country being a meagre three percent it was informed that Nuclear energy is highly cost
intensive and it has also to be seen in the context of energy contribution growing in other traditional sector through
capacity creation. Nuclear energy generation involves higher iterative process due to high order risk to ensure reduction
of occurrence of risk or to ensure improbability of occurrence of risk.  Incidentally the Nuclear power sector in the
country has zero accident record since 1968. In addition, availability of raw material uranium of 238 category is scarce
and India has deposits of U235 only and conversion of U 235 to 238 is also a cost intensive process.
 
6.12.4    The committee also sought an assurance against occurrence of a Chernobyl type accidents.  In this context, the
Committee was reassured that Chernobyl type technology is not licensable, and the NPCIL follows an extremely
transparent policy besides, having a sound system of in built periodic safety audits and stock taking.
 
6.12.5   In addition, the NPCIL is also learning from accidents in other countries.Moreover, as a member of IAEC India
is bound by their safety and other provision of Nuclear Power use and hence accidents are near improbable.
 
6.12.6    The Committee was also informed that the capacity utilization is about 87 percent  and there is a continuous
improvement of capacity factors.
           
6.12.7   The Committee was informed that one of the reasons for the slow growth of nuclear power in our country has
been the indigenous technology development phase that the nuclear power programme had to go through. Nuclear
power plants are very complex and require millions of smaller and bigger items/components to be designed, fabricated
and assembled. The licensing of nuclear power plants involves a complex regulatory process in which all the safety
aspects are checked. The nuclear power plants have been installed in advanced countries by sharing of technology
developed by different countries and using their fabrication capabilities. On account of the restrictive trade barriers and
technology denial regime prevalent for India, all the development had to be done within the country and this took time
initially.
 
6.12.8     The Committee was also apprised that Nuclear power has no significant avenues for overseas financing. It has
to rely on Government budgetary support in combination with domestic borrowing and internal surplus. A programme
of setting up of 10,000 MWe of nuclear power capacity by 2000 was formulated. There were problems on the
availability of financial resources during the VIII Five-Year Plan. Therefore, this programme could not be implemented
as envisaged.

6.12.9   The Committee was also informed the realization of dues from the SEBs has been a problems in the past. With
the acceptance of the MS Ahluwalia Committee Report by the states, the problem is likely to be under control.
However, the settlement of the part dues in terms of long maturity bonds puts a considerable pressure on the liquidity of
the company.
6.13     OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
 
6.13.1    The Committee was pleased to note that NPCIL had been performing extremely well since its inception.
 
6.13.2    The Committee also observed that having regard to the vital sector in which the unit is operating the structure
of the MOU should be more appropriately geared to this factor.  It was observed the focus on financial performance
being iterated in the MOU should be altered to shift the focus on more important factors of national interest. Hence the
MoU should accord higher weightage to performance parameters relating R&D, contribution to defense, contribution to
Indian Space Research Programme, Disaster Management and Relief efforts.
 
6.13.3    The Committee felt R&D, especially in the areas of import substitution in terms of development of new
materials as well as new process technologies, should be accorded much higher weightage in the interest of impetus to
Indian Nuclear Programmes.
 
6.13.4    This apart, the Committee felt that since the MOU is a mutually agreed document on performance parameters, a
focus shift in the contribution of Government for this type of PSE is also imperative.  The performance parameters of
the Department of Atomic Energy in the MOU should emphasis on more tangible factors like facilitating more in
enabling the company in recovering dues from SEB.
 
6.13.5  The committee also felt that MOUs should contain weightage for energy efficiency and resource efficiency
efforts as they also are to liable to reflect in the Balance Sheet of the Company under the Companies Act.
 
6.13.6    The Committee also felt that since the unit is operating in a strategic sector, it is imperative that it has a sound
policy for retention and upgradation of skills of its Human Resource.  This is more than imperative for a unit like
NPCIL having regard to its strategic contribution to India’s defence and infrastructure sector. It is therefore felt that the
weightage for HRD should also be higher.  At the same time the excellent expertise and human resource base should
also be exported in the form participation in safety audit teams constituted by IAEC, mutual inspection teams etc
 
6.13.7   Also higher weightage should be accorded in the MOU for safety parameters besides, developing fail safe
technologies and excellent safety record and also the environment of high improbabity of risk.  
 
6.13.8  Ecological and environmentally sustainable operation is also a vital area of concern for Nuclear Power. 
Weightage to this should also be accorded appropriately.
 
6.13.9  As regards introduction of systems upgradation like Extra Resource Planning etc, the Committee observed that
the NPCIL is having its own LAN systems and felt little need for a performance enhancing systems application like
ERP.  In this context, it is the considered view of the Committee that NPCIL, which is working in high tech sector,
needs to be alert to organizational decays and take remedial measures through process reengineering of its work
systems. Hence, MOU weight should also be accorded for this appropriately.
 
The Committee feels that considering the self-reliant manner in which nuclear power has been developed, Government
should provide higher financial allocation and resources for the growth of Nuclear power.

IL BACKGROUND OF MOU SYSTEM

2.1 The Department of Public Enterprises in its Background Note on the MoU system stated that the
MoU system was introduced as a major policy initiative by the Central Government as an important tool
to improve the performance of the Central Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs). The New Industrial Policy
of 1991 laid greater emphasis on the MoU system requiring all PSEs to be brought under the ambit of
the MoU system. Beginning with four PSEs in 1987-88, the MoU system has now been extended to a
large number of PSEs. By 2000-2001, 108 PSEs had signed the MoUs.

2.2 It was stated that the main objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of the
PSEs by imparting increased autonomy and accountability and to provide a method of evaluation of the
performance of the managements of the PSEs in an objective and transparent manner. Further, the
objective of providing clarity of goals to be achieved by PSEs is another dimension of the MoU system.

2.3. The Committee has noted that there is a High Power Committee (HPC) at the apex level, headed
by the Cabinet Secretary which is basically a policy making body for the MoUs. This HPC consists of
Secretaries of all nodal Departments of Government such as Finance, Expenditure, Planning
Commission and Programme Implementation, etc. The HPC undertakes the evaluation of the
performance of the PSEs and in addition the HPC also provides a forum to resolve inter-ministerial
issues.

2.4 To assist HPC in this task and also to provide the technical inputs and to finalise the MoUs, there
is an Advisory Body called Adhoc Task Force (ATF), it was stated. The members of the ATF are drawn
from various fields having vast experience in their areas and include retired Secretaries, Chief
Secretaries, top experts in different disciplines like finance, management, science and technology, and
prominent academicians. This body provides neutrality and objectivity to the MoU system.

2.5 The Department has also informed that under the present set up there is a small MoU Division
under the Department of Public Enterprises, Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, which
co-ordinates the entire exercise of finalizing the MoUs in respect of all the PSEs numbering 108. In
addition to finalizing the MoUs, the MoU Division is also responsible for the evaluation of performance
of PSEs, both on the basis of the provisional as well as the audited results.

http://164. 100.24. 167/book2/reports/indus/83rdreport.htm 1/27/05


83rd Report Page 5 of 15

2.6 Explaining about the process of preparing MoUs, the Department have stated that the MoU
process starts with the issuing of guidelines by the DPE to the PSEs/Administrative Ministries for
drafting the MoUs. The PSEs prepare their MoUs on the basis of these guidelines. These draft MoUs
are then discussed with the Administrative Ministries and in the Boards of the PSEs. They are then
submitted to the DPE. DPE prepares background papers and its comments on each draft MoU keeping
in view the past performance of the PSE, its future potential, the industry scenario and the economic
environment of the PSE, it was added. It was further stated that these draft MoUs are discussed in the
MoU negotiation meetings where the ATF members, managements of the PSE, officials from the
Administrative Ministries and the representatives from nodal Government Agencies like Ministry of
Finance, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation and Planning Commission are also
present. The MoUs and the targets are finalised in these meetings through mutual discussions.

EXPORT CREDIT GUARANTEE CORPORATION
_OF INDIA LIMITED (ECGC)

L PROFILE

1.1 Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. (ECGC) was set up in 1957 by the
Government of India to support and strengthen the export promotion efforts of the country. The
corporation provides insurance cover to exporters against non-receipt of the payment for their exports
due to commercial and political risks. Export Credit Insurance seeks to create a favorable climate in
which exporters get timely and liberal facilities from banks. For this purpose, the corporation issues
policies and guarantees. The Registered and Corporate/Head Office of the corporation is located at
Mumbai. There are five regional offices at Mumbai, Chennai, Bangalore, Kolkata and New Delhi and 26
branches are also located in various cities in the country.

1.2... ECGC offers various policies which include standard policies, specific policies, financial
guarantee, transfer guarantee, overseas investment etc. The corporation has designed following five
types of standard policies to provide cover for shipments made on short-term credit :

Shipments (Comprehensive Risks) Policy — to cover both commercial and political risks from the date of

shipment.
Shipments (Political Risk) Policy — to cover only political risk from the date of shipment.

Small Exporters Policy — to cover both commercial and political risks or only political risk from the date
of shipment for the use of Small Exporters.

Contract (comprehensive Risks) Policy- to cover both commercial and political risks from the date of
contract.

Contracts (Political Risks) Policy — to cover both commercial and political risks from the date of
contract.

1.3 Specific policies are offered to provide continuous cover on the shipments of raw material,

http://164. 100.24. 167/book2/reports/indus/83rdreport.htm 1/27/05


83rd Report Page 6 of 15

consumer goods and consumer durables for which credit period does not exceed 180 days. Contracts for
export of capital goods or tumkey projects or construction works or rendering services abroad are not of
a repetitive nature. Such transactions are therefore insured by ECGC on a case - to — case basis under

specific policies.

1.4. Inorder to encourage banks to give adequate credit and other facilities for exports and protect
them from losses on account of their lending to exporters, ECGC provides financial guarantees which
include packing credit guarantee, export, production, finance guarantee, post-shipment export credit
guarantee, export performance guarantee, and export finance (overseas lending) guarantee. The
company also provides transfer guarantee, overseas investment insurance etc.

Il MISSION OF THE COMPANY
To support the Indian Export Industry by providing cost effective insurance and trade related

services to meet the needs of the Indian export market.

tm. OBJECTIVES OF THE COMPANY
To encourage, facilitate and develop trade between India and other countries.

To provide adequate export credit insurance cover, comparable to similar covers available to exporters
in other countries so that Indian exporters would be able to save themselves from losses that may arise
due to credit risks both commercial and political and also be in a position to maximize their export

business.

To provide the banks in India with export credit guarantee with a view to enable them to extend
adequate credit facilities to the Indian exporters both in pre-shipment and post-shipment stages.

To provide investment insurance to Indian investors undertaking investments in foreign countries

To operate the various schemes in such a manner that the Corporation would generate enough surpluses
to enable it to meet any losses that may result from unforeseen political situations.

To introduce new product lines so as to diversify into trade related services.

future plan of ECGC in context of the liberalization of the Indian economy and in view of the opening of
the insurance sector within the purview of (Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority) IRDA.

in 1991-92 to Rs.330.45 crore in 2001-02 showing a growth of 269 percent . On asked whether ECGC

current year to raise it from the present level of Rs. 415 crores to Rs. 440 crores.

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE

6.1 The Committee is of the view that ECGC should expand the range of its activities to cater to
medium and small-scale exporters. The Committee recommends that ECGC should endeavour towards
specialization based on customer segmentation based on customer size, which has become a necessity in
the present circumstances.

6.2 The Committee after examining the performance of ECGC within the MOU parameters is of the
opinion that weightage should be given to the role played by ECGC in providing impetus to exports in
the small-scale sector. The Committee feels that the SSI sector makes a marked presence in the export
market and comprises a part 45 percent of the India’s exports. The Committee strongly recommends that
ECGC should introduce some special scheme to promote exports from the SSI sector.

6.3. The Committee during the course of the deliberations felt that the customer requirements are
changing and demand for cost effective and efficient service on global standards is growing. The
Committee strongly recommends that ECGC should take immediate steps to become a strong customer
oriented organization.

The Committee is of the opinion that the total exposure in terms of maximum liability underwritten by
ECGC is disproportionate to the present capital base of ECGC. The Committee recommends that

National Film Development Corporation Ltd. (NFDC) is a Public Sector Enterprise set up in

1975 under the companies Act, 1956.The company was restructured during 1980 by the merger of the
erstwhile Indian Motion Picture Export Corporation (IMPEC) and Film Finance Corporation (FFC) and
the company emerged as Central Agency to promote good cinema in the country. Over the years, NFDC
has provided a wide range of services essential to the integrated growth of Indian cinema Besides
producing and financing films NFDC exports Indian films all over the world and imports commercial
films, Tele-films and serials for distribution and exhibition in the country. Other technical services
provided by NFDC include recording and dubbing, production equipment hiring, subtitling of films,
video duplication, video production, postproduction etc.

XII. OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee was of the opinion that in today’s world the impact of mass media is tremendous.
However, commercial considerations should not be the sole criteria for production of films. The
Committee strongly feels that films, which are socially relevant, must get preference in NFDC.

The Committee during the course of deliberations was of the opinion that NFDC should play a more
active role towards the popularization of Indian Cinema at the international level. The Committee
recommends that NFDC should provide support to both Indian films and Indian Directors to enable
them to get international exposure and success.

The Committee is of the considered opinion that the film festivals being organized by NFDC are mainly
held in major metropolitan cities. The Committee recommends that film festivals should be held in
smaller towns so as to propagate and promote Indian cinema and to provide wider audience.

The Committee feels that NFDC should help in promoting regional films so as to enable them to get all
India viewer ship. The Committee recommends that NFDC should help in the distribution/exhibition of
regional films by providing Hindi/English subtitles.

The Committee is of the opinion that Indian Cinema cannot remain isolated from the global cinema and
hence steps to bring good quality foreign cinema must be made. The Committee recommends that
NFDC should bring in good quality foreign cinema to India.

The Committee was informed that resource constraint has been a major factor hampering the growth of
NFDC. The Committee feels that with the grant of Industry status to the film industry financial
institutions can finance the production of quality films The Committee strongly recommends that
government should take up the matter with the financial institutions so that more loans are extended
NFDC.

REPORT 
         The Sub-Committee IV for Ministry fo r Agro and Rural Industries at its meeting held on 14 th  
March and 41h April 2002 decided to  study the implementation of Pr ime Minister Rozgar Yojana
(PMRY in the States of Andhra Pr adesh, Karnataka and Kerala. The Sub-Committee visited the States 
of Andhra Pradesh Karnataka and Kerala from 201h to  271h June 2002 and held discussions with the 
officials of  Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries, Stat e Government and Banks on issues pertaining to
PMRY. 
  
PMRY - AN OVERVIEW OF THE SCHEME 
  
1.1    The Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana was launched on 2nd Oct ober, 1993 with a view to providing
self-employment opportunities to educated unemplo yed youth in the country. The scheme was made 
operational with effect from Is t April, 1994. Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojanawas launched on 2nd
October, 1993. The scheme was designed to provide employment to more than  a million persons by
setting up seven lakh micro enterp rises during the Eight Five Year  Plan (1993-97), through industry, 
services and business routes. The scheme was operated in urban ar eas only during 1993-94, and in both 
urban and rural areas of the country from 1994-95 onwards. From 1994-95 the erstwhile-Self-
Employment Scheme for the Educat ed Unemployed Youth (SEEUY) was merged into PMRY. During
the Eight Plan a total of 7.75 lakh cases were sancti oned and out of these, lo ans were reported to have
been disbursed in 6.52 lakh cases as reported by the Reserve Bank of In dia (REI). Until now, nearly 15
educated unemployed youth have benefited from th e scheme. The PMRY is continuing in the Tenth
Plan period.

against a target of 2.20 lakh benefi ciaries, as many as 2.62 lakh cases  were sanctioned, and in 1.45 lakh
cases loans were disbursed as per the available reports from REI. Furt her, to enhance the coverage and

1.3    The target envisaged for 1999-2000 was 2.20 lakh beneficiaries. Against this target, 1,14,587 cases 
have been sanctioned, and disbursement took plac e in 59,845 cases as reporte d upto the month ending
December, 1999. The Target for 2002-03 remains at the level of Rs.2.20 lakhs, as was the case on 2001-
02. 
  
1.4    The Committee observes that the target (2.20 lakh beneficiaries) set for PMRY is too low to have
any significant impact on the creati on of employment opportunities in the country. This issue weighted
on the Committee's discussion with of ficials of State Government, Mini stry of Agro & Rural Industries
during its visit to Andhra Pradesh, Kamataka, Kerala. The Committee no ted that the target fixed each
year for PMRY has remained st atic during the last three year s i.e. for 2000-01, 2001-02 and 2002-03 
only 2.20 lakh persons were to be c overed under PMRY scheme. This figure, when divided between the
states and thereafter, among districts of each state, is like a drop. Th is figure is too minuscule to have
any noticeable impact on the unemployment scenario in a country of millions. 
  
1.5    The Ministry of Small Scale Industries, with whom the matter was taken up explained that the 
fixing of target was based on two aspects: - 
(a)
    Basic Target which is fixed, and is based on th e State's population as in 1991. This target is 
given by the Planning Commissi on, and is based on the employm ent potential and the numbe r
of unemployed registered with Employment Excha nge. An annual. target of 2.2 lakhs is given
for 2002-03, on an all India basis. This is communicated in March every year, for the next year.
(b)   Additional Target: This is vari able and is fixed on the basis of recovery position during the
previous year, and the performance in the previous year. This is communicated during May. 
         The Committee was also informed that th ere is a Government of Indi a guideline that 125 per cent
of target must also be achieved. 
  
1.6    However, the Committee was of the view that  the overall target for PM RY should be increased so
that states could be given enhanc ed targets, and more and more people can be brought under the ambit
of the scheme each year.

2.1    During the course of the Committee's meeting held at Hyde rabad, Commissioner of Industries
replied that Andhra Pradesh state that the scheme with a high target of around 33,000 and the number of
sanctions have been declining since with accumulation of NPAs. 
  
2.2    The Committee was further informed that th ere are a number of reasons  for under achievement o f
tile target under PMRY which are as under:- 
  
(a)  Banks complained that there is generall y delay in communicating PMRY targets to them,
which results in delay in grounding of the unit. Also, selection of beneficiaries is done only on
specific dates. The delay in comm unicating target of the banks le ads to delay in sanctioning o f
loans and subsequent disbursal of loans to the beneficiaries. Target is communicated in two
installments, which results in delay in its implementation. 
  
(b)  It is generally seen that beneficiaries take up si milar or same lines of  activity, which makes it
unviable. Autorickshaws, photocopy shops, STD booths etc were cite d as examples. Banks
hesitate to sanction loans for activities of simi lar nature as these activities reach a saturation
point which is a major reason to the failure of the scheme. 
  
(c)  Most beneficiaries go in for trade and business activities. 
  
(d)  Percentage of overdues to total loans is 67 per cent, which is a matter of great concern. 
  
(e)  Absconding entrepreneurs who divert funds and close shop are also a matter of concern. 
  
(f)   From the entrepreneurs' side, request for change in activ ity results in delay in getting
approvals. 
  
(g)  Marketing of products is a problem area which entrepreneurs find difficult to surmount. 
  
8.      Mounting NPAs under the PMRY scheme is a problem to be addressed immediately. The
representatives of Government of  Andhra Pradesh apprised the Comm ittee that the following measures
were being taken for overcoming the problems:- 
  
(a)  A list of viable schemes is being identifie d. Project profiles on thes e lines of activities are
being prepared. 
  
(b)  List of eligible beneficiaries in each area, mandal wise, is being maintained. 
  
(c)  Technology link with instit utions is being thought of. A me ntion was made of RUDSETI o f
Karnataka and some districts of Andhra Pradesh, which provide training to beneficiaries. 
  
(d)  Deputy Tahsildars are employe d for recovery of dues. Andhra  Pradesh is the only state doing
so. 
  
(e)  Monitoring is being done by Industry Promotion Officer. 
  
(f)   Awards have been constituted for best Industry Promotion Officer. 
  
(g)  Advertisement campaign for PMRY will be undertaken.

2.3    The Committee observes that there is a great diff erence between applicat ions recommended and
cases sanctioned in Andhra Pradesh. The downtrend in the number of sa nctions is alarming, and the gap
between the number of applications  and disbursals has been increa sing in Andhra Pradesh. As against
the national average, achievement of the target under the scheme be ing 86.3 per cent, the gap of 50 pe r
cent between the target and its achievement in Andhra Pradesh showed a dismal performance. The
progress of the PMRY in Andhra Pradesh depicted a sharp decline in the number of sanctions though the
target remained almost static. (33,600 for 1999-2000, 33,800 for 2000-01 and .33,200 for 2001-02). 
  
2.4    A gap in the PMRY between sanctions and di sbursal of loan was also  seen in Andhra Pradesh,
Against the 16,782 applications sanctioned, only 13,309 cases were disbursed loan during 1999-2000, 
and against 14,857 sanctioned cases during 2000-01, only 12178 aspirants were disbursed loans. 
  
2.5    The Committee observed that timely communication of targets s hould be made and specific dates
for selection of entrepreneurs should be communicated. As regard s large number of beneficiaries
choosing activities which become unviable, the Committee suggests th at counselling of applicants to
choose from agriculture and allied activities should be done. 
  
2.6    The Committee also observ es that coverage of SC/STs unde r the Scheme is not upto the norm
stipulated up Government of India i.e. 22.5 per cen t for SC/ST. Against the all India average of 15.9 pe r
cent, Andhra Pradesh has recorded representation for these categories as 16.9 per cent during 1998-99, 
21.3 'per cent during 1999-2000, 17.5 per cent during 2000-2001 and 15.1 per cent during 2001-02. This 
has to be brought to the stipulated norm. 
  
RECOVERY OF LOANS
 
  
2.7    The recovery scenario in A ndhra Pradesh a dismal picture. Avai lable records indicate that during
the half year ended Marc h, 1999 it was 41.1 per cent; during th e half year ended March, 2000 it was
36.8 per cent and during half year  ended March, 2001 it was 37.9 per cent. During the half-year ende d 
September, 2001 it was 38.8 per cent The representatives of State Government apprised the Committee
that Deputy Tahsildar had been specially deputed  to make recovery of loans from defaulting
entrepreneurs. 
  
2.8    The Committee, during the course of the interaction wished to know if any study on viable projects
in each district was undertaken. The Commissioner of Industries Andhra Pradesh replied that this
exercise was undertaken, and project profiles on identified lines of activities were being prepared. 
2.9    The Committee observes that in order to improve rate of gr ounding of units it was necessary to
rectify the high percen tage of NPAs as mounting NPAs were one of the reas ons for high mortality rate
of PMRY projects. The Committee obs erved that NPAs to large industr ies can not be equated with the
NPAs under the PMRY as the percenta ge. of NPAs in PMRY sector wa s but a small percent of total
NPAs in the country. Out of total NPA of Rs.18000 cr ores, small sector owed only Rs.8,000 crore. NPA
for PMRY, therefore, was only negl igible. The Committee, therefore,  suggests that bankers should be
encouraged to finance self-employment schemes as this would directly increase employment. 
  
SURVIVAL OF PMRY UNITS 
  
2.10 The Committee was informed by the Commissioner of Industries, Andhra Pradesh that the average
rate of survival in Andhra Pradesh is 60 per cent, and that mortality rate was high in business and trade
sector. This was because the beneficiary abandons his activity af ter a short period. In the absence o
f
fixed assets they are not able to pump in fresh investment, nor can they approach banks/Financial
Institutions for fresh loans. He opi ned that service oriented units s hould be encouraged, as the survival
rate in the service sector was hi gh whereas the survival rate  in business sector was onl y 30 per cent. He

SURVIVAL OF PMRY UNITS 
3.6    The Committee was informed that PMRY units find it hard to sustain themselves in the face o f
inherent features and weaknesses facing them. Abandonment of activ ity by some entrepreneurs midway
is one reason. Another reason for non viability of projects is willful  default by candidates. In some
cases, there is non-availa bility of certain raw ma terial and inadequte demand for the products/services
and lack of infrastrcutural facilities. 
  
3.7    The Committee recommends th at training programmes should be  conducted for successful setting
up of productive activities by the beneficiaries th rough training establishments of the banks and also
through institutes such as Rural Development Self Employment Trai ning Institutes (RUDSETIs) and
Syndicate Institute of Rural Entrep reneurship Development (SIRDs).  Sponsoring agen cies should also
extend escort services/infrastructural facilities to make the projects viable.

4.12 It is borne out by experience that the success rate is  higher when the applic ant possesses required
training on the vocation prior to starting the enterpri se. Necessary training inputs should be given to the
prospective applicants before sponsoring the a pplications. Besides, DIC and other governmental
agencies may also be associate for imparting trai ning at the pre-application stage. The modules fo r 
training need to be reviewed and revised periodically to suit the requirement of new entrepreneurs and in
keeping with the market scenario. 
  
4.13 The Committee finds that although at tempts were made to achieve quantitative targets in the case
of PMRY, no serious effort was made  to achieve qualitative targets. Entrepreneurs have to face many
hurdles like power connec tions, frequent inspections, lack of infrastructure, while embarking on an
enterprise. The scheme is not a smooth for a beginner. Moreover, th ere are other schemes like REGP
which offer more incentives/concessions/subsid
y to the entrepreneurs and prove to be more allurin g to

lower age limit requires to be increased to bring mo re mature youth to the scheme, the Committee feels.
                                                                                               (Para 4.6) 
         The Committee observes that though th e ceiling on project cost unde r PMRY has been increased
from Rs.l Lakh to Rs.2 Lakhs with effect from  1999-2000; for activities other than business, no 
perceptible increase in the amount of the average loan disbursed is  observed. This may indicate that
either there is a predominance of business activities in the cases sanctioned, or banks have taken a
routine target-oriented approach in  the implementation of the scheme with little care for the actual
requirement of funds for setting up micro-enterpris es. There is concern that  activities are being unde r 
financed which lead to their una vailability and their misuse ri ght from the very beginning. The
Committee, therefore, advise that Model Project Profiles should be prepar ed in every district on
successful activities and banks could release th e financing, according to  these model profiles.
                                                                                  (Para 4.7) 
         The Committee, therefore, observes th at permanent sales outlets should be set up at Block /
Taluk/District levels. The Government may provide infrastructure, including space and staff for running
such sales outlets.                                                            (Para 4.8) 
         The Committee finds that not enough has been done to popularize the scheme. The Committee
observes that- all possible measures should be taken to ensure adequate publicity to the scheme to create 
greater awareness in order to invite  applications from elig ible candidates in greater numbers. This will,
in turn, ensure a wider choice during selection of candidates. Fu rther, the Green Channel (Single
Window) system introduced at the dist rict level should be made more effective in assisting more and
more beneficiaries to come forwar d for starting micro-enterprises. 
                                                                                        (Para 4.9) 
         In order to attract more and more educated youth to the scheme, the Committee feels: 
.     Subsidy ceiling of Rs.7500 be raised to Rs.15,000 subject to a minimum of 15 per cent. 
.     The ceiling on income (Rs.40,000) may be enhanced to Rs.50,000 to Rs.60,OOO so as to
enlarge the selection zone. 
(Para 4.10)
         Frequent review meetings by DIC, al ong with supporting bankers to take stock of the assisted
projects, may go a long way in imp roving the working of the micro enterprises and enable the banks
borrowers to take corrective steps at the earliest stage wh erever required. This is  expected to improve
the success rate of the assisted projects.                                    (Para 4.11) 
         The Committee recommends that Distri cts recording better rec overy performance should be
targeted for better coverage under the scheme.                                                      (Para 4.14) 
         Central Government have laid empha sis on agro and village indus tries by creating a separate
Ministry of Agro and Rural Indust ries. To give a meani ngful impetus to Agro & Rural Industries, the
Committee recommends setting up of  Centre -State forum on A&RI where under the Officers of the 
Central Govt. would meet the Stat e Industry Deptt., District Industr ies Centre, industry associations,
entrepreneurs, and banks from time  to time to get feed back about  the credit flow, infrastructural
facilities, and other difficulties faced by the Agro and Rural Industries, and formulate possible solutions.
The Committee hope that the Centra l and State Government should jo in hands in bringing more and
more people under the ambit of the Agro and Rural Industries.

REPORT
 
1.Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited (HSCL) is an offshoot of the Construction Division of Steel Authority 
of India Ltd. ( SAIL). The company was incorporated in 1964 with the prime objective of creating in Public Sector an
organisation capable of-taking-up   the construction of  modern  Steel Plants in the country. HSCL has executed works
in Steel Plants right from inception till commissioning, viz, Bokaro Steel plant, Vizag Steel Plant, Salem Steel Plant and
was  associated  with the expansion and modernisation activities of Bhilai Steel Plant, Durgapur Steel Plant, IISCO
(Burnpur)  as  also Bhadravati Steel Plant.  With the decline  in traditional work-order , the company  diversified its
activities  in  other sectors like  power , coal, oil and  gas and also  infrastructural facilities like  roads/highways,
bridges, dams, underground-communication and transport system besides  industrial and  township  complexes
involving  high degree of planning, coordination and modern sophisticated techniques. The Company gained experience
in the areas like civil works of plant building, structural fabrication and erection in industrial plants, and erection of
Equipment in the Steel Plants. As SAIL expanded its activities, activities of HSCL also expanded.  Apart from activities
in SAIL, the company expanded its activities in other areas, like civil works for buildings, other than SAIL, Dam
Construction'. Bridge construction, coal handling plants, road construction, stadium complexes, school buildings and
industrial townships etc. The company also gained experience in planning & coordination in steel & non-steel sectors.
1.2       The authorized capital of the company has been raised from Rs.20.00 crore to Rs.150.00 crore on approval of 
Government of India through the financial restructuring-cum-financial assistance package sanctioned to the company. 
Similarly, the paid  up  capital  has also been increased from Rs.20.00 crore to rs.117.10 crore.
1.3       The Ministry of Steel  informed the Sub -Committee that  HSCL suffered   in 1970s primarily   due to two
reasons . The first factor was the sudden  increase in work force between 1970-79 from 4,100 to 26,537.  Of this,
Bokaro unit alone   accounted for 12,600.  This  was due to the  crisis created when a large number of public sector and
private  companies engaged by Bokaro Steel   failed and left their  work sites leaving behind  their workforce.  Due to
pressure, both from the Government and from the steel plants.  HSCL  had to take over these works along with the
workforce, in order to  complete the works within the   stipulated time.  The other major factor responsible for the
company's decline was the lack of   substantial activity in the  steel sector.   The works awarded to HSLCL by the steel
plants  after 1974 were  not adequate  to sustain the additional recurring liabilities, mainly due to increase wage bills on
account of statutory hikes including  revision of pay and increase in the number of workforce.  As a result of the above
factors,   the company began to incur continuous losses from 1978-79 onwards (except 1985-86) and  as on 31.3.1999
the accumulated loss stood at Rs.1383.28 crore.  Another  factor  which  also contributed to the downgrading of the 
company is the huge  loss suffered by HSCL on Libyan works, undertaken under  Government  of India  protocol,  due
to reasons beyond the control of the  company .
 
1.4       The Committee notes that the reasons as placed  by the Ministry of Steel, for the suffering of  HSCL.  The
Committee is of the  opinion  that  lack of vision for  human resource management and  lack of a concrete policy  led to
and sudden increase in work force in HSCL.  The Committee further  opines  that HSCL's present suffering is due to
error of judgment and some elements were beyond  the  control of   management   and Government due to prevailing 
circumstances, lack of managerial vision and manpower policy added to the woes  of HSCL.
