2.2.      The Committee, while taking note of the current financial performance of HSCL  expresses its concern over its
pathetic conditions,  and is of the view  that  HSCL  needs  improvement for  better financial   performance.  HSCL 
requires a  new vision, new managerial  will and effective strategy for the  continuance  of  its existence.
3.         FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE -CUM-RESTRUCTURING PACKAGE
3.1       With a view to bail out the company from its financial crisis, a comprehensive financial restructuring proposal
was approved by Government of India/CCEA in  9
th July, 1999.  The revival  package provided  several financial
assistance/exemptions  which, inter-alia, included :-
Conversion of plan loans  of Rs.97.10 crore as on 31.3.99 into equity
Grant of moratorium on repayment  of and interest holiday on all Government  of India    loans upto 31.3.99 for 10
years.
Waiver of interest accrued and outstanding on all GOI loans as on 31.3.99 amounting to around Rs.975.17 crore
Non-plan loan of  Rs.79.33 crore during 1999-2000  for payment of statutory dues with moratorium on repayment and
interest holiday for five years subject to a review at the end of  five years.
Exemption of corporate tax in 1999-2000 on  account of windfall profit due to waiver of interest on loans.
Continuance of Government  guarantee of Rs.92.00  crore, Rs12.00 crore  cash credit  and  Rs.80.00 crore bank
guarantee  facilities, with waiver of guarantee  commission of one per cent .
It is expected that HSCL will rationalise its manpower through VRS scheme and necessary funds for the same will be 
raised from banks.  The Government will provide guarantee and full interest subsidy  for raising loan of Rs.318.36
crore   during the  three  years  i.e. 1999 -2000 to 2001-02 for separating  2000 employees per year.
 
3.2       The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Government for approving the  financial restructuring
proposal.  Considering the  fact that resources are limited the  sanctioning    of revival  package  having financial
implication is a  considered decision of the Government.  Committee also appreciates the Ministry of Steel for its
consistent    efforts in persuading the Ministry of Finance for  giving   revival package  to  HSCL.   The  Committee
notes the provisions  of revival package for  HSCL.
4.         Implementation of status of revival package
4.1       As regards the status of  implementation of  financial-cum-assistance  restructuring  package, the  Sub-
Committee was  informed by  the Ministry of Steel that action has already  been taken on   point (i) to (iv).  In respect 
of the issue  regarding (v) exemption from payments of corporate tax on  account  profit   due to waiver of interest on
loan  has been taken  up with Secretary, Department of Revenue (Ministry of Finance)and (vi)  State Bank of India,
Indian Bank and Indian overseas Bank have disbursed  loan of Rs.209.82  crore, Rs.56.38  crore and  Rs.56.16 crore
respectively to HSCL  and (vii) around  7106 employees have been  separated.
4.2       The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of Steel has taken action  on all provisions contained in the 
revival package.  The Committee hopes that efforts  of the Ministry of Steel in  persuading   the Department of Revenue 
for exempt  of  corporate  tax for HSCL would have a positive impact on the financial performance of HSCL.  The
Committee further  hopes that  consequent upon the  separation of  7,106  employees and reduction in the wage bill, the

financial ratio of the company  would further improve.
4.3       Consequent upon the implementation of the revival package the accumulated loss of the company   came down
to  Rs.532 crore as on March' 2000. The Turnover of the company has fallen from a peak level of Rs.416 crore in 1996-
97 to Rs.238 crore in 2000-01. The loss for the year 2000-01 is expected to be around Rs.65 crore. Major reasons for the
fall in turnover is due to the fact that  the expected demand  has not taken place due to sluggishness in the Steel Sector
activities. The total turnover in Steel Sector has reduced from 70 pr cent  to 36 per cent.
4.4       The Committee understands that it is but natural that the accumulated loss of the company would come down
once the Government  grants waiver of interest Government loans, so far the same is a book-entry and it hardly has any
reflection on the actual financial performance  of the company.

5.2       The Committee observes that financial assistance-cum-restructuring package  as proposed by the Ministry of
Steel and so approved by the Government was not as  comprehensive so as to mitigate the accumulated loss and total 
liability of HSCL.  The company continues to rein in adverse financial scenario and disadvantages in  general because
implementation of the revival package would  respond  only  if approved  measures are  taken in time for total  and
comprehensive restructuring of the company.  HSCL  needs total  overhauling  and complete and comprehensive 
restructuring in one  go as partial  package and  delayed implementation  defeats   the whole  idea, approach and  action.
5.3       At present, the company has 5997 skilled technical and non-technical personnel on its roll.  The expenditure
towards salary  and wages in 2001-02 is estimated to be about Rs.63 crore against Rs.146.09 crore in 1998-99.  The
actual loss of Rs.172.55 crore in  2000-01 was expected to come down to Rs.133 crore in 2001-02.  The  company
cannot stand on its own with wage  and statutory dues accumulating  to around Rs.205 crore as on 1.2.02 .   A proposal
has been put up to the Finance Ministry  by the Administrative Ministry for favourable consideration.  It is a harsh fact
that with gradual reduction in margin due to fierce   competition in the  present   market economy situation, the
company can not sustain the salary burden of 6000 employees at the turnover level of Rs.275.00 crore.  In view of the
above, the  company proposes to obtain Government guarantee for a further loan of Rs.250.00 crore to separate another
5000 employees.  This would enable the company to manage with a manpower figure of around 1000 at an annual
expenditure of  about 12 crore towards salary and wages.
5.4       The Committee is of the view that once the comprehensive restructuring package is effectively implemented
HSCL  would acquire  sufficient   resilience   and synergy to work even against fierce competition.  The Committee
recommends that HSCL management should strive in this regard. 
5.5       The Sub-Committee wanted to know the reasons as to why, despite the implementation of Financial Assistance
cum Restructuring package as sought by the Ministry of Steel in tandem with HSCL management and as approved by
Government in July, 1999, the accumulated loss of HSCL stood at Rs. 532 crore as on March 2000, and the expected
loss for the year 2000-2001 was Rs.65 crore. The HSCL management stated that the loss of Rs. 532 crore as on
31.3.2000 and another Rs.65 crore as on 31.3.2001 is mainly attributable to the insurmountable factors which include:-
Turnover could not be raised to the level required as per the restructuring proposal; 
Lack of work orders from Steel Plants due to continuing decline in Steel Industry;
Recession in construction Industry;
 Delay in getting loan for VRS;
Under-utilisation and idling of manpower and resources at Steel Plants.
5.6       The Committee is constrained to express its concern over the fact that financial assistance given for 
restructuring  package  could not be implemented in the  expected   manner and the outcome    thereof   is not  as
expected.   The Committee notes the  reasons  for failure of revival package,  although it is not fully envisaged with the
reasons for  failure  of  revival package  as advocated by the Ministry of Steel.  For the  revival of the company, HSCL
management has to procure work order despite ups and downs in Steel Industry and HSCL management  should not
face  much  difficulties as Government   is giving  due importance  to the construction sector.  The committee  is  of the 
view that optimum utilisation   of manpower and  resources at the  disposal of company is the responsibility of HSCL
management.

6.         Reasons for  partial failure of  Financial Assistance -cum- restructuring package
6.1       The Ministry of Steel  informed the Sub-Committee that  the Restructuring package could not yield the desired
result and advocated  the under mentioned detailed reasons for the partial failure of the restructuring package: -
Delay of about eleven months by commercial bank in the sanction and disbursement of the first phase of loan for VRS
amounting to Rs.210 Crore, forcing the company to carry idle wages.   In the revival plan it was envisaged to separate
2000 employees per year beginning with 1999-2000 but the loan amount was only disbursed in June, 2000 due to late
sanction. As a result, the actual separation under VRS could be effected only thereafter.
The projections in terms of profit & loss as contained in revival package were made with regard to the prevailing market
condition at that time. Since then, the market condition have shown a down turn and even big companies like SAIL have
been incurring losses.
Most of the works undertaken by HSCL are being sub-contracted primarily because of the age profile of its employee
and also the difficulties faced in their redeployment on work sites which are scattered all over India. Most of the receipts
of HSCL are passed on as payments to Sub contractor, thereby leaving a very marginal amount for utilisation towards
meeting overheads like salaries /wages etc.
HSCL has diversified its operations in the non-steel sector as jobs from the steel sector had virtually not coming up. The
margins in the diversified areas are very low, and this  means that HSCL would continue to incur losses.
HSCL has been replacing its  obsolete equipment in order to execute the works efficiently at site. During the years
1999-2000 and 2000-2001 equipments for an amount of Rs.35 lakhs and Rs.2.38 crore respectively were purchased.
Further in 2000-01, order for one excavator cum loader for Bokaro Unit for Rs.71 lakhs have been placed during the
year.
 
6.2       The Committee,  while taking note of the detailed reasons for partial failure of  Financial Assistance
restructuring package, is constrained to express its concern.  The Committee  is of the view that HSCL  management
could  have well  managed and controlled  the problems being faced by  HSCL. The Committee views that replacement
of obsolete equipment in HSCL  should have  positive  impact on the operational efficiency of company  rather than  
deterring   the implementation of revival package.  Moreover, HSCL management should chalk out  a strategy for better
margin of profit. The Committee opines that HSCL management while implementing VRS should keep in mind the age 
profile in the company  so as to retain capable and   efficient  the work  force  to undertake  the job.

7.0       HSCL becoming a sub-contracting company
7.1       Replying to the Sub-Committee's query regarding HSCL becoming a sub-contracting company from a
construction company resultant and the possibility of sustenance of company under changed circumstances, the
management stated that the company has to resort to sub-contracting to augment the order book position in the face of
stiff competition from the construction sector.  It also has to offset difficulties like severe cash crunch to deposit
EMD/SD etc. and funds for procurement of raw materials and other inputs.  Sub-contracting is also necessitated due to
the fact that shifting manpower and other resources from steel plants to short duration projects is not only expensive but
also invites social and other local resistance.  Moreover, the age profile of the employees is also a deterrent in carrying
out the works departmentally.  Low margins due to competition and inadequacy of related expertise and skill are also
strong factors compelling adoption of sub-contracting system.
7.2       The HSCL management clarified that the company has neither become, nor has any plans to become out and out
a sub-contracting company.  It has a rich team of experienced engineers, workers, technicians and a strong fleet of
construction equipments, as its backbone.  In most cases, the company executes the jobs giving maximum possible
departmental inputs combining with it the strengths of the sub-contractors.  The extent of departmental inputs varies
according to location and nature of work.  As of now, the downward trend has been witnessed and therefore, given the
difficult circumstances enveloping the Company, the process is expected to remain the way it is for some more time. 
Till then, the primary concern of the company would be the payment of salary and wages to its employees as well as
liquidation of all other liabilities.  Once out of this predicament, the company's performance is bound to increase
through better utilization of equipments, supervision, design, procurement and monitoring besides direct execution as
much as possible.  Under the changed scenario and market economy, the system of sub-contracting (with maximum
departmental inputs) cannot be altogether discarded.  The execution arrangement, as elaborated above, is practical and
sustainable, if the liabilities reduce. 
7.3       The Committee understands the  compelling  circumstances under which HSCL has to adopt the system of  sub-
contracting  business pattern but   it is also an open secret that sub-contracting   gives low margin for HSCL than if the
work done by the company itself.  The  Committee  is of the view  that VRS  offer  by HSCL  to its employees would
take care of keeping with itself the workforce consisting of  productive age profile and  willing to undertake
work/assignment from whatever concern its coming.  The Committee feels that  direct undertaking of work by HSCL
staff would give larger margin to HSCL and thus opening scope for profitability of HSCL, therefore, it would be better
that the  system of sub-Contracting  is replaced by direct involvement of HSCL employees,  sooner than later.

9.3       Since inception and over the years, majority of the resources and infrastructural facilities had been built up in
PSU Steel Plants.  However, the continuing decline in the steel sector during the last several years has cast a shadow of
uncertainty on the question of sustenance of the company.  During the earlier years, steel plant projects were being
awarded to HSCL on nomination basis.  As a time progressed, the special status of the company with SAIL Steel Plants,
for the construction which the company was framed, got eroded. With the introduction of "Internal award Procedure" by
which  HSCL are exposed to unreasonable competition.  This makes bagging jobs in steel plants further more difficult. 
Inspite of the scope of jobs of AMR, operation maintenance, waste disposal, slag processing and scrap recovery in the
steel plants, HSCL's role has been marginalized .
 
9.4       The Committee is of the view that  HSCL deserves a better deal in SAIL with Government  mediation, therefore
the Committee recommends  that  all the project as well as  AMR and operational jobs, within the execution capacity of
HSCL, should be offered on nomination on priority basis to HSCL.  This would enable the company to utilise its
infrastructure, set up over the years at SAIL plants and  meet  the expenses of the company. Award procedure  of SAIL  
should be relaxed suitably   for preferential treatment   to HSCL.  The  company may have  long term
arrangement/understanding   with SAIL on the basis of quantum of job  assured for award.   The Committee further
recommends  that a certain portion of the construction jobs in the Infrastructural sector be assigned to HSCL  on 
nomination basis,  at   least during  the initial  years of planned revival.  Purchase preference  to PSUs should be  strictly
adhered to.  Presently the PSUs/Government Department   are not  uniformly following the system.  The dismal balance
sheets of the company, for several years now, have made customers apprehensive in pre-qualifying HSCL for their
prospects.  Judging  the merit  of the situation, respective Administrative Ministries may issue necessary directives not
to disqualify HSCL for quoting, based on the financial performance of last  few years. HSCL should be granted
relaxation in registration formalities with Government   Departments for  taking up work. HSCL should be exempted
from submitting EMD for taking up work with Government departments and PSUs. HSCL's  experience in construction 
of roads in the integrated steel plants should be  considered   as qualifying criterion for High way work and matter may
be taken up  with the  Ministry of Road Transport and  Highways.

12.0     Rationalisation of   Manpower
12.1     The Sub -Committee was informed that the Company started with a modest strength of 95 employees in 1964-65
and thereafter increased to 26,537 in 1978-79. Most of the surplus manpower of SAIL was inducted into this Company.
The strength thereafter started reducing and came to a level of 11,654 in 1999-2000. The strength has further been
reduced to 7302 in 2000-01, with many people opting to separate under the VR Scheme. In 2001-02 further separation
has taken place and the strength as on 01.07.2001 is 6318. In contrast to the Turnover, the manpower which has
experience in Steel Sector only is concentrated in the Steel Plant Units of the Company and accounts for 81% (5132 out
of 6318). The Head Office of the Company at Kolkata has 327 employees, and is dependent on income generated by
productive units. The details of pending wages and salaries as on 30

14.0     Second Revival Package for HSCL
14.1     The Sub-Committee understands that the plans under the revival package sanctioned in July'1999 did not
materialise due to sluggish activities in Steel Sector, which is the expertise of the Company. The turnover in the Non-
Steel Sector do not contribute sufficient margins to the company as the work has to be further sub-contracted due to lack
of expertise with the Company. The margin available to the Company in this Sector is just sufficient to take care of the
small manpower stationed in these units, who perform only supervision of the work. On account of the circumstances in
which the Company is placed, there was an urgent need to downsize the manpower strength of the Company to a level
of 1200 numbers. This meant that another 4800- 5000 employees had to be provided with VR. The Company will
require an assistance of Rs.250 crore for this purpose. The company is experiencing a peculiar situation where it has to
face the agitation of employees due to non-payment of salaries and wages. Therefore, in continuation of earlier requests
made to Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Steel has again requested Ministry of Finance to consider the following reliefs

COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
 
The Committee notes that the reasons as placed  by the Ministry of Steel, for the suffering of  HSCL.  The Committee is
of the  opinion  that  lack of vision for  human resource management and  lack of a concrete policy  led to and sudden
increase in work force in HSCL.  The Committee further  opines  that HSCL's present suffering is due to error of
judgment and some elements were beyond  the  control of   management   and Government due to prevailing 
circumstances, lack of managerial vision and manpower policy added to the woes  of HSCL.
 
( Para 1.4)
 
The Committee, while taking note of the current financial performance of HSCL  expresses its concern over its pathetic
conditions,  and is of the view  that  HSCL  needs  improvement for  better financial   performance.  HSCL  requires a 
new vision, new managerial  will and effective strategy for the  continuance  of  its existence.
( Para : 2.2)
 
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Government for approving the  financial restructuring proposal. 
Considering the  fact that resources are limited the  sanctioning    of revival  package  having financial implication is a 
considered decision of the Government.  Committee also appreciates the Ministry of Steel for its consistent    efforts in
persuading the Ministry of Finance for  giving   revival package  to  HSCL.   The  Committee notes the provisions  of
revival package for  HSCL.
 ( Para 3.2)
 
Implementation status
 The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of Steel has taken action  on all provisions contained in the  revival
package.  The Committee hopes that efforts  of the Ministry of Steel in  persuading   the Department of Revenue  for
exempt  of  corporate  tax for HSCL would have a positive impact on the financial performance of HSCL.  The
Committee further  hopes that  consequent upon the  separation of  7,106  employees and reduction in the wage bill, the
financial ratio of the company  would further improve.
( Para 4.2)
 
The Committee understands that it is but natural that the accumulated loss of the company would come down once the
Government  grants waiver of interest Government loans, so far the same is a book-entry and it hardly has any reflection
on the actual financial performance  of the company.
 ( Para 4.4)
 
The Committee is happy to note the  savings on the specified  overheads due to  measures undertaken by HSCL 
management to rationalise administrative expenditure.   The Committee hopes that the efforts to rationalise
administrative  expenditure would continue.
( Para 4.8)
 
The Committee observes that financial assistance-cum-restructuring package  as proposed by the Ministry of Steel and
so approved by the Government was not as  comprehensive so as to mitigate the accumulated loss and total  liability of
HSCL.  The company continues to rein in adverse financial scenario and disadvantages in  general because
implementation of the revival package would  respond  only  if approved  measures are  taken in time for total  and
comprehensive restructuring of the company.  HSCL  needs total  overhauling  and complete and comprehensive 
restructuring in one  go as partial  package and  delayed implementation  defeats   the whole  idea, approach and  action.
 ( Para 5.2)
 
The Committee is of the view that once the comprehensive restructuring package is effectively implemented HSCL 
would   acquire  sufficient  resilience   and synergy to work even against fierce competition.  The Committee
recommends that HSCL management should strive in this regard. 
 
( Para 5.4)

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorized
by the Committee, hereby present this Eighty-sixth Report on Performance Review of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation
Ltd. (MSTC).
2.      The Committee on Industry constituted Sub-Committee for Ministry of Steel to examine the Performance Review
of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd. (MSTC). The Sub-Committee visited Kolkata on 17th to 20th July, 2001 and
interacted with the Management of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd. (MSTC).
3.      The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 14th March, 2002 heard the Secretary, Ministry of Steel and official of
MSTC. The Report has been prepared on the basis of on the spot-study by the Sub-Committee-I for the Ministry of Steel
of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry and interaction with the Secretary, Ministry of
Steel and officials of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd. (MSTC).

REPORT
         MSTC Limited (formerly known as Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd.) was incorporated as a Public Limited
Company under the Companies Act, 1956 on 9 th September, 1964. The status of the company underwent change in
February, 1974 to that of a subsidiary of Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL). In the year 1982-83, the corporation
was converted into a Government of India Company transferring the shares of SAIL to the President of India. It was the
Canalizing Agency for import of Carbon Steel Melting’s Scrap, Sponge Iron, Hot Briquette Iron and re-rolled scrap till
February, 1992. It was also the canalizing agency for import of ships for breaking till August, 1991. Presently, the
company undertakes disposal of ferrous and non-ferrous scrap arising from integrated steel plants under SAIL/RINL
etc. and disposal of scrap, surplus stores, etc. from other public sector undertakings and Government departments and
also import of ferrous and non-ferrous scarp, coke, finished steel and petroleum products. MSTC is the only Central
PSU under the Ministry of Steel to issue bonus shares.

3.0    MAIN ACTIVITIES
3.1    The Sub-Committee was informed that MSTC has manifold activities which include (i) import (ii) export (iii)
Supply of raw material to actual users (iv) supply of materials as parallel marketer and (v) Scrap/Obsolete/Surplus
disposal on behalf of plant organizations. The company has four wings for its activities namely 
(i) International marketing (ii) Domestic Marketing (iii) Management services and (iv) Finance/HRD. Head office
located at Kolkata, the company has four regional offices at Kolkata, New Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and branch offices
located at Bangalore, Vizag, Bhopal, Vadodara, Rourkela, Bokaro, Surat and New Mangalore. The Company has two
major spheres of activities i.e. Domestic Marketing and International Marketing.
3.1.0Domestic Marketing
3.1.1While a subsidiary of SAIL, MSTC started acting as selling agent of IISCO, RSP, BSL for disposal of their scrap
arising and thus started its Domestic Marketing activity. In 1993, after being de-linked from SAIL, MSTC extended its
activities to other PSUs, Government departments etc. The objective of DM is to maximize availability of indigenous
scrap by including the principals to mobilize and sell their scrap arisings/rejected/ condemned/surplus/spares/capital
equipments etc. so that the same can be recycled. The disposal action is taken in such a manner that the maximum
possible price is realized in totally transparent manner by selling the materials through open tenders, public auctions etc.
This activity was given importance only after decanalisation. The annual volume of business that was Rs.210 crore in
1992-93 reached at Rs.600 crore in 2000-2001.

         (iv)    Projects for investment with marketing/procurement rights identified investment made in KISCO,
investment in SJK under consideration; and
         (v)    Imports resumed with widened basket in 1997-1998, Rs.82 crore in 1998-1999, Rs.285 crore in 2000-2001.
The import was expected to cross Rs.300 crore mark in 2001-2002.
5.4    The Committee observes that the activities of MSTC has undergone noticeable change with the changing scenario
of steel industry, change in the Government policy i.e. from canalisation to the de-canalisation of imports and in
accordance with market perspective. The MSTC, which acted earlier as a selling agency for SAIL in respect of their
melting scrap arising, has started to carry the business with the other Government PSU when SAIL started selling
melting scrap directly. MSTC went, rightly, for strengthening of direct-marketing when the Government policy stood
for de-canalisation of import. Although the performance of MSTC suffered to some extent during these phase of
tumultuous change, however, it is the managerial skill which led MSTC for changing business gear and it is the
concerted employees’ commitment which has got a bearing on the physical and financial performance of the company.
The Committee acclaims the performance of MSTC and hopes that an all out effort on the part of the management and
employees would continue to improve the financial performance of the company to a new zenith.

13.0  PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY MSTC
13.1  Sale Tax Structure
         13.1.1Pointing out the lacuna in the Sales Tax Structure, MSTC management informed the Sub-Committee that a
provision in the recent budget allows the State Governments to impose central sales tax on declared goods at
a rate higher than 4% and also empower them to impose multi-point tax. If the States use these powers, this
will make the job of trading extremely difficult, while a uniform system of VAT will be ideal, uniformity in
the matter of sales tax i.e. one point tax whether CST of LST, shall go a long way in helping traders
particularly the trading houses carrying on trading in more than State in the country.
         13.1.2The Committee understands the problems being faced by trading organisation due to prevalence of multi-
point tax-structure. Therefore, the Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Steel should take up the
matter with the Ministry of Finance and State Governments. The proposal of uniform system of VAT and
one-point tax may be examined and if found feasible, steps in this regard may be taken at the earliest.
13.2.0         Requirement of submission of end-use certificates for imported melting scrap
         13.2.1As regards the provision for requirement of submission of end-use certificates for imported melting scrap,
the Sub-Committee was informed that on import of melting scrap, the end use certificate is required to be
submitted by the actual users within six months. The main reason for this is to eliminate the misuse of scrap
imported for melting, being used for re-rolling. As a trader, MSTC sells such melting scrap to actual users
only but have to depend on the actual users to submit end-use certificate issues by Central Excise
Department after the melting scrap sold to them has been consumed. In the event of actual users’ failure to
obtain end-use certificate from the Central Excise, MSTC has to pay higher rate of duty on the material
imported. This requirement should, therefore, be withdrawn.
         13.2.2The Committee is of the opinion that the Government should evolve alternative effective mechanism to
check the misuse of scrap imported for melting, being used for re-rolling.

for imported melting scrap. If the Ministry of Finance remains unmoved the provision may be made for

13.3.0         Requirement of availing services of trans-chart for hiring ships for imports
         13.3.1The Sub-Committee was apprised that as per existing procedure, PSUs are to import materials on FOB basis
and shipping arrangement is to be made through Ministry of Shipping (Trans-chart). In case Trans-chart is
unable to arrange shipping, necessary waiver is to be obtained by PSUs form Trans-chart before finalising
contract on C&F basis. Import contracts by MSTC are finalised at very short notice. Since it is seldom
possible to fix a vessel through Trans-chart in the short time available, MSTC is compelled to continue
imports on C&F basis for shipload cargoes. It would be in the fitness of things, especially in the liberalized
scenario, to do away with the requirement of approaching Trans-chart.
         13.3.2The Committee understands that since MSTC finalise import contracts usually in a short span of time so it is
difficult on the part of MSTC to fix a vessel through Ministry of Shipping (Trans-chart). Therefore, the
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Steel should take the matter with the Ministry of Shipping and
help MSTC out by doing away with the requirement of approaching Trans-chart.
13.3.3The Committee notes that MSTC is one of the few Government companies which has successfully withstood
the impact of post liberalization era by changing its strategy according to the need of the situation. The
Committee hopes that the Ministry of Steel would extend a helping hand to the company in sorting out its
problems so that it can fetch a better price from the prospective buyers.

production and is a trading company, however, steps taken towards modernisation and restructuring would help in
improving its operational efficiency and managerial effectiveness. The Committee is of the firm view that
modernisation in the process and system of working of the company would have a definite bearingon the physical and
financial performance of the company. The steps taken to modernise and restructure the communication and expansion
in the domestic as well as international marketing division would yield positive fruits in the functioning of the company,
the Committee feels so. The Committee further feels that the efforts made on the part of MSTC management for
enlarging import basket would add to the profitability of the
company.                                                                                                                            (Para : 4.7)
 
PERFORMANCE OF MSTC
         The Committee observes that the activities of MSTC has undergone noticeable change with the changing scenario
of steel industry, change in the Government policy i.e. from canalisation to the de-canalisation of imports and in
accordance with market perspective. The MSTC, which acted earlier as a selling agency for SAIL in respect of their
melting scrap arising, has started to carry the business with the other Government PSU when SAIL started selling
melting scrap directly. MSTC went, rightly, for strengthening of Direct-marketing when the Government policy stood
for de-canalisation of import. Although the performance of MSTC suffered to some extent during these phase of
tumultuous change, however, it is the managerial skill which led MSTC for changing business gear and it is the
concerted employees’ commitment which has got a bearing on the physical and financial performance of the company.
The Committee acclaims the performance of MSTC and hope that an all out effort on the part of the management and
employees would continue to improve the financial performance of the company to a new
zenith.                                                                                           (Para : 5.4)
MoU RATING OF THE COMPANY
         The Committee observes that MSTC is coming out of the woods and doing excellent performance as is reflected
from MoU rating as awarded by Department of Public Enterprises after taking into various parameters of performance
into consideration. The Committee wishes its best for MSTC for continuing its excellent performance in forthcoming
years and hopes that MoU system would always act as a catalyst to improve the physical and financial performance of
the company.         (Para : 6.3)
PROJECTS / SCHEMES / DIVERSIFICATION PLANS AND FINANCIAL REQUIREMENTS
         The Committee is pleased to note that MSTC management is giving due consideration to diversification plans and
entering into joint ventures. The Committee is of the opinion that in the prevailing market Competitive era,
diversification of activities’ and projection of business through partnership/joint ventures has almost become a corporate
culture. MSTC is moving in the right direction by adopting the canons of modern days business practice. The
Committee hopes that MSTC, whether in existing structure i.e. as a PSU or in the post divested phase would continue its
efforts towards adopting the prevailing precepts and strategy in accordance with changing market scenario.                     
(Para : 7.4)
         The Committee notes that financial provision for completion of plans/schemes of MSTC and at the same time
hopes that all the plans and schemes would be completed without time and cost overrun.                (Para : 7.5)
OUTSTANDING ISSUES BETWEEN MSTC AND M/S HARSCO. CORPORATION, INC. USA AND ISSUE OF
DISINVESTMENT
         The Committee observes that all no-going disputes between MSTC and its partner M/s Harsco Corporation Inc.
USA should be resolved with the good offices of Ministry of Steel and SBI caps should evaluate the value of shares of
FSNL to facilitate the negotiation process at the earliest. So far as the disinvestment of 100 per cent Government
shareholdings in MSTC through a strategic sale in concerned the committee desires that the Department of
Disinvestment may, in line with decision taken in regard to disinvestment of NALCO and MOIL, consider to give
MSTC employees/an opportunity to purchase atleast 5 per cent share in MSTC as a measure to allay fears among
employees and generate a sense of organisational belongingness and commitment among
employees.                                          (Para : 8.6)
INTERIM TURN AROUND PLAN

diversification of imported basket has a positive bearing on the performance of MSTC and hopes that introduction on e-
auction for domestic marketing division would go a long way in improving further the physical and financial
performance of the company.           (Para : 9.2)
PROCUREMENT OF WORK ORDER FROM SAIL, RINL AND RAILWAYS
         The Committee recommends that MSTC management should strive its best to procure workorder from SAIL,
RINL and Railways. The Committee desires that MSTC management should also approach steels units in private sector
for work-order. The Committee hopes that introduction of E-auction portal by MSTC management would help MSTC to
procure workorder from all around.                                                                                                (Para : 10.6)
         The Committee is of the firm view that the concept of inter-PSUs co-operation should be advocated by the
Ministry of Steel to lend a helping hand to other PSUs in the areas of mutual interest. In this regard the Ministry of Steel
may act promptly as a facilitator and help MSTC in the procurement of work-order from SAIL and RINL.(Para : 10.7)
         The Committee further recommends that MSTC management and the Ministry of Steel would continue to take up
follow-up action with the Ministry of Railways (Railway Board) on continuous and regular basis for procurement of
work-order. The Committee desires that the Railway Board should give due consideration to the request of MSTC
management by giving preference to MSTC.                                                                                          (Para : 10.8)
         The Committee desires that the Ministry of Steel in its Action Taken Note of the present Report would furnish the
details of efforts made by Ministry of Steel as facilitator to MSTC in procuring the work-order from SAIL, RINL and
Railways alongwith the quantum of work-order so received.                                               (Para : 10.9)
HUMAN RESOURCES MANAGEMENT OF MSTC
         The Committee notes that there is no surplus manpower in MSTC at the moment and MSTC is managing in its
activities with a total manpower of 280. The Committee is pleased to note that MSTC management is adopting the
strategy of redeployment of manpower in order to have optimum utilisation of manpower. The Committee hopes that
MSTC is adhering to the principle of right man at right place at right time which would certainly help in improving the
performance of the company. The Committee also expects that MSTC management would examine the labour
productivity in term of turnover/Sales/profit and in human resource as per requirement.                                          (Para :
11.2)
SWOT ANALYSIS OF MSTC
         The Committee observes that MSTC management has given due importance to the significance of SWOT-analysis
in the general working of the company. The Committee appreciates MSTC management for adhering to the basic
principles and practice of management. The efforts of re-defining of SWOT-analysis on the part of MSTC management
to a praiseworthy step and the Committee hopes that MSTC management would continue to reorient its SWOT-analysis
on per changing industrial and economic scenario and chalk out its further strategy as per the commends of outcome of
SWOT-analysis.                                                                                                                            (Para : 12.3)
         The Committee is of the opinion that MSTC management should take advantage of its strength as the company has
minimal fixed overheads expenditure due to optimum manpower with expertise from SAIL, equipped with modern
telecommunication and computer. The Committee is pleased to note that MSTC has  good track record for executing
impacts contracts due to its goodwill in the domestic and international market. Banking upon its company,
goodwill/track-record, MSTC management should make efforts to enhance its market share in domestic as well as
international market.         (Para : 12.4)
         The Committee opines that with the induction of liberalisation policy bureaucratic procedures and regulation has
been done away with. However, MSTC management in tandem with the Ministry of Steel should point out in the ATN
of the present Report the bureaucratic hurdles and Government control having adverse imports on the marketing
capacity of MSTC. The Committee is of the opinion that MSTC management should have a re-look on the areas of
weakness in the SWOT analysis and should take adequate steps for overcoming its weaknesses i.e. induction of latest
technological developments, streamlining of the main activities positioning of right man at right place in right time,
redrafting of corporate goal in the internal market etc.                                                                                            (Para :
12.5)
         The Committee recommends that MSTC management would explore ways and means to capitalise on
opportunities for better financial performance of the Company and it is being hoped that the Ministry of Steel would
extend all possible help to MSTC in this regard. MSTC management may explore the possibilities of MSTC entering
into domestic/international joint venture strategic alliance, explore new governess for activities of the company and
consequent changes in the object clearance of the company in order to infect synergy in the overall working of the
company.  (Para : 12.6)
         The Committee further recommends that MSTC management should chalk out strategy for getting rid of threats

Sale Tax Structure
         The Committee understands the problems being faced by trading organisation due to prevalence of multi-point
tax-structure. Therefore, the Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Steel should take up the matter with the

REQUIREMENT OF SUBMISSION OF END-USE CERTIFICATES FOR IMPORTED MELTING SCRAP
         The Committee is of the opinion that the Government should evolve alternative effective mechanism to check the
misuse of scrap imported for melting, being used for re-rolling.                                         (Para : 13.2.2)
         The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Steel should approach the Ministry of Finance (Department of
Excise) for withdrawing the provision for requirement of submission of end-users certificate for imported melting scrap.
If the Ministry of Finance remains unmoved the provision may be made for early submission of end use certificate by
the actual users’ and in case of default, a certain the penalty may be imposed on the defaulter. The Committee is of the
view that MSTC should not be subjected to imposition of higher rate of duty for the default committed by the actual
users.         (Para : 13.2.3)
REQUIREMENT OF AVAILING SERVICES OF TRANS-CHART FOR HIRING SHIPS FOR IMPORTS
         The Committee understands that since MSTC finalise import contracts usually in a short span of time so it is
difficult on the part of MSTC to fix a vessel through Ministry of Shipping (Transchart). Therefore, the Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Steel should take the matter with the Ministry of Shipping and help MSTC out by
doing away with the requirement of approaching Transchart.                                                                           (Para :
13.3.2)
         The Committee notes that MSTC is of one of the few Government, companies which has successfully withstood
the impact of port liberalization era by changing its strategy according to the need of the situation. The Committee
hopes that the Ministry of Steel would extend a helping hand to the company in sorting out its problems so that it can
fetch a better price from the prospective buyers.                                                                                           (Para : 13.3.3)

Report
            The Refractory Industry in India is more than century old and the growth of this industry is closely inter-linked with the
development and growth of steel industry as more than 75 per cent of the total refractories produced in the country are consumed by
steel industries. Refractories contribute around 5 per cent   towards the total cost of steel making.  Under the changing scenario of
globalisation and liberalization, steel makers are facing stiff competition in the market, therefore, Steel Industry is  left with no  other
alternative than to produce the best  quality at the least cost.  The Steel Industry has started to demand  superior grade refractories
required for blast furnace, secondary refining and continuous casting units of steel industries which has posed challenges to the
refractory industry.  The emphasis by the industry in the recent years has been towards import substitution and production of special
items like magnesia carbon, slide gate refractories. 
1.1       Bharat Refractories Limited (BRL) was originally incorporated as a subsidiary company of Bokaro Steel Ltd. as the
production unit of (BHRP) which was earlier acquired by Government of India in 1972 and placed under the management of Bokaro
Steel Limited. Consequent upon restructuring of the Public Sector and steel industries on 1
st May 1978, Ranchi Road Refractories
Plant (RRRPL) at Ramgarh, which was under the control of erstwhile Hindustan Steel Limited and Bhilai Refractories Plant was also
transferred to BRL.  India Firebricks and Insulation Co. (IFICO) which was taken over by Steel Authority of India Ltd., with effect
from December, 1976, was also transferred as a subsidiary of BRL with effect from the date of restructurings.  At present, Bharat
Refractories Ltd (BRL) has four units, namely;
(a)    Bhandaridah Refractories Plant, Bhandaridah;
(b)   Ranchi Road Refractories Plant, Ramgarh;
(c)    Bhilai Refractories plant at Bhilai; and
(d)   IFICO Refractories Plant at Ramgarh.
1.2 The company is engaged in the manufacture and supply of various kinds of refractories not only to the integrated steel plants, but
also to the mini and medium steel plants.
1.3       The Committee notes the stages involved in the   formation of Bharat Refractories Ltd.  (BRL)  and hopes   that BRL
management would leave no stone unturned in assessing the   strength of all the four units of BRL and chalk out a short and long
term strategic course of action for early turnaround of company as a whole.  The Committee recommends that BRL management
work to ensure that all four units of BRL are making efforts towards the common mission for achieving common organizational goal
and are contributing to the physical and financial performance of the company.  None of them should    prove a burden on the
company.
2.0
              Capital Structure

recommends that the BRL management and the Ministry of  Steel  should examine  and assess the capital structure of BRL, from
time to time, and suggest  measures  for capital restructuring ,in such a way, that BRL  achieves the break -even point and economy
of  scales ensuring maximum   Return on Investment (ROI).
 
 
3.0       Sickness of BRL and IFICO.
3.1       The Sub-Committee was informed  that  BRL and  India Fire Bricks  and Insulation Company  (IFICO)  were sick due to
under mentioned  reasons  and came under the purview  of Sick Industrial  Companies (Special Provision) Act,  1985 and was
referred to BIFR in 1992:-
 
(a)
         Obsolescence of machinery technological indiscipline and underutilization of capacity.
(b)         Managerial inefficiency and low  man-power   utilization.
(c)         Shortage of working capital  resulting into delay  in the procurement  of raw-material ..
(d)         Erratic power supply.
(e)         Changing   demand pattern of  refractories  etc.
3.2.      The Committee notes the reasons for BRL  and IFICO  becoming sick and coming under the purview of BIFR in  1992.  The
Committee observes that due attention for  revival of BRL was not considered at the appropriate time  and that  is the reason why
BRL continued  to make losses year  after year.  What  other result might be expected, from a loss making company which continued
to operate with  obsolescent machinery;    under utilisation  of  installed capacity;     low labour- productivity and shortage of capital ,
than falling  in the  net of BIFR.  BRL missed the ( the first  opportunity for revival), the Committee concludes.
4.0       IDBI's Revival Scheme
4.1       IDBI was appointed  the  operating agency to formulate revival scheme which was  approved by BIFR in January, 1997.  The
revival package consisted of financial relief granted by Government of India, which are enumerated a below:
i
                Waiver of interest per cent  on loans amounting to Rs.61.64 crore;
ii               Conversion of 50 per cent  plan loan (Rs.39.76) into equity and the remaining 50 per cent  of loan R.39.76 crore) into
fresh loan bearing interest @ 12 per cent  p.a. with interest holiday for 3 years, and moratorium on loan repayment for 4
years;
iii             Conversion of non-plan loan amounting to Rs. 12.05   crore into 7 per cent  non-cumulative preference shares
redeemable in ten years; and

3.                 As all units except BRP were sick at the time of takeover, Amalgamation and modernisation required substantial

4.

received by the company is   carrying   interest @ 15 per cent p.a. with penal interest of 2.75 per cent
4.4       The Committee  observes  that since IDBI's revival package had  no cash assistance to BRL as working capital  on the
assumption that with its revised capital base and net worth position,  BRL   would be in  a position to raise working capital and

chances of increasing its production as well as improving its product  mix  for better   sales realisation . The Committee understands
that it is because of the slow down in the steel industry .The demand for refractories had not been of the level expected. It is but
natural that, in the above scenario, the company was unable to generate internal resources so as to meet its plan and non-plan
expenditure.  BRL ended 1997-98 with a cash loss of Rs.14.33 crore and   the same adverse trend persisted during   1998-99.
4.5       The Committee understands that the general recession in steel industry in addition to BRL’s inherent problems i.e. under
utilisation of installed capacity, interruption in power supply, problems in the procurement of raw-material due to lack of working
capital followed by non -implementation of IDBI's   revival scheme led to the continued dwindling in physical and financial
performance of the company.
5.0       Second Revival Package for BRL
5.1       The management explained that   the Continued cash loss incurred by BRL, capital liquidity position, huge accumulation of
outstanding dues coupled with resentment of workers due to non-revision of wages had severely affected production and sale
realisation.  Due to paucity of funds and inadequate assistance from Government, most of the plant and machinery outlived their
effective life and required immediate replacement.  Taking into consideration all these factors the Ministry of steel formulated the
second revival package for BRL. This revival package included: -
i
                Grant of non-plan   loan Rs.400 crore for meeting revised wage bill during 1998-99,
ii               Grant of non--plan interest   free loan of Rs.16.00 crore during 1998-99 for meeting the working capital interest
holiday on existing loan as on 31.3.99 till 2007-2008;
iii             Moratorium on loan repaying for existing loans for another four years i.e. till 2003-2004;
iv             and Government of India  guarantee for  enhancing the  working capital limit  to Rs.24.00 crore. 
5.2       The second revisal package   for BRL was approved by the CCEA in its meeting held on 21.1.99.  Necessary non-plan
provision of Rs.20.50 crore was made   in RE 1998-99.
5.3       Contrary to all hopes the Second revival packages for BRL failed because of the following inherent problems of the company
were not attended to: -
i                Low labour productivity due to excess manpower
ii               High cost of production due to high operating cost and increase in the price of input but decline in the price of
refractory items.
iii             Under utilisation of production capacity due to obsolete machinery, inadequate working capital and low work orders
from steel industry due to decline in demand of conventional refractory items.
iv      Continued monthly loss as a result- of quoting selling price at contribution margin by the company due to stiff
competition.

7.0       Problems being faced by Refectories industry 
7.1       The Sub-Committee was given an understanding that the growth of Refractory Industry is closely inter-linked with the
development and growth of steel industry as more than 75 per cent of the total refractories produced in the country are consumed by
steel industries while 15 per cent are used by Cement & Glass Industries and rest goes for Non-ferrous metal and petrol-chemical
sectors.  Refractories contribute around 5 per cent   towards the total cost of steel making.    During the last several years, the demand
of superior grade refractories required for BOF, secondary refining and continuous casting units of steel industries posed challenges
to the refractory producers.  The emphasis by the industry in the recent years is towards import substitution    and production of
special items like magnesia carbon, slide gate refractories, submerged nozzles, shrouds.  Monoblock stoppers, low –cement castables,
dense silica bricks for tall coke ovens, etc. The choice of refractories for steel making depends on various factors like achieving
reduced fuel consumption, increased furnace capacity, increased furnace life and availability and improved product quality.  The
future of refractory industry lies in continued development of improved bonding in basic and high alumina materials, advances in tar  
pitch bonding and impregnation and development of resion bonding. Monolithics special those incorporating low cement, carbon/.
Graphite emerged and relatively high performance materials.  Besides there is greater emphasis for greater energy efficiency. The
changing attitude of present day consumers is laying more importance on the availability of furnace, cleanliness of steel, ultimate cost
benefit, even if the initial investment were high.  This may be reckoned from the fact that during the last three decades, the
improvement in refractories quality has led to about 50 to 60 per cent decrease in specific consumption of refractories, whereas the
turnover of refractory units has been steadily rising.
 
7.2       The Committee is of the view that, since 75 per cent of the total refractories produced in the country      are consumed by steel
industries and steel industry is demanding superior grade of refractories, the Ministry of steel should facilitate the refractories
industry in general and BRL in particular to     undertake adequate research work for production of such superior grade of refractories
which suits the requirement of steel industry.  The Committee   recommends that research work in refractories industry may take into
consideration the requirement of steel industry which inter-alia include reduction in fuel consumption, incurred furnace capacity,
incurred furnace   life and availability and improved product quality.
 
7.3       The major factors that have led to decline in refractory consumption are increased stringency on the quality of refractory
products and improvement of quality along with improved operational parameters. The operating data of SAIL and their perspective
planning as indicated below for the next decade are indicators of the trend in steel sector.

7.4.      The Sub-Committee wanted to know whether it is a fact that technological improvement in steel making has affected the
entire refractories industry and unhealthy competition has led to price war, if so, the measures that could be undertaken to improve
the physical and financial performance of refractories industry in general and BRL in particular. The BRL management informed the
Sub-Committee that improvement in Steel making Technology alongwith development of superior quality refractories has reduced
the consumption of refractories per ton of steel in the country, which has particularly created a price war situation. Impact of this
during last three years resulted in price reduction to the tune of 20 / 25 per cent every year leading to a situation as on date when
some of the products are priced at almost raw materials cost.
7.5       The Committee observes that technological improvement in steel making has not only led to the increasing demand   of
superior quality refractories and reduction in total consumption of refractories but also generated a price war situation   and unfair
trade price due to excessive competition among refractories producers.  The Committee is of the view that improvement in steel
making technology is a welcome and necessary   development for betterment   of steel industry while reduction in total consumption
of refractories is an unavoidable development and it may be hoped that with the sign of recovery in steel industry the demand of
refractories would increase.  So far as the situation of price was due to excessive competition   is concerned, the Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Steel should take up the matter to ensure that healthy competition should prevail in the Refractories
Industry and competition should not result into unfair trade   prices.  The price of the refractories product be allowed to be determined
by the free market forces of demand and supply.

further recommends   that   the Ministry of Steel should act as a facilitator and guide the BRL management to undertake measures for
maximisation of profit.

10.2.2.Refractories for continuous casting system (RCC)
A feasibility   Report  for Refractories for continuous casting system (RCC) has been prepared by the M/s MECON,
appointed  as consultant.  The technical know-how  for the production of continuous casting refractory  has already been  obtained 
by the company from M/s Shinagawa Refractores  Ltd., Japan.  With the   technological changes in steel sector leading to the
reduction of consumption of  conventional refractories and demand for the refractories for  continuous casting system ways and
means would however have necessarily to be found for setting  up of the project for the  survival  of the company. The company
proposes to set up the project through joint venture utilising the existing facilities at IFICO. Refractories Plant . In view of the same,
a  provision of Rs.10.90 crore has been made in the BE 2001-2002  with a budgetary support of Rs.0.50 crore.
10.2.3  The Sub-Committee wanted to know the  current status of BRL plan to set up a continuous Casting Refractories Plant in joint
venture  and the original estimated cost and current cost for setting un the same ,the management stated that BRL floated open tender
and one Party namely MONNET ISPAT LTD. offered their proposal to become joint venture partner and this has been forwarded to
the Ministry. The proposal is for 60 : 40 percent equity participation by Monnet &BRL and for signing MOU on this basis. BRL
asked permission of Ministry of Steel which is awaited. The BRL management  informed the Sub-Committee that the  original cost of
the project was about Rs. 23 crores as done by MECON in 1992 but later on in 2000- 2001 the cost escalated upto 38 crores when a
separate Company in joint venture was thought.  Replying to the Sub-Committee's query regarding the proportion   of the 
Government equity and the sources to raise the required fund the BRL management stated that BRL's equity part of 40 per cent
would be adjusted by the cost of land and Technology transfer cost alongwith some fund from plan loan to be sanctioned by Govt of
India in 10th 5 year plan .
 
10.2.4  BRL is not  in a position to generate sufficient  internal  resources to meet the cost  of the project.  BRL proposed  to make the
project for a joint venture.  In order to obtain a joint venture partner, BRL floated open  tender  and only one party viz., Monnet Ispat
Limited responded for the same for 60:40 equity participation  by  Monnet and BRL.   The  proposal is under consideration   of the  
Government Chairman-cum-Managing Director, BRL have also  discussed   with Managing  Director, Ferro scrap Nigam Ltd.  for 
their participation in the project which is under scrutiny stage at Ferrro scrap Nigam Ltd.  which is also a public sector undertaking
under the Ministry of Steel.
10.2.5  The   Committee is of the considered view that setting up of Continuous Casting System (RCC)  is long  overdue .The  
Standing  Committee on Industry has  recommended   in its earlier reports for setting up of refractories for  Continuous   Casting 
System at the earliest for ensured survival of the company.  The RCC has got the merit of positive  feasibility report as prepared by
M/s  MECON and the technical know-how as obtained from M/s  Shinagow Refractories  Ltd.,  Japan.  The   technological changes
in steel  making process leaves little scope for demand of conventional refractories and  opens the  avenues    for refractories  for
Continuous Casting System.  All   these factors   necessitate    the setting up of RCC, sooner the better, since  original   estimated
cost  i.e. Rs.23 crore has  already overrun  to the tune of Rs.38.00 crore .  The only   deterring  factor  earlier was the lack of fund for

13.0     Tax Structure
13.1     Pertaining to the Sub-Committee's query as  to what extent the existing tax structure is beneficial in the interest of refractories
industry  and the steps  which could be undertaken for rationalization of tax structure,  the BRL management stated that most of the
raw materials required for manufacturing of high tech refractory items are not available in the country as such import of huge
quantity of these materials is a must. There has been some rationalization of tax structure during the budget of 2001- 2002 while
custom duties of three items namely D-B-M, Fused Magnesite & Sea Water Magnesia was reduced to 15 per cent. Thereby giving
some relief to Refractory industries. However, there are various other raw materials like B-F-A, W-F-A, Tabular Alumina graphite &
fume Silica required for high Tech products needs the same relief to enable Indian products cost effective & competitive in price
compared to foreign suppliers.
 
13.2     During the budget presentation for 2001-02 relief on  Sea Water Magnesia, Fused Magnesia and Dead Burnt Magnesia  was
considered  by the Government of India and the same has been reduced to  15 per cent   plus 4 per cent surcharge. During the budget  
presentation of 2002-03 , the duty on  Brown fused Alumina, Sintered Alumina, Silicon Carbon,  Graphite etc., was  reduced to 30
per cent .  However, the  refractory bricks  imported from outside is charged 25 per cent   custom duty,   Reduction of custom duty an
input material  to 50 per cent of the finished bricks import duty would be suitable for refractories industry.

superior quality refractories  and reduction in total consumption  of refractories but generated  a price war situation   and unfair trade 
price due to excessive competition  among refractories producers.  The  Committee is of the view that improvement  in steel making 
technology is a welcome and necessary   development for betterment   of steel industry while  reduction in total consumption of
refractories is an unavoidable development and it may be hoped that  with the sign of recovery in steel industry the demand of
refractories would increase.  So far as the situation of price was due to  excessive competition   is concerned, the  Committee 
recommends that the Ministry  of Steel should take up the matter  to ensure that  healthy  competition should prevail in the
Refractories Industry  and competition should not result  into unfair trade   prices.  The price of the  refractories product be  allowed
to be determined  by the free market  forces  of demand and  supply.

            The Committee understands the problems  being faced by refractories industry  arising due to imbalance between
manufacturing  cost and selling price.  The Committee observes that the price of the finished  products has been  drastically reduced
(ranging from  30 to 44 per cent ) whereas there is a  trend in increase in  the price structure of input materials ( ranging from 5 to 17
per cent ).  This is the  double loss  to the refractory  industry  and under the   said  circumstances any  industry is bound to  be
affected.  Therefore, the Committee is of the view that refractories industry in general and BRL  management   in particular should 
chalk out a two pronged strategy  i.e. one  to arrest  the  fall in the selling price of refractories and   to reverse the trend  and other
strategy is required to  minimise the cost of production so that  the `margin of profit' for refractories industry may increase.  The

REPORT

Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited (RINL) commonly known as Visakhapatnam Steel
Plant (VSP), is the first shore-based integrated Steel Plant set up in India at a distance from
the major raw material sources, viz. metallurgical coal and iron ore . Being shore-based it
has the advantage of easier import of input materials like coking coal, lime-stone ete., and
casier export of finished products. The location is also expected to help industrialistion of
the region. VSP has been set up with several latest technologies for the first time in the
country, such as 100 percent continuous casting of liquid steel, dry quenching of coke
with auxiliary power gencration facilities, 100 percent Cast House Slag Granulation in
Blast Furnace and Torpedo Ladle for transporting liquid hot metal.

2.0 RINL INDEPENDENT FROM SAIL

21 RINL was originally conceived as a unit of Steel Authority of India (SAIL) to
augment its long product capacity and service its southem market, The facility was envisaged
with sourcing of raw material from National Mineral Development Corporation ( NMDC),
which was also a part of SAIL at that time, and a jetty was also envisaged for its imports and
exports. The announcement of VSP as part of SAIL was done in April 1970, the foundation
stone was laid in January,1971, the Indo-Soviet agreement was concluded in June, 1979 and
the revised DPR was prepared in 1980. In 1982, Government of India decided to carve a
separate holding company for VSP, and RINL was formed as a separate PSU under Ministry
of Steel in February ,1982.

2:2 RINL has been operating as a separate PSU primarily for the following reasons :

i to have healthy competition with the public sector
ii to improve efficiency of its operations in a competitive eavironment
iii to be accountable for its own financial performance, ete.

23 The Committee notes the contention of RINL management that RIN has been
Operating as a separate and independent PSU (independent of SAIL) for imbibing
competitive resilience in plant, injecting operational efficiency and having the benefits of
being accountable for its own financial performance.

24 The Committee, however, recommends that the Government may like to examine and
explore the possibility of merger of SAIL and RINL and take concrete step in this regard, if
the move consolidates long stcel making capacity in the country.

2.5 In the Committee's meeting held on 4% April 2002 (on Demands -for Grants 2002-
03), the Secretary, Ministry of Steel expressed his views on RINL in the following words:-

+ Coming:to some of ihe other plants, | am pleased to inform the Committee that some of our
PSUs have done well. The RINL, Vizag, which at one time seemed to be running in losses,
now appears to be slightly coming around which is extremely encouraging. They have
reported running in excess of the installed capacity on all fronts. They have reported cash
ancl for last year. They are expected to report much higher cash this year. The net loss,
which had come down from Rs. 561 crore in 1999-2000 to Rs. 291 crore in the year 2001-02,
we estimate that it would be in the region of Rs.125 crore only. The net loss would be down
to Rs. 25 crore, | था happy to inform that in our reviews of plant and its operations, they have
done well. I would say that they have done extremely well. We are happy with the manner in
which they have been able to bring the plant out which was initially in very, very deep
woods."

million tonnes. Then there was another one of 1.5 million tonnes. Total | think is 3.45
million tonnes steel. Finally, it was settled at 2.25 million tonnes as compared to Korea,

for 3 million tonnes. This year we have done three million tonnes and in the near future it

3.2 The Government approved the proposal to set up RINL in June, 1979 with production

20.0 MANAGEMENT BY OBJECTIVE (MBO)

20.1 Till 1992, the Indian Steel industry had never been a market driven outfit. With the
Opening of economy under globalization and liberalization policy of the government, the
contro] era came to an end and all the Public sector steel plants had to suddenly face the
“Chill winds of competition”, Organisations that acquired a competitive edge were able to
survive and others were destined to wither away.

20.2 Furthermore, with the South East Asian crisis, Soviet disintegration and increased
dumping of steel by China/CIS countries at cheaper rates had affected the domestic as well as
intemational markets and all major producers were compelled to reduce their production
volumes and steel prices, Added to it, the plight of the long product producers like RINL in
the country was far from viable with cut-throat competition from secondary producers and
ship breaking industry on one hand and Tecessionary trends all over the world on the other.



=

20.3 In the above scenario, any organization to survive and grow has to approach its
internal and external environment with innovative initiatives and utmost responsiveness to get
results in the quickest possible way, RINL was no exception. From the later part of 1997,
Situation in the market began to worsen. RINL at the same time has to face the problems in
both the internal and external environments. Equipment needed attention, morale of
employees was at a lower ebb and marketing strategies, systems and procedures which were
catering to the needs of controlled product regime were no longer valid in changed
environment. With the result that RINL had to formulate an objective oriented action plan to
address the vital issues and halt the downslide of the organization. Some of the issues which
needed immediate attention were:

1 Equipment health;

capital repairs of all major production units;

iii Actions required to improve the employees’ morale and confidence;

iv sensitise marketing field officers to the tasks ahead and review its decision

making process

20.4. In the light of the above, the company had to address objectively each of the issues
and introduce changes to improve the performance of the company. Detailed action plans
were formulated and implemented to bring 4 transformation in the performance of the
company. The actions taken were :

1. all the capital repairs were taken up on schedule to bring back the equipment in
good health;

ii All the systems and procedures were reviewed and revamped to make the
decision making more faster and at the same time transparent;

iii Marketing setup both at headquarters and branches were strengthened;

iv A strict control on administrative expenditure was introduced;

Discipline on the shopfloor was strengthened alongwith technological discipline;

vi Usage of metallurgical wastes and recycling had been stepped up to contain the
cost of production; and

vii Regular sessions were conducted with employees to लाला! their views for
tumingaround the organization. In addition to these, the departmental
communication (Samalochana) meetings were conducted to improve the
performance of the departments. "ACCESS" scheme was introduced to enable
the employees to directly offer their views to the Chief Executive of the
company.

20.5 With the result, the company has been doing exceedingly well not only in production
but also in improving its market share both in domestic and international markets. Also,
RINL became an example for other steel producing companies to emulate. A total
transformation has been brought in the functioning of the organization about which can be
seen in the company of improving its financial performance year after year and is fast
marching ahead for a “tumaround™.

20.6 The Committee is pleased to note that RINL management is re-orienting its corporate
goal asperthe canons of changing scenario's of steel industry due to on going process of

‘model PSU’ for other Steel units to follow suit. RINL has, rightly, selected the Key

freight charges. Since 1995-96, withdrawal of this extra freight charge formed a part of the

23.6 In the meeting of the Sub-Commuttee held on 12" September, 2001 on the subject of
“Key Concern Areas of Steel Industries and promotion of steel consumption in various sectors
of economy ", the issue of inflated freight charge was discussed in detailed. Participating in
discussion Shn R.N. Malhotra, Chairman, Railway Board expressed his views 1-

"On the ‘questions of concessions, I would like to say that we are prepared to
consider any request from any manufacturer for certain concessions which will help them and
Which in tum would help the Railways But Sir, by reducing our revenue, we can not help
anyone, If they are prepared to give us an undertaking that if we reduce the freight on the
KK Line by a certain percentage, they will be able to give us so much of extra traffic, we can
consider it.”

23.7. Interjecting in the discussion, the Secretary, Ministry of Steel expressed his opinion
in following words:-

+ the question that has been raised with regard to the KK Line related to movement of
iron ore from Bailadilla, which is used by the Vizag Steel Plant. It has a very long history.
It is not really a question of incremental traffic. The operative issue here is that 65 per cent
additional freight charge was put at a certain point of time because that line was specifically
created for the movement of iron ore from point A to point B, with an understanding that if
the level of freight crossed six million tonnes, this additionality would be removed. The
situation today is that, as against the 65 per cent enhanced rate that was being charged, the
current enhanced rate is 30 per cent, and the traffic generated on that line, today, s 12 tonnes.
We can not have a persistent kind of an incremental situation going on. We understand that at
a point of time, the line was constructed for captive use, and additional charges were levied in
order to make it viable for the Railways. Once a certain threshold of traffic generation has
been achieved, the incremental rate should not apply. That was the original understanding.
One cannot have a situation wherein because there ts an incremental rate, in order to reduce
it, you must have incremental traffic. The fact that rate was brought down from 65 per cent
to 35 per cent and now to 30 per centis, itself, a recognition of the understanding on which

v7



this 65 per cent was charged. Now, as _] that understanding, that additionality factor
should now go. This is the issue that has to be examined.

23.8 Responding to the argument of Secretary, the Chairman, Railway Board, added :-

" The Additionality which was charged earlier was for several reasons. The first
reason was that because it was a hilly area, with sharp edges and curves, the construction cost
of rails was very high. The second reason was that we had put surcharge on movement of
any traffic on that line because of the fact that in place of one locomotive, which is normally
required on a plain terrain, we had to put three locomotive in place . So, the cost of operation
also was very high. Also, the electricity bill for the operational of this line is five times
higher than what it would cost in the case of a line on the plain. Now, how do we recover
that cost? We cannot go on reducing our revenue, unless there is a commitment on the part
of the steel plants that they will be able to sell so much of extra stee! and thus give us that
much of extra traffic.”

23.9 The Secretary, Ministry of Steel further added :-

" The K.K. Line is an issue where there is difference in Perception between the
Railway Board and the Steel Ministry . It will be useful to have a re-look and see whether
there is any justification for reducing this further additionality, In fact, quite recently, the
NMDC, which is a profit-making PSU under this Ministry, had offered to take over the line
on a captive basis and bear the cost, because they are of the view that the cost additionality
that is being charged, is unjustified Unfortunately, that was not acceptable to the Railways.
But the basic issue is that the movement of freight is the business of the Ministry of Railways
and not of the NMDC or the Steel Industry. 1 feel that this matter has to be dealt with in an
impartial manner. It may be useful to get the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, the NMDC and the
Railways to jointly look at this issue and, in fact give a joint working paper on this.”
