ACCEPTED REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT
Para 5.4
Status of Navratna and Miniratna companies
RECOMMENDATION
  The Committee notes that Non-Official Directors for Navratna and Miniratna PSEs have benefited immensly due to
the status assigned to them. The Committee feels that the Department of Public Enteprises should undertake all possible
steps to introduce professionalism in these Public Sector Enterprises so that they are able to face challenges of changing
times and able to develop competitive edge.
Para 5.5

92nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/92ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:19:50]
RECOMMENDATION
  The Committee, however, proposes to undertake a study to know how far Directors of MoU signing PSEs are given
sufficient power to enable them to take quick decisions in their business related matters and formation of joint venture
etc. in India and abroad.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
  Steps have already been taken for professionalising the Boards of Navratna and Miniratna PSEs. A Search Committee
was set up for selecting non-official part-time Directors for Navratna/Miniratna PSEs. The delegation of enhanced
financial powers to the Navratna and Miniratna PSEs is subject to the condition that the Boards of these PSEs are
professionalised by inducting at least 4 non-official Directors in the case of Navratnas and at least 3 non-official
Directors in the case of Miniratnas. These non-officials are eminent persons drawn from various disciplines like
technocrats, management experts and consultants, professional managers in industry and trade, etc.  Induction of non-
official professionals through the Search Committee mechanism is a countinuous process.
  The MoU system is based on the principle of enhanced autonomy and accountability. Accordingly, the Boards of MoU
signing PSEs enjoy certain financial and operational autonomy within the guidelines. As and when the Committee
desires to undertake the study, this Department will provide requisite assistance to coordinate it.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
  The Department of Public Enterprises has informed about the steps taken about the professionalization of the Boards of
Navratna and Miniratna companies. But it has not stated how far they have been successful to face the challenges of
changing time. The Committee needs the detailed breakup of the composition of Boards of Navratna and Miniratna
companies to have an insight with regard to professionalization of Boards and how far they have played proactive role.
Para 5.9
RECOMMENDATION
The Committee is of the opinion that the grant of Navratna and Miniratna status should not be a one-time affair. The
Committee is of the view that the Navratna/Miniratna status should be reviewed periodically and those PSEs, which
underperform as compared to their targets should be denied Navratna/Miniratna status.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
  The government has already taken a decision to introduce the mechanism to periodically review the Navratna and
Miniratna status of the PSEs. An Apex Committee headed by the Cabinet Secretary is to regularly review their
performance for which a detailed format has already been circulated to the PSEs and the Administrative Ministries.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
The Committee notes that a mechanism has been introduced to periodically review the Navratna and Miniratna
status of PSE and the administrative Ministries for the purpose. The Committee wishes that it may be apprised about the
feed back received from the PSEs and Ministries in response to the said circular and actions taken by the Department of
Public Enterprises thereon.
Para 5.10
RECOMMENDATION
The Committee also recommends that greater financial, operational and managerial autonomy should be given to
Navratnas/Miniratnas PSEs so as to enable them to take independent decisions.
ACTION  TAKEN  BY  THE  GOVERNMENT
Through the Navratna and Miniratna scheme enhanced financial, operational and managerial autonomy has already
been granted to the PSEs. However, an institutional arrangement has already been set up to review the working of the
scheme and the need for grant of further autonomy will also be considered under this arrangement.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION

The Committee stresses that it should be apprised of the results of review done so far of the  scheme of the enhanced
financial, operational and managerial autonomy granted to the PSEs.                                                 
Para 6.2
Counselling, Retraining/Redeployment, Setting up of New Centres/Addition of Nodal Agencies
RECOMMENDATION
The Committee feels that the initiatives taken by the DHI to counsel, retrain and redeploy the employees of CPSEs
are laudable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that greater focus on proper implementation and regular
monitoring of the above scheme is required to make it more effective at the ground level.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
DPE would strive for further improvement under the CRR Programme. For regular monitoring of the programme,
the Monitoring Cell set up under the CRR Programme has been in close touch with the Nodal Training Agencies and
Central PSUs for proper implementation and monitoring of the programme. Regular field visits have been made to the
Nodal Agencies and locations of the training imparted in order to closely watch and monitor the programme, have the
feed back from the beneficiaries and also to meet the Central PSUs in the surroundings so as to create a cohesive
environment for the CRR programme. Besides, at the local level provision has already been made for setting up of
Coordination Committee consisting of the Members from Central PSUs, Nodal Training Agencies and credit institutions
so that the issues can be discussed and sorted out locally.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
The Committee wishes to know number of visits have so far been made to the nodal agencies and locations of the
training and details of feedback received from the beneficiaries and results achieved after meeting the Central PSUs in
the surroundings. The Committee further wishes to know whether coordination Committee at local level consisting of
Members from Central PSUs, Nodal Training Agencies and credit institutions has since been formed, if so, at how many
places and results achieved therefrom.
Para 6.6
RECOMMENDATION
The Committee is of the opinion that with the increase in the number of employees opting for VRS, the programme
for retraining and redeployment of these employees requires tremendous technical expertise. The Committee has been
informed that training agencies have been identified throughout the country to rehabilitate workers who have retired
under the VRS scheme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Public Enterprises should
exercise greater monitoring over the working of these agencies and ensure that effective training depending on the
actual job market conditions is imparted.
ACTION  TAKEN  BY  THE  GOVERNMENT
Visualizing the professional/technical expertise required, the selection of the Nodal Training Agencies have been
made in such a way that it should cater to the need of the restructured employees. Both the Central PSUs as well as
Nodal Training Agencies, who are the key elements of the CRR programme have been advised to draw up the training
modules for 20 days/30 days/40 days in such a manner that should cater the individual needs of the rationalised
employees of CPSUs. They should also take into account the market opportunity available, the strength and weakness of
the trainees, the resources required for that particular project that the trainees would be taking up and the capacity of the
individual concerned etc. Besides, constant monitoring alongwith field visits by officers of Monitoring Cell, DPE are
made so as to have first hand feed  back from the beneficiaries and the difficulties/suggestion, if any are put into place
so as to bring further improvement in this programme. However, recommendations of the Committee have been noted.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
The Committee recommends that Department of Public Enterprises should play a proactive   role in the matter and
watch the quality of training programme, guide the trained persons in taking up projects in consultation with the Small
Industries Service Institutions and have meetings with the Credit Intitutions to facilitate availability of required funds.

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this Ninety-Third Report on the Action Taken by the Government on the
Recommendations contained in the 75th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry on Demends for Grants (2002-2003) pertaining to Ministry of Small Scale Industries.
2.      The 75th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry was presented to Rajya
Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 14th May, 2002.
3.      The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted the report at its
meeting held on the 11th December, 2002.
NEW DELHI ,
11 December, 2002;
         
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER 
Chairman,
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry.
REPORT
        The Ninety-Third Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
Recommendations contained in the 75 th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry on the Demands For Grants (2002-2003) pertaining to the Ministry of Small Scale Industries which was
presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 14th May, 2002.
2.     Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained in the
Report. They have been categorized as follows:
        (i) Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Government:- Para 3.8, 4.5, 4.6, 5.3, 6.7, 7.5,

        (ii)    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government’s

        (v)   Observations/Recommendations at a Glance. (Chapter–V).

as mentioned in Chapter – I of the Report.

7.     The details of the ATR is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.
CHAPTER-I

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED

WTO OBLIGATIONS
Para 3.8
Observation/Recommendation
        The Committee further observes that it is essential to create greater awareness about the obligations India has to
fulfil under the WTO regime and their impact on various sectors. There is a need to have adequate preparedness for
WTO compliance. The Committee recommends that regular interactions between the Government and SSIs should take
place for this purpose. Special cells with legal backup may be created and strengthened to deal with WTO related
problems of SSIs in concerned Government Department and industry associations.
Action Taken/Comments
        With a view to create awareness among the SSI units/Associations, etc. on WTO Agreements and their
implications, Ministry of SSI & ARI organized 28 one-day Sensitization Workshops all over the country. The
Ministry also organized 16 one-day workshops on Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) during 2001-2002 with
the assistance of WIPO and 16 Seminars all over the country to disseminate information to the SSI
Associations on Anti Dumping Procedures.
        A WTO cell in the office of DC (SSI) was set up on 15 th November, 1999 with the objective to keep abreast with
the recent developments in WTO, disseminate information to SSI units and their Associations, coordinate with other
Ministries and Departments, prepare the policy for SSIs in line with the WTO agreements, organize WTO Workshops
especially for SSI units at macro & micro level in the Small Scale Sector to enable the small/tiny sector to understand
the WTO agreements. With a view to assist the SSI Sector on legal matters a panel of legal experts on WTO matters has
been created at the Office of the DCSSI to assist the entrepreneurs in filing anti-dumping and IPR related cases.
RESTRUCTURING OF NATIONAL SMALL INDUSTRIES CORPORATION FOR DEVELOPMENT OF
SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES
Para 4.5
Observation/Recommendation
        The Committee recommends that in response to challenges and opportunities arising out of globalisation, new
responsibilities envisaged for SIDO like gathering latest information regarding WTO Agreement, WTO sensitization
and strategy building programmes, anti-dumping proceedings, etc. need to receive priority consideration. In this context,
action for upgrading sub—sector specific schemes for technology transfer and exports need to be taken care of.
Appropriate HRD strategies need also to be paid attention. Government should work out restructuring of NSIC in the
light of suggestion made by M/s Ferguson and Co. (Consultant) to achieve the above objectives.
Action Taken/Comments
        This Ministry is getting sectoral studies conducted in areas having a strong SSI presence to formulate a pro-active
strategy and to fine-tune the existing policies and programmes. Five sectoral studies have already been undertaken with
UNDP assistance of US $ 20,000 on Hand tools, Medicinal Biotechnology, Glass and Ceramics, Bicycle parts and
Flavour and Fragrance. The Ministry also financially supports Industry Associations to develop monitoring mechanisms
on the performance of four selected product clusters in terms of growth, removal of QRs, surge in imports, etc. These
Associations/Clusters are CII-Food Processing and Machine tools; FISME – Shaneel; and Kishangarh Marble
Association – Marble respectively. The work on these projects has since been started.
        The Ministry has also formulated a “market Development Assistance for SSI Exporters” SSI-MDA Scheme to
enhance exports by the SSIs. Under the scheme financial assistance upto Rs. 1 lakh is given to SSI Associations for
initiating anti-dumping investigations.
        M/s A F. Ferguson & Co. were asked to prepare an operational plan keeping in mind the various activities of NSIC
as approved by the Ministry after discussion with the share holders. M/s A.F. Ferguson & Co. has since finalized the
operational plan which was submitted to this Ministry in July, 2002. The operational plan was put up to the Board of
Directors in their meeting held on August 2, 2002. After approval of Plan by the NSIC Board and Government, it will
be put in operation.
DEVELOPMENT OF CLUSTERS
Para 4.6

Observation/Recommendation
        The Committee feels that more attention needs to be given to the development of clusters for facilitating sustenance
and growth of existing enterprises. Pooling the strengths of several enterprises in a similar line of activity produces
synergetic effects. The Committee, therefore, recommends that consortia of SSIs for common purchase of raw materials,
common branding and access to large complex markets should be set up for promotion of small scale sector.
Action Taken/Comments
        Under the Integrated Technology Upgradation and Management Programme (UPTECH) for technology
upgradation of small scale industries, 9 clusters were taken up for development in the Ninth Plan. Development of 5
clusters based on Herbal/Aromatics Plants at 5 different places in the country is also being taken up.
        In addition, 4 National Programmes for the Development of Toy, Stone, Lock and Machine Tool Industries have
been taken up under UPTECH scheme during Ninth Plan for technology upgradation, in collaboration with UNIDO.
        Further, UNIDO, under the cluster development programme, has identified 7 more clusters. A Steering Committee
has been set up under the Chairmanship of AS & DC (SSI) for implementation and guidance. Apart from this, a project
– ‘Support to the Country Effort to promote SME Cluster Development’ for technology upgradation clusters has also
been taken up in collaboration with UNIDO.
        Sub Group on Marketing, Export and Partnership of the Working Group on Small Scale Industries (SSI Sector) for
Tenth Plan (2002---2007) suggested adoption of consortium approach in which the NSIC could play a significant role.
Consortia formed by small units should have the facility of guidance by way of availability of information in time etc.
and these consortia be encouraged to develop brands of their own. Since, the initiative to form these consortia is to be
taken by SSI units, the Government would provide due support and encouragement to such efforts.
PROMOTION OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES SCHEMES

        The Committee feels that in order to enhance the competitiveness of the SSIs, it is essential to provide to it
technical assistance alongwith other basic inputs for production such as power, fuel, raw materials and credit at
reasonable prices. The Committee has been apprised that various Tool Rooms like Central Tool Room and Training
Centre (CTR & TC), Kolkata, Central tool Room, Ludhiana, Central Institute of Hand Tools (CIHT), Jalandhar, Central

Action Taken/Comments
        The prudential norms on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning are objective and are based on
the record of recovery in each bank. In terms of extant instructions, a non-performing asset (NPA) is defined as credit
facility in respect of which the interest/or instalments of principal has remained overdue for a period more that 180 days.
With a view to moving closer to international best practices and to ensure greater transparency, it has been decided to
adopt the 90 days overdue norm for identification of NPAs w.e.f. 31st March, 2004. According to the RBI, as a matter of
policy, Relaxation is not granted in the NPA norm on the basis of sector, scale of operation and industry.
        The norm for recognition of loan impairment has been introduced by the RBI after due consideration and is in
keeping with international best practices. The RBI is of the view that since our financial system is also under scrutiny
from various international agencies it would not be feasible to depart from these norms without affecting the confidence
of the international financial and capital markets. Besides, 90 days norm will come into effect only after a considerable
lapse of time i.e. 31st March, 2004. Hence, both banks and the industry will have sufficient time to adjust to the new
requirements.

shall be eligible for exemption from provisioning requirements. The has been introduced to ensure that banks do not
hesitate in granting additional facilities to sick SSI units.

Technology, Science and Technology (Department of Bio-Technology), Department of Scientific & Industrial Research,

Plan Working Group on SSI also recommended setting up Incubation Centres for which it has suggested an outlay of
Rs. 1000 crores. The Report of the Working Group has been sent to the Planning Commission for their consideration.

        The Committee recommends that Ministry of Small Scale Industries should vigorously pursue with the various
Ministries/Department the setting up of incubation centers under their Ministries/Departments. The Committee wishes
to know the details of response received from the various Ministries/Departments in this regard.

sanction or rejection thereof and the reasons for rejection.

        The Committee also recommends that SSIs, branches of Banks should display prominently on the bank counters

        The Committee wishes to know the bank-wise information about the display in their branch premises the details of

ACCELARATED DEPRECIATION TO SSI UNITS
Para 9.7
Observation/Recommendation
        The Committee observes that removal of Quantitative Restrictions has brought Indian industry face-to-face with
foreign products, which are technologically far superior. Moreover, technical barriers to trade are emerging as major
non-tariff barriers to access the markets of the developed countries. Therefore, Indian industry, particularly to SSI
Sectors need support to upgrade to the high technical standards set by the developed countries. Accelerated rate of
depreciation may be allowed to SSIs units on purchase of plant and machinery for technology upgradation.
Action Taken/Comments
        This Ministry has launched the Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for technology upgradation of the SSIs in
certain select products/sub-sectors and the banks have been advised about the Scheme for providing financial assistance
accordingly. Banks have also been instructed to develop schemes to encourage investment by SSI units in technology
upgradation and harmonize the same with SIDBI.
        Additional depreciation @ 15% has been allowed on new plant & machinery for setting up new units or expanding
installed capacity of existing units by at least 25%, in the Union Budget 2002-03.
Further Recommendation

ANTI-DUMPING MEASURES
Para 11.2
Observation/Recommendation
        The Committee recommends that on account of almost all products coming under Open General License (OGL)
list, the Government may further strengthen that anti-dumping mechanism so that remedial measures may be initiated
expeditiously. Countervailing duties and safeguard duties may be imposed in order to protect domestic producers from
cheap imports. It may not be possible for SSIs units to function in such a competitive market. However, if they want to
grow from SSI level, all facilities available to them should continue for at least five years.
Action Taken/Comments
        The WTO Cell in the Office of DC (SSI) has taken up the matter with Directorate General of Anti-Dumping &
Allied Duties, Department of Commerce, Ministry of Commerce & Industry, to take appropriate action to further
strengthen the Anti-Dumping mechanism and to impose countervailing duties so as to initiate remedial measures
expeditiously. The matter was also taken up with Director General of Safeguards, to take appropriate action in order to
protect domestic producers from cheap imports. Under the Mission for the Millennium, this office had conducted an
exercise to study the compatibility with the WTO Agreements regarding the various support measures and schemes of
this Ministry. This was done in consultation with the Trade Policy Division, Department of Commerce, and Ministry of
Commerce & Industry. It is opined that all the schemes are WTO compatible.
        The Director General of Safeguards has already taken up action in respect of 12 products for investigations. So far,
safeguard duties in respect of 7 cases have been imposed.
        This Ministry has recently formulated a Market Development Assistance (MDA) Scheme to enhance the exports by
the SSIs. Under the Scheme, financial assistance of participation in international exhibitions, overseas study, tours,
assistance towards the production of publicity material, market studies etc. is given. Under the aforesaid Scheme,
financial assistance upto Rs. 1 lakh is also given to SSI Association who have initiated anti-dumping investigations.
        Majority of the Schemes and Programmes being implemented by the Government for the growth and development
of SSI Sector in India are continuous and perpetual as regards their periodicity. The period-specific Schemes like
Reimbursement of expense incurred on ISO-9000 Certification would continue till the end of Tenth Five Year Plan
period (March 2007); the Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme was envisaged for a period of 5 years ending
September, 2005; the Scheme for setting up of Training Centers by industry Association was envisaged to be in
operation for an initial period of 5 years w.e.f. 2001-02 and extension thereafter will be considered on the basis of
performance and success of the Scheme. The support to the SSI sector in the form of various benefits incentives offered
through different Schemes would be available beyond 5 years also, therefore, the recommendation of the Committee to
continue the benefits available to the SSI sector for at least 5 years is in-built in the support measures already.
Further Recommendation
        The Committee desires that the Committee’s recommendation that if SSI Units want to grow from SSI level,
all facilities available to them should continue for at least five years and the Ministry’s reply thereto to the effect that the
benefits  available to SSI Sector for at least five years which was inbuilt in the support measures, would continue for
those SSIs who wanted to grow above the SSI level, should be given wide publicity through a suitably worded circular,
Press Releases and electronic media.

        In order to revive sick industries. The committee recommends further:-

        The Committee recommends that unless State Governments play a proactive role in creating infrastructure for

3.0   The Committee thereafter, took up auto policy for discussion. The Chairman apprised the Members that the
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry had recommended in its 59th Report that the Government should
formulate an Auto Policy in view of the ongoing liberalization of the economy and W.T.O. Obligations. In response to
the Committee's recommendations the Department of Heavy Industries in its action taken note has informed the
Committee that Government of India has brought out an Auto Policy on 7th March, 2002.
3.1   The Chairman stated that the Committee on Industry took up the auto policy for detailed discussion as the policy
laid down certain recommendations for the growth of the Industry. Since most of these recommendations required
actions by the Ministries other than the Department of Heavy Industries and so far these recommendations had not been
translated into real Government Policy.
3.2   The Chairman apprised the Members that the Committee had already taken up the matter for discussion and in this
regard the Committee had held two meetings on 24th June and 16th July, 2002. Based on the discussion held on 24th
June, 2002 a questionnaire was prepared and replies thereon was obtained from Department of Heavy Industries. In the
Meeting held on 16th July, 2002 the Committee had interacted with Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI);
Society of India Automobiles Manufacturers (SIAM); Automotive Tyre Manufacturers Association (ATMA); and
Automotive Component Manufacturers Association (ACMA); Prozon Inc. (manufacture of Fuel saver). Apprising the
Members the details of discussion held in these two meetings, the Chairman spelt out the scope for discussion in auto
policy which inter-alia  included import of second hand imported cars; lack of testing facilities; foreign direct
investment, research and development; construction of bus-body building; terminal life policy; lifting of quantitive
restriction; using spurious items and related 'e' mark issue; excise duty on tyre and concession on imported tyre; Ban on
used tyre; difficulties due to octroi on 5-6 States, switching over from tube tyre to tubeless tyre; encouragement to small
car industries; infrastructure import tariff; environmental aspects etc.
3.3   The Committee, thereafter, discussed in details the aims of Auto Policy which aimed at to promote integrated,
phased, enduring and self-sustained growth of the Indian Automobile Industry. The Committee discussed also the
objective to Auto Policy which inter-alia include promotion of a globally competitive automotive industry; exalting the
sector as a lever of industrial growth and an employment; Establishment of an international hub for manufacturing small
affordable passenger cars and key centre for manufacturing tractors and two wheelers in the world; ensuring a balanced
transition to open trade at a minimal risk to the Indian Economy and local industry; modernisation of the industry by
facilitating indigenous design, research and development; steering up India's software industry into automotive
technology; development of domestic safety and environemental standard at par with international standards; assisting
development of vehicles propelled by alternative energy sources.

INTRODUCTION

obligations and mutual responsibilities of both the parties are clearly specified indicating the intensions and the objectives to be achieved.
The main objectives of the MoU system were to improve the performance of the PSE through enhanced autonomy and accountability. It
was also envisaged through the system to provide clarity of goals and objectives to be achieved.

global scenario, drastic reduction of customs duty has opened the door for export of less costlier chemical products to the country. In the
year 1991-92 the rate of customs duty on organic chemicals was 150%, which was brought down to 30% in the year 2002-03. At the
same time C&F international prices of phenol and Acetone have come down to $390 to $310 per metric tonne in March, 2002 from $700
and $500 per metric tonne in March, 2000 respectively.
1.5  The Committee was also informed that the other factors responsibile for limiting the growth of chemical industry are as under:
        1.   Dumping of cheap products in the country.
        2.   Inadequate infrastructure facility (road, rail, port)
        3.   High cost of finance (interest rates are high)
        4.   Uneconomic size of plants (due to erstwhile licensing system)
        5.   High power cost (utility costs are high)
        6.   Inefficient process technology
        7.   Basic Feed Stock prices are high
        8.   Cascading effect of various taxes and duties
        9.   Stringent labour laws
II. MoU System in HOCL
2.1  The commitments and the mutual responsibilities of the Government and the PSE are clearly defined in the MoU system. The targets
are finalised before the beginning of the financial year and the performance evaluation with respect to these targets is carried out only at
the end of the year. The focus under the MoU system has shifted to achievements of results. Ministries have begun to withdraw from
their tendency to control by procedures. MoU has therefore increased operational autonomy of the enterprise.
2.2  Through the MoU system an effort has been made to strike a balance between the static and dynamic performance parameters. While
the static parameters in the form of financial/physical targets are essential to make the PSEs financially viable, the dynamic parameters in
the form of productivity, marketing efforts, modernization, technology upgradation, quality control, project implementation, R&D,
customer satisfaction and HRD are included keeping in view the growth of the PSEs on a long term basis. By emphasising on the
dynamic parameters and comparing the performance with the private sector, the MoU system made an attempt to help the PSEs to face
competition.
2.3  Recently, the strategic issues and benchmarks have also been introduced to make the MoU system more dynamic. This is a step
towards the direction of helping the PSEs to become global players and to face the competition in a situation of globalisation.
2.4  The performance evaluation under the MoU system is carried out only at the end of the year, however, the Administrative Ministries
undertake quarterly/half-yearly review of performance. With introduction of MOU system, the discussions during these meetings is
reportedly become more focused. This has led to higher quality of debate about the performance of the PSEs.
2.5  By making a distinction between the managerial performance and the performance of the enterprise under the MoU system the
judgements on the performance of managements of the PSEs have become much more fair. This has been very good for the morale of the
employees who know that gross generalisation about public secotor is unfair.
2.6  HOCL signed its first MoU with the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers in the year 1991-92. The effectiveness of signing of MoU
by the HOCL can be gauged from the following facts:
          1.   Several projects (capacity expansion & diversification) implemented with a capital outlay  upto Rs. 50 crores within the Board's
powers under the authority delegated to MoU signing  PSUs.
          2.   The physical performance review/evaluation resulted in continuous growth.
          3.   Inclusion of additional dynamic parameters in MoU ensured sustained overall growth.
          4.   Earlier protective environment in duty structure ensured continuous growth in company's physical and financial parameters.
          5.   Drastic reduction in the duty and consequently withdrawal of duty protection resulted in revision of MOU parameters including
the emphasis on five main core products for performance evaluation criteria.

price of its products. The company was suffering from small size of plants, high power and interest rate, low labour productivity and
lower margins. It was mentioned that it was difficult for HOCL to achieve long term economic viability without substantial injection of
new funds to revamp the operations at global scale.
2.9  In view of the drastic reduction of import duty and availability of cheap import, a contrasting situation has emerged. The company
has a good performance record as per MoU rating. If we go by MoU rating it          cannot be said that it has failed in its pursuit of results,
but its operational losses gives an impression that if the losses continue it will be on the road towards its closure. In this regard, the
mention of the mission of signing the MoU and Government's responsibilities is relevant. The mission of signing the MoU by HOCL
with the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers is to retain the leadership in chemical business and emerge as a global player. Moreover,
Part II of the MoU mentioned that Government would provide all possible help to safeguard the interest of the company. Department of
Public Enterprises has also stated that the strategic issues and benchmarks   have also been introduced to make the MoU system more
dynamic and this is a step towards the direction of helping the PSEs to become global Players and to face competition in a situation of
globalisation. In such a situation, the Committee feels that in view of the ground reality, the Government should come out with a scheme
to help the company to come out of the woods. Otherwise, the high sounded words enshrined in the MoU document will remain a pious
desire while the company with a good track record would make its journey towards its doom.

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
3.  The Committee after having the interaction session with HOC and going through all reading material supplied by it marks the
following observations/recommendations:-
3.1  The Committee after examining the performance of HOC within the MoU parameters is of the opinion that weightage should be
given to the role played by HOC in developing those chemical derivatives, which are being imported at exorbitant prices.
3.2  The Committee is of the opinion that dumping of cheap chemical products from the countries like China is a major reason for the
deteriorating performance of the indigenous chemical sector industry. The Committee recommends that Anti dumping mechanism be
activated to ensure cheap import and the Government should take up the matter with the designated authorities in this regard.
3.3  The Committee was concerned to note that adequate steps to make the Indian Chemical Industry  globally competitive have not been
taken by the Government. The Committee is of the view that adequate steps to establish world scale capacities for achieving economies
of scale be taken.
3.4  The Committee also observed that having regard to the vital sector in which the unit is operating the structure of the MoU should be
more appropriately geared to this factor. It was observed the focus on financial performance, which is being reiterated in the MoU, should
be altered to shift the focus on more important factors of national interest. Hence the MoU should accord higher weightage to
performance parameters relating R&D Development of Import subsidies etc.
3.5  The Committee recommends that Department of Public Enterprises should support any move made by the Ministry of Chemicals and
fertilizers for securing loan/budgetary support etc. to help the company. The Committee also stresses that the Ministry of Chemicals and
Fertilizers being the administrative Ministry should take appropriate steps in this regard on a priority basis. The Committee hopes that the
Ministry will come forward to lend its helping hand to the company in this hour of need.
3.6  The Committee, after having interactions with the CMD of HOC, advocates the following remedies for making chemical industry
globally competitive:
        1.   WTO safeguard measure to be adopted to protect Indian industry against dumping
        2.   Technology upgradation
`       3.   Amendment of labour laws
        4.   Duty-free import of catalyst
        5.   Establish world scale capacities for economies of scale
        6.   Adequate infrastructure facility of international standard
        7.   Reduce power cost
        8.   Reduce cost of finance
        9.   Amalgamation and merger of units
      10.   Basic Feed Stock to be made available at FOB prices delivered to user industry

more appropriately geared to this factor. It was observed the focus on financial performance, which is being reiterated in the MoU, should
be altered to shift the focus on more important factors of national interest. Hence the MoU should accord higher weightage to
performance parameters relating R&D and Development of Import subsidies etc.(Para 3.4)
The Committee recommends that Department of Public Enterprises should support any move made by the Ministry of Chemicals and
Fertilizers for securing Loan/budgetary support etc. to help the company. The Committee also stresses that the Ministry of Chemicals and

Ministry will come forward to lend its helping hand to the company in this hour of
need.                                                                                                                                  (Para 3.5)
The Committee, after having interactions with the CMD of HOC, advocates the following remedies for making chemical industry
globally competitive:

          4.  Duty-free import of catalyst

the Committee, hereby present this Ninety-fifth Report on the Inter-PSU Cooperation in Engineering and Construction

NEW DELHI ;

DR.  P.C. ALEXANDER
 Chairman,
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry.
 
REPORT                                       
CHAPTER-I
INTRODUCTION
1.1   At the time of India’s Independence in 1947, the country had been facing a plethora of problems, which needed to be
tackled in a planned and methodical manner. Primarily, our country being an agrarian economy had negligible industrial
base, low level of savings, inadequate investment with virtually no infrastructural facilities. A large population was below
poverty line and inequalities prevailed in income, levels of employment coupled with lack of trained manpower, which led to
regional imbalances.
1.2   In order to attain the industrial growth, a big initiative was needed from the Government as the private sector had neither
the necessary resources in terms of funds, managerial and scientific skills nor the will to undertake risks involved in large
long gestation investment. In view of the wide range of problems faced by the country on its economic, social and strategic
fronts, it became a necessity to deploy the public sector as an instrument for self-reliant economic growth to overcome the
industrial backwardness. In addition, the adoption of Indian constitution also identified two major National missions, namely
needing self reliance and social justice in the chapter IVof the Constitution.
1.3   Hence, Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 was amended in time with a emphasis on   strategic role in the economy.
Massive investments have been made in last five decades to build a public sector. Many of public sector enterprises
successfully expanded production, opened up new areas of technology and built up a resource of technical competence in a
number of areas.
1.4   Some of the major objectives of setting up public enterprises had been as under:
l     To ensure rapid economic growth and industrialisation of the country and create necessary infrastructure for
economic development;
l     To earn return on investment and thus generate resources for development;
l     To promote redistribution of income and wealth;
l     To create employment opportunities;
l     To promote balanced regional development;
l     To assist the development of small-scale and ancillary industries;
l     To promote import substitutions, save and earn foreign exchange for the economy; and
l     To create national wealth for larger public good.
1.5   In order to improve the portfolio and performance of public enterprises in a liberalised economy, and also involve
private sector participation be nation building the Government of India announced on  24
th July 1991, as a part of the
Statement on Industrial Policy a Statement on Public Sector  Policy also. The Statement contains the following decisions:-
(i)    Portfolio of public sector investments will be reviewed with a view to focus the public sector on strategic, high-tech
and essential infrastructure. Whereas some reservation for the public sector is being retained, there would be no bar
for area of exclusivity to be opened up to the private sector selectively. Similarly, the public sector will also be
allowed entry in areas not reserved for it.
(ii)    Public entreprises which are chronically sick and which are unlikely to be turned around will, for the formulation
of revival/rehabilitation schemes, be referred to the Board for industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) or
other similar high level institutions created for the purpose. A  social security mechanism will be created to protect
the interests of workers likely to be affected by such rehabilitation packages.
(iii)   In order to raise resources and encourage wide public participation, part of the government’s share-holding in the
public sector would be offered to mutual funds, financial institutions, general public and workers.
(iv)   Boards of public sector companies would be made more professional and given greater powers.
(v)   There will be a greater thrust on performance improvement through the Memoranda of Understanding (MoU)
system by which managements would be granted greater autonomy and will be held accountable. Technical
expertise on the part of the Government would be upgraded to make the MoU negotiations and implementation
more effective.

NINETY - FIFTH  REPORT COMMITTEE  ON  INDUSTRY
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/95threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:21:51]
(vi)   To facilitate discussion on performance, the MoU signed between Government and the public enterprises would be
placed in Parliament. While focusing on major management issues, this would also help place matters on the day-
to-day operations of public enterprises in their correct perspective.
1.6   As per the announcement in the Industrial Policy Statement and also in the Budget Speech of  July  1991 in order to
raise resources. Encourage wide public participation and promote greater accountability, the government equity in selected
public enterprises was to be offered to Mutual Funds, Financial Institutions , workers and general public.
1.7   The main elements of the present government policy towards public sector enterprises are:
l     Bring down government equity in all non-strategic  PSEs to 26 percent or lower, if necessary;
l     Restructure and review potentially viable PSEs;
l     Close down PSEs which can not be revived; and  
l     Fully protect the interests of workers.
1.8   A development of this nature had an immediate impact on the prospects of several public  sector units. Overnight, the
“Sellers’  Market’’ was converted into “ Buyers’ Market’’. The industrial units, where investments ran into hundred of
thousands of crores of rupees were allowed to go to the wall to lay waste investments sunk in the past. The impact can further
be gauzed from the fact that 66 industrial PSEs whose net worth had become negative and had become sick were registered
with BIFR  as  on 31.6.01 and a number of PSUs were closed. In the circumstances the endeavour ought to be to extract
whatever output is extractable from installed industrial capacity if these products have a ready market within the country and
that should be the justification enough for the process of production in these units not being permitted to come to halt.
1.9   The Committee in its 17
th report on “Industrialisation of Backward  Areas and the State of the Capital Goods Sector’’
while dealing with the impact to liberalisation on the Indian industry observed as follows:
        “ This state of ambivalence will perhaps contiune for some while. In the meantime, it will be instructive if limited
experiments could be tried out pursuant to various suggestions offered to the committee. One such suggestion is for common
productions planning by a group of sick public sector units located in reasonable proximity to one another and specialising in
a similar range of products by interacting closely with one another and ensuring that the output of one units is accepted as
input in a neighbouring units and vice versa, both units , it is claimed could significantly improve the prospects of their
survival. Should that be the case, even banks and financial institutions might decide to change their general approach.’’
1.10However, neither the government  nor the PSEs took any initiaive to make a serious effort to translate the suggestion into
reality. Sub-committee-III  for Ministry of Heavy  Industry and Public  Enterprises of Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry under the convenorship of Dr. B. B.Ramaiah, while doing an exercise on the study of the
instrument of MoU signed by the Central PSUswith their administrative Ministries, also observed that no weightage had been
given to inter-PSUcooperation in the MoUs. The Committee felt that in the new economic scenario the collaborative
approach amongst the PSUs under various Ministries should be evolved without compromising the competitive spirit and
quality.
1.11The committee further observed that liberalisation and globalisation has had an impact on the overall industrial scenario.
Transition form a closed economy to a free market economy has meant opening of floodgates of unforeseen troubles for
some of these PSUs. These PSUs should be given enough elbow room to adapt themselves in accordance with the new
realities. They  need an impetus for sustaining mutual cooperations in respect of their works order position,  R&Dand
technological development , etc. This could be addressed through inter-PSUcollaborative approach.
1.12This shall not only ensure a better-coordinated and healthy relationship between these PSUs but also address issues of
better responsiveness, better quality of product, better degree of adherence to delivery schedules and cost effectiveness.
This will also in a way encourage R&Defforts of the supplier PSUs enabling them to upgrade and update their products,
services and technologies to the needs of the client  PSUs and departments as well as foster other synergetic endeavour
like concurrent engineering drawing to Delivery collaboration etc.
CHAPTER-II
 INTERACTION WITH THE PSUs
2.     A meeting was covered on the 14 th October 2001   at  Hyderabad   to interact with the CMDs of Engineering and
Construction schemes.    On  the issue of inter-PSU, cooperation most of the CMDs present in that meeting stated that the
member PSUs should cooperate and coordinate with each other so as to explore the possibilities of permanent mechanism for
cooperation in respect of work orders, export orientation, sharing of R&D experiences, forming of Joint venture, etc.
        The viewpoints expressed by the representatives of PSUs are given below:
3.     BHEL
3.1   BHEL has been following a policy of procuring materials/items from PSEs who are technically qualified and meet

NINETY - FIFTH  REPORT COMMITTEE  ON  INDUSTRY
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/95threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:21:51]
delivery and quality requirements as this is essential to make the competitive intensity in the opened –up market. Regarding
implementation of the purchase preference policy, BHEL includes purchase preference clause in its NIT (Notice Inviting 
Tender). The PSEs , which meet the required techincal conditions and specifications of quality, deliveries etc. are further
considered for order placement. BHEL also procures material on the basis of long-term  Memorandum of
Understsnding/public/rate contracts negotiated with PSEs such as SAIL, Hindustan  Zinc, Indian Oil  Corporation etc.
Similarly in the area of machine tool services, HMT and HEC have been given preference by BHEL for condescending and
modernisation contracts. Wherever possible, construction services have also been taken from PSEs like Bridge and Roof,
NPC, NIDC   etc. Last two PSEs are currently involved in a Rs 6 crore civil works contract for blade shop at BHEL,
Haridwar.
3.2   During the last year (2000-2001), around  Rs 410 crores of contracts were awarded by the BHEL to PSEs including Rs.
54 crores to central PSEs under the engineering and construction sectors. During the last three years, orders placed on central
PSEs under the engineering and construction sectors were Rs. 152 crores.
3.3   BHEL is continuing to pursue Inter-PSU cooperation as outlined above. Whereas the orders placed on BHEL by other
PSEs in the last three years on the basis of purchase preference has been only to the extent of Rs. 328 crores for non-power
sector areas, BHEL has awarded contracts worth Rs. 600 crores to other PSEs on purchase preference basis. Majority of
tenders placed by various petrochemicals etc are on competitive basis. There are many possibilities of business operation
which can be exploited provided such an opportunity is given  e. g. partnership in manufacturing defence equipment with
Ordnance Factory Board, with RITES  and other railways organisations for railways equipment, locomotive, etc.
3.4   On its part, BHELhas taken steps to enhance cooperation with other  PSEs by entering into MoUs and organising
customer focus groups. It has entered into MoU with Bhakra Beas Management for renovation, modernization and
upgradation of hydro sets. Recently in September 2001, an MoU has been entered into with EIL with the objective of jointly
addressing certain identified areas of business. Utilising the complementary strengths of the two organisations, BHEL has
also organised a marketing and project management group at Mumbai to service certain segments of ONGC’s requirements
for modernisation and renovation of off  -shore and on-shore  drilling equiment and platforms.
4.     HEAVY  ENGINEERING  CORPORATION
4.1   Heavy Engineering Corporation was set up as a temple of modern India in accordance with the Nehruvian dream to
provide strong industrial bases for the country. In the manufacturing facilities of casting, forging navigation and machining
has been created all under one umbrella and it became the biggest integrated engineering complex of South Asia and it is one
of the very few such set-ups all over the world. There are only a few countries over the globe that have facilities comparable
to Heavy Engineering Corporation. They treat this type of industry as a crown jewel among their heavy industries in respect
of the engineering capability and self-reliance to the nation. In spite of many odds and world wars they were safeguarded
against devastation
4.2   Heavy Engineering Corporation’s facilites were cerated basically to cater to the needs of core sector steel industry. 
Nation’s planners envisaged that by the turn of the last century India would acquire the capability to produce 100 million ton
steel to meet its projected demand and to establish such complexes this company was created not only to arrest the drain of
foreign exchange but simultaneously to establish world-class manufacturing setup specifically to cater to this objective. The
company supplied more than 5.50  lakh  tonnes of equipments for steel plants.
4.3     Apart from steel sector, this company also caters to the need of other sectors namely mining,  coal,  aluminium,  power,
railways,  defence and other areas like nuclear, atomic and space research.  
4.4   It has supplied mining shovels, which constitute backbone and are the most commonly used prime mining equipment in
open cast mining of various subsidiaries of coal India Ltd. spread over the coal-mining belt of the nation. It is among the very
few companies in the world that manufacture heavy duty crushers used for ore- processing . More than 60 percent of this
company’s products are of import substitution in nature and it supplies to many PSUs and other government organisations.
4.5   It has contributed in products of strategic importance in the areas of defence, nuclear and space. These are fields which
are either difficult to get or the country would have paid exorbitant price for such items. This has become more significant
when the country has to face the embargo on high technology components items from USA and other developed world after
Pokhran experiments.
4.6   It has entered into technical collaboration agreements with leading manufacturers in the world,  observed, assimilated 
and  Indianised the same to widen technical Knowledge base of India. Thereby it also created technically competent pool of
manpower in other organisations both private as well as public sector all over the country. As the talent in this company went
out over the years, in search of better prospects in their careers.
4.7   Quality  remained the hallmark of this company’s  products and received commendations from foreign experts. In 
2000-2001  it produced ultra clean steel for some strategic defence need and properties achieved were much superior to the
foreign specifications.
4.8   As the priorities  changed, the nation’s plans didn’t materialise and economy did not pick up to the desired level. It too

had to pay heavy price in the form of un-utilised capacity right from its inception. Commercial viability became significant
after the initiation of economic reforms since 1991. Added to this, recession in the capital goods sector caused further harm in
procuring orders for its survival.
        Some problems specific to this company, which need redress, are:
l     Huge infrastructure has been created and the same remains under-utilised.
l     It is being denied orders by other PSUs on the ground of its negative net worth.
l     Tailor-made stringent and unreasonable specifications are framed by PSUs to deny orders to this company in

l     Some PSEs even do not open the bids of others without proper justifications. It is forced to submit EMD and
securities prior to bid opening on par with others in spite of credentials of being established supplier of many of the

l     It is denied its due payments and the payment issues are put into complex disputes and delays by other PSUs.
l     Instead of mutual cooperation through synergising their capabilities and abilities, PSUs are engaging in working
against each other.
l     Foreign collaborations for technology by more than one  PSU for the same product leads to additional drainage of
foreign exchange through licence fee, royalty and higher import.
5.     NATIONAL  INSTRUMENTS  LTD.
5.1   The Company is engaged in design, development, manufacturing and marketing of opto-mechanical and opto-electronic
instruments, both for civil as well as defence use. The company in India is good brand equity and is also an accredited and
registered supplier of equipments and instruments to defence establishments.
5.2   
Present Purchase Preference 
        The present purchase preference is applicable for PSUs purchase in case of value of Rs. One crore or more. Under
existing policy, there is no purchase preference to PSUs as such, excepting that in case of any  PSU/  government
organisations quoted price is higher by  10  percent with reference to the lowest bidder, the tender  PSU/ government bodies
are called for price negotiation and given an opportunity to lower their price at the level of the lowest bidder.  Therefore the
PSU/ government organisations, unless they actually became the lowest bidder are not entitled to get on a contract and hence
not entail any preference.
5.3   In case of National  Instruments Ltd. the tender that generally comes out and the  company responds to at all is less than
Rs 1 crore.   So the company is not able to derive any benefit because of the value ceiling, i.e. Rs.1crore. In case a purchase
made by this company, the procurement quantum/value of each tender is much lower than  Rs1 crore and as such, the
company is not in a position to extend its benefits to any  PSU/ Government departments.
5.4   Necessity of Purchase Preference
        The company earnestly feels that there is a distinctive necessity of purchase preference applicable to  PSUs/
government  departments.
5.5   The purchase preference if it has to be beneficial to this company the value limit of tender and that is purchase should be
Rs 10 lakhs and above. Since the cost structure of PSUs/ Government organisations are to absorb some social costs/
overheads, apart from the laid down wage structure required to be followed, as compared to the private sector, threrfore to
stand in the competitive market it is necessary that the price preference should be allowed to all PSUs in their bids to other
PSUs and that should at least be 9-10 percent.
5.6   It is also felt that it should be mandatory to all  PSU/  government bodies that certain part of the total annual purchase is
to be purchased /Procured directly from other PSUs eligible to supply.
6.     IRCON
6.1   Lease Export of Machinery and Equipment
        The Indian projects exporters temporarily  export some construction equipment from India for a particular project
abroad and on its completion, may have to shift the same to another project, either in the same or another country and it may
finally be more than five years before such equipment  is imported back into India. As part of the current rules, such re-
import attracts customs duty even though no export benefit may have been availed at the time of export. Levy of customs
duty on import of such machinery and equipment on which exports benefits had been availed is understandable and is
appreciated  but levying import duty on equipment and machinery which was temporarily exported without having exports
benefits, defies common sense. This needs to be quickly rectified.
6.2   Similarly, certain equipment/machinery may be exported from India for overseas leasing purpose without any export
benefits and may have to be re-imported and after particular leasing business is over. For example, IRCON had

NINETY - FIFTH  REPORT COMMITTEE  ON  INDUSTRY
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/95threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:21:51]
imported/exported some metre-gauge diesel locomotives on lease from Indian Railways for further sub-leasing to the
Malaysia Railways. However, all along , the locomotive remained on the books of Indian Railways. No export benefits,
whatsoever, had been availed. Surprisingly, customs authorities are levying 40% customs duty on locomotives in all such
cases where re-import is done after five years. Such leavy of customs duty will seriously jeopardise import and leading from
India. It is understood that this problem has arisen due to an amendment to section 25 clause (2) through the Finance Act
1999as a result of which the Central Government’s power to allow exemption of import duty under the Act, is restricted to
goods of strategy or secret nature or for charitable purpose. Hence, it is requested that this clause be suitably amended as to
restore the power of the government for exemption of customs duty on import of such machinery and equipment on which no
export benefits has been availed at the time of temporary export.
6.3   Providing a Freedom and Flexibility to the PSUs to form and offer attractive Voluntary Retirement Schemes
        IRCON is a consistently profit-making company under the Ministry of Railways. However, due to heavy recruitment in
the early stages, the company is burdened with more than 700 surplus staff in various categories. AVRSwas framed in
accordance with income tax rules and also the Government guidelines and offered to the employees from time to time. The
response has not been very encouraging.
6.4   Based on our experience it is felt that there is need to make the scheme more attractive. For this purpose, some
amendments may be required in tax rules and also the Government guidelines.
6.5   As section 10 (10C) of the Income Tax Act  1961 read with rule  2EA  of the Income Tax Rules 1962,  the amount
receivable on account of retirement should not exceed the amount equivalent to three months salary for each completed year
of service or three months per year of remaining service for superannuation. A further ceiling upto Rs. 5 lakhs has been
placed by the Finance Act 2000.
6.6   These limits are too law. After implementation of revised scales of pay both in the CDA as well as IDA scales of pay,
the limits mentioned above operate in such a manner that even for a 20-22 years of service, employees only in a very low
scale of pay fall within the eligible range. This restricts the scope of the scheme very much.
6.7   Even in the case of those who were eligible, the amounts are too meagre to act as an inducement. An amount equivalent
to five to six months pay per years of completed service or balance service subject to a ceiling of Rs.10  lakhs may be
considered reasonable. If judiciously invested, this amount of VRS package may provide them months return of 70-75% of
the normal monthly wages. With this they may feel reasonably secure to opt forVRSand look for alternative avenues of
income to make up for the monthly shortfalls.
6.8   Due to existing scheme being an unattractive one, the surplus employees have to be continued in employment. As a
consequence, the organisation continues to bear not only the cost of the  monthly wages but also an avoidable attendant cost
on housing , office, transport , electricity, LTC, statutory bonus,  contribution to P.F., medical expenses, etc. The total cost to
the organisation thus comes out to be much more than the bare cost of employee alone. It would be more economical to offer
VRS terms and reduce surplus staff than to continue to bear the avoidable cost perpetually. In fact, indirect benefits would
also accrue by way of increased efficiency with lesser number of staff.
6.9   Needless to say, the separation package should be such as can reasonably be expected to enable an employee to make a
new beginning in life. Also, the separation package should have a more humane face.
6.10Further, the Income Tex rules and government  guidelines on VRSshould be such that they promote VRSscheme. At
present, the rather lukewarm response to the scheme suggest that there is need for serious reconsideration.
6.11It is appreciated that some PSUs may not be able to afford more liberal voluntary retirement schemes. However, PSUs
which can afford to pay more attractive separation package, should be allowed to frame more liberal schemes so as to right
size the manpower establishment in order  to face the increasing competition.
6.12It is, therefore, necessary that current provisions of Income Tax Rules including the Upper ceiling of 5 lakh are
considered for modifications as suggested above.

CHAPTER-III
CONTENTIOUS  ISSUES  CONCERNING  THE  PSUs
25.   Implementation Issues and Suggestions
25.1Any attempt for Inter-PSU cooperation should take into account the interests and meet the requirements of ultimate
consumer in the opened up economy, for example PSEs in the infrastructure sector should be able to join hands and deliver a
project to the satisfaction of customers within reasonably qualifying conditions. The implementation of such a policy requires
orchestrated efforts and to be successful requires policy directives from the owner, the Government of India, to the concerned
ministries and PSEs under them.
25.2Many of the users sector PSEs such as those in power sector and also SEBs specify their own venders for procurement of
certain equipments and also prescribe approval of sub-vendors. This condition often works to the detriment of the PSEs.
25.3Within the PSEs themselves, both the suppliers and end-users, there is need for increased cooperation and understanding
in terms of provisions such as suitable risk sharing in respect of penalty clauses as well as field trials  of new products
developed etc.
25.4It has been observed in certain instances that PSEs, which developed products linked to a single dominant customer
which is another PSU and make long-term fixed investment in equipment technology, manpower, etc, do not get to realize
adequate returns due to sudden drop in order inflow (In case of BHEL are Turret casting, SRGM Locos etc.).
26.   Purchase Preference for Central PSEs
26.1The genesis of purchase preference to PSEs lies basically in better utilisation of assets and facilities created at great cost
to the economy to enable the country improve its GDP growth. At present the role of private sector especially in the
infrastructure, basic goods and other core sectors of the economy, is limited. The public sector investment still far outweighs
the private sector investment and as such, better utilization of the public sector assets will have beneficial impact on the
overall economic growth, which has been assisted by continuation of purchase preference policy.
26.2The premise that private sectors and MNCs could be constrained from bidding with the continuation of purchase
preference is not factual. There is also no linkage between purchase preference scheme and quality of products, as any
company including PSEs bidding for purchase under ICB has to first meet the qualifying technical and quality requirements.
Also, there is no impact on the project cost as PSEs have to match the lowest bidding price (L1) and provided thier own
prices within 10% of L1.
26.3In the context that PSEs are not truly Board managed as in the case of private sector, the policy of purchase preference
has served the purpose of neutralising some of the disadvantages faced by them. However, in the present business
environment, there is need to expedite the process of transformation of PSEs to autonomous Board managed companies so
that the need of such preferences can be obviated. This premise is evident from the fact that as PSEs gain competitive
strength, when purchase preference is not being used.
27.   Policy Issues
27.1In this background, the inter-PSE cooperation could fit in only if such cooperation is based on factors such as

competitiveness, meeting technical requirements, adherence to reasonable qualification criteria etc., especially in case of
International Competitive Bidding (ICB) tenders. These are hallmarks of today's business environment in the opened up
economy where public sectors not covered under administered price regime have to compete with Indian private sector and
multinational companies at times even on unequal footing. Therefore, as a pre-requisite, any inter-PSE cooperation has to
have a directive from the centre and a mandate for being operational and successful.
27.2Most of the public sector enterprises in the industrial field were created for catering to the infrastructure  needs of the
country where investment from private sector was not forthcoming. As such, if at all there is going to be any structured inter-
PSE cooperation, it should cover all the areas of infrastructure etc. by utilizing their synergies rather than catering to only the
inter-PSE needs in the engineering and construction sectors.
27.3With the opening up of the Indian economy, sectoral policies are no more seamlessly linked and every company has to
compete with every other company for getting business in India as well as abroad. In this scenario inter-PSE cooperation
should be directed by a Government policy framework on the subject which should ensure that policy pronouncements and
their implementation are beyond the purview of WTO provisions but also competition law, which is equally applicable to
PSEs, may also come in the way of mutual cooperation unless validated by a national policy framework.
27.4However, inter PSE cooperation for maximizing the business among public sector units and utilizing the assets created at
great cost to the country is a desirable objective at the national level, which will have positive impact on the economy. While
ensuring that this objective is realised, it is also necessary that the PSEs be enabled to become competitive, for which a policy
framework should be in place to ensure availability of critical inputs such as technology flows, which are particularly
necessary for PSEs in the engineering and construction sectors.
27.5Suggestions to improve the viability of PSUs
l     PSUs should form a consortium or enter into a joint venture partnerships to exploit their potential strength in the
best manner so that they can compete with MNCs.
l     There should be central coordination committee to guide and encourage PSUs to pull up their resources and form
consortium.
l     There should be a central coordination committee to bring together buyer as well as seller PSUs across the table to
sort out their issues/disputes.
l     There should be an overseeing mechanism and laid down policy to stop duplication of foreign collaborations for
similar products by different PSUs.
l     Since the large infrastructure is not fully utilized, purchase preference should continue.
l     Dealings amongst the PSUs Should be more transparent and documents resulting to decision by one accessible to
the other.
27.6Authorising MDs of MoU signing PSUs to approve overseas tour programmes of the functional Directors
27.7Based on Cabinet approval, DPE had agreed to authorise MDs of MoU-signing-PSUs to approve overseas tour
programme of the functional Directors. Subsequently, on the instructions from the Ministry of Heavy Industry, the DPE had
withdrawn these powers with the result that proposals for overseas visits of even functional directors of all PSUs have to be
sent for minister's approval.
27.8More than 50 per cent of IRCON's annual business comes from overseas operations. It is to be appreciated that IRCON
basically contracts the company and clients are required to discuss urgent contract projects related issues with the top
management of the contract or company at a very short notice of 2-3 days. The normal procedure of obtaining approval from
the concerned Minister takes anything from two to three weeks, with the result that it becomes embarrassing to explain to the
client about delay in coming for meeting/discussion.
27.9It is therefore suggested that while tour programmes of MDs of MoU signing companies may still be approved by the
concern Minister, authority of MDs in MoU signing PSUs to approve overseas program of the functional directors should be
restored at the earliest so as to remove this handicap.
Observation on Purchase Preference
27.10 From the above background it is absolutely clear that the very aim of the Government to implement the philosophy of
purchase preference in the true spirit is defeated when more than one PSU bidders participate for a job, since the situation
leads to competition amongst the bidding PSUs undercutting each other and possibly submitting cost ineffective proposals.
Even if there is one PSU bidder for a particular job, and PSU customers prepared to give a purchase preference to the bidding
PSUs, in absence of the proper level playing field, it sometimes becomes impossible for the bidding PUSs to match the price
of L1 bidders in the private sector. In fact, in tender enquiries of PSU customers, more often do not mention purchase
preference clause. Not only this, bid qualify and consequent requirements framed in such a way e.g. minimum turnover
figures and profitability for three consequent financial years prior to bid submission date etc. match, i.e., some PSU bidders

27.11 To the entire background and philosophy of setting up of various PSUs several years back as compared to many private
sector companies and multinationals, who had very definite advantages of entering the field later need to be pragmatically
understood to ensure proper level playing field to PSUs.
Global Tenders
27.12 Many of the major PSUs particularly in coal and power sector had been issuing global tenders even for range of the
equipments that are available indigenously with established manufacturing and product support/service facilities and the
products are already established with purchaser PSU for a long time. Even though such global tenders may provide for
purchase preference to central PSUs, the following anomalies still exist which require to be addressed to for providing level
playing field and implementing the govt. policy in letter and spirit.
(a)   Price preference of 15%: against all global tenders, MNCs are eligible to participate and this amounts to
international competitive bidding. In such ICB where purchases financed by multilateral agencies like IBRD, ADB
etc. bids offering the goods manufactured in the purchaser's country with minimum 30% value addition on ex-works
price quoted and that production facility has been extended at least since the date of bid submission and considered
under group 'A' category. The fully imported offers are considered under group 'C' category. For the bids under 'A'
category, there are domestic price preferences of 15% on CIF value of imported goods (amount of customs duty and
other import tax that a non-exempt importer would have to pay for importation of goods offered under 'C' category or
15% of CIF value of goods offered, whichever is low) in evaluation. If group 'A' of domestic bidder thus becomes L1
in evaluation, after considering 15% price preference, group 'A' domestic bidder will not get contract at the bid price
quoted. This facility of 15% price preference to indigenous goods evaluation is not available in respect of global
tenders, where competition will be from international bidders, same in line with World Bank tenders. This facility of
15% price preference is to be extended by Government of India to all global tenders.
28.   Bid Currencies
28.1In IBRD and ADB tenders, indigenous bidders are allowed to quote in foreign currency also and are paid in currency
quoted. This is not being allowed in domestic and global bids and indigenous manufacturers are asked to quote price in
rupees only, whereas in case of imported offer evaluation is done by converting the foreign currency bids into Indian Rupees
at the exchange rate, as applicable on the date of bid opening; the actual outgo will be at the rate as applicable on the date of
payment against shipments though L/C.
28.2Hence domestic bidders particularly where import content is substantial (meeting the minimum value addition of 30 pc)
should be allowed to quote in foreign currency also for import content and subject to same type of evaluation as applied in
fully imported equipment. Payment should also be made to domestic bidders for the foreign currency portion in equivalent
rupees, at the exchange rate applicable on the date of supply, without asking for further confirmation on documents.
29.   Special Additional Duty
29.1As per policy, SAD is applied at 4% on all imports and the same is non-MOD vatable. In the case of indigenous offer,
particularly where the value of import content is high, SAD is paid on import content and in addition, CST is also charged at
4% on the ex-factory price plus FD. Thus, indigenous offers will be in a disadvantageous position when compared to the
imported offer in total evaluation to the extent of CST.
        The following points need consideration
(a)     Purchase preference to be given for domestic offers onIy between established non-PSE sector and established
PSE sector including joint ventures in the later case, subject to value addition being minimum 30%.
(b)   In case of global tenders, domestic bidders should be given 15% preference as allowed in the case of
international competitive bidding, in addition to purchase preference.
(c)   Domestic bidders to be allowed to quote in foreign currency plus Indian Rupees when import content is of a
high value and payments to be made by purchasing PSE to selling PSE in equivalent Indian Rupees, for
corresponding foreign exchange value at the exchange rate as applicable on the date of supplies.
(d)   Purchase policy is to be extended for another three years that is up to 31st March 2005.
(e)   All tenders issued by the central PSUs and Government departments (central and state) for goods and services
of more than one crore value should incorporate purchase preference clause strictly in line with the government
guidelines and extend the same to a bids offered by selling PSUs as mandatory.
(f)    In case of global tenders, the tender document should contain 15% price preference in evaluation and if
domestic central PSE offer becomes L1 with this price preference, the order should be placed on the central
PSE at the quoted price.
29.2Exemption to PSUs should be given from submission of Earnest Money deposit. In lieu of draft/cash/B.G., PSUs should
be allowed to submit indemnity bond.
