9.6 (ii) The Committee, therefore, finds that foreign investment and technical collabora­
tion has been approved in Industrial Sector relating to even Food Processing Industries to 
the tune of 8472.2 millions of rupees without any consideration for the growth of indigenous 
industries in this Sector. Food Processing Industry have to a large extent depend on the local 
ancillary small scale and village and cottage industries and thereby there is no safeguard for 
the survival and development of such industries. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that :-
fa) disinvestment by PSUs and the funds accrued on account of the disinvestment 
should be utilised for reviving, and restructuring of the sick PSUs. The demand for 
grants and performance budget are totally silent on this aspect; 
(b) foreign investments should be approved in areas where we are yet to develop the 
technical know-how and depend upon foreign technology, The Government should 
ensure that foreign investment is earmarked for industries in the export sector to 
boost up the export of our industrial production. It should not disturb and dislocate 
the existing industrial growth of the country in the long run. The foreign 
collaboration should be identified for industries where we are lagging behind in 
international market. The Committee regrets to note that the demand for grants for 
the Department of Heavy Largest Industry does not perceive this situation and no 
funds have been allocated to organise and regulate foreign investment in our 
industrial sector particularly in the PSUs which we have developed and grown over 
a period of several decades but for which the present infrastructure for further 
development could not have been there; 
(c) every effort should be made to ensure that all the eight· benches of Board for 
Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) are made functional and the cases of 
sick PSUs pending before them are disposed off expeditiously to minimise the drain 
on the public funds. The Demands for Grants of the Department and the 
Performance Budget do not reflect any concern on the depleted strength of the 
BIFR benches and the expenditure and efforts to be made by the Department to 
make them functional; 
(d) the details of disinvestments made by the Public Sector Undertakings, undertaking­
wise, should be compiled by the Department and the data relating to the sale prices 
of shares, undertaking-wise and the amount of money so collected and spent, 

undertaking-wise may be collected may be furnished to the Committee for further detailed 
examination in order to allay the misgivings in the minds of general publia that the shares 
were sold at throw away prices by some Public Sector Undertakings; and 
(e) concrete steps should be taken by the Department to ensure that foreign investors 
are not allowed to dump their unsold products in India to the detrement of 
indigenous industries. 
9.6 (iii) MUL Incidentally , the Committee finds that the CISF was providing security at 
Maruti Udyog Limited at Gurgaon since 1983. In June 1992, MUL became a non­
government company and it was felt by MUL that the continuance of CISF would probably 
not be possible. MUL looked for alternative arrangements. It was found that Group 4 
Securities India (P) Ltd. was the best. Group 4 Securities is an international security 
company with operations in 40 countries. It started operations in India in February 1990 and 
has six branches in India. After a period of familiarisation and training the Group 4 
contingent has taken over security responsibility for MUL plant w.e.f April 1, 1993. 
The Committee notes with regret that even in the matter of switching over the Security 
network, Maruti Udyog Limited had to opt for an international security company thereby 
opening the door to a multinational company for a job for which trained and adequate 
manpower and resources were available within the country, if it was a necessity to dispense 
with the security cover provided by CISF, local talent and manpower could have been 
engaged by Maruti Udyog.

of exports 28 per cent of the exports are directly done from the units in the small scale

The performance Budget of the Department is silent on the steps taken by it to check the 
downward graph. The Budget estimates for the year 1993-94 for this item is reduced to 40 
crores compared to 45 crores in the preceding year inspite of escalation in prices. 
This is a scheme to benefit educated unemployed youth with low income families and 30% 
of the beneficiaries are from SCJST categories. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the scheme should be implemented with all the available resources so as to ensure that the 
benefits envisaged under the scheme for self-employment provided to large number of 
persons and more funds are allocated. 
9. 7 (ii) Small Scale Industries: A sum of Rs .• 190.40 crores has been provided in the 
Budget Estimates for 1993-94. The revised estimates of 1992-93 were to the tune of Rs. 
147.41 crores. The Development of Small Scale Industries is organised through Development 
Commissioner of Small Scale Industries of the Department. The Committee finds that on 
administration and maintenance of the office of the Development Commissioner an amount 
of Rs. 3.68 crores is provided in the Budget Estimates with a component of 3.10 crores as 
non-plan expenditure. Rs. 58 lakhs are only for plan expenditure on two items i.e. publicity 
for 40 lakhs and for modernisation of library for 18 lakhs in the Budget Estimates. 
Comparing the budget figures for an important item like training which is 3.41 crores with 
that of the expenditure on the maintenance of the office of Development Commissioner, it 
may be seen that expenditure priorities are not on sound lines. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that every step should be taken to regulate the expenditure on this item and 
the money thus saved may be earmarked for other developmental item(s) of the Small Scale 
Industries. 
9. 7 (iii) Khadi and Village Industries: Khadi and Village Industries have been earmarked a 
sum of Rs. 525.64 crores in the current year Budget Estimates compared to 352 crores in the 
last years revised estimates. The Khadi and Village Industries cover a vast majority of our 
population in different areas of the country and primarily cater to the needs of our 
economically weaker sections. The Khadi and Village Industries generate vast potential for 
local employment and if given correct direction and infrastructural support, Kha.di and 
Village Industries can be more helpful in our rural economy. The Committee, however, 
finds that inspite of budgetary support, Khadi and Village Industries have not been able to 
compete in the open market and stand on their legs. The reasons , therefore, have to be 
studied and perceptive planning is to be made to make a beginning so that Khadi and 
Village Industries become self-sufficient in their functioning in all respects. The Commit tee 
finds that no thought is given in the Demands for Grants and there is no expenditure on this 
account. The Committee therefore , recommends that the priorities of expenditure may be 

re-fixed and monetary allocation be made. The Committee further recommends that every 
effort should be made to ensure that Khadi and Village Industri es do not suffer from 
shortage of financial resources, lack of infrastructural support and bureaucratic red-tapi sm. It 
is essent ial that the problem of marketing of the finished goods is taken on top priority. The 
Government should issue instructions at least to their Departments that Khadi/Village/Small 
Scale Industries Products are purchased for their requirements on the pattern of encourage­
ment given for Handloom cloth. The other point the Committee emphasises that it should be 
made obligatory on the part of the establishments of such industrie s to pay minimum living 
wages to the employees. The Committee further recommends that concrete steps are to be 
taken to ensure for the general health and welfare of the workers. Co-operatives in the field 
are to be activised and finished goods are marketed for adequate return. The Committee is 
aware of the fact that rural masses are not gainfully employed throughout the year. Some 
programmes for motivating the rural masses to utilise their spare time in engaging 
themselves in such industries are to be devised. The Committee finds that though a sum of 
Rs. 525.54 crores has been earmarked in the Budget Estimates for this item yet no money 
has been allotted for motivating people and for awareness programm es on the role and the 
utility of Khadi and Village Industries to rural masses. The programme for training 
undertaken by the Department also lacks perception. The Committee opines that prog­
ramme for training should be so designed and chalked out so as to give on the spot training 
and guidance by mobile training personnel in the first instance to familiarise the rural masses 
about various projects/schemes under Khadi and Village Industrie s. The initial phase may 
inrer-alia include ground level information about project, equipment, finance and marketing 
facilities for finished products. Once this phase of training is completed and the masses are 
motivated and assured of additional revenue to the person or to the family then additional 
training programmes as envisaged by the Department in the Budget Estimates would yield 
positive results. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the thrust of the training 
programme should be reoriented and grouped into two phases as mentioned above. 
The Committee trusts that its observations and recommendations will receive serious 
considerat ion for implementation.

6. Taken into account the documents and other material made available to it and oral evidence tendered before 
it the Committee concludes as under :-
6.01 The Performance Budget of the Ministry of Mines for the year 1994-95 states that the Ministry is 
primarily responsible for the regulation and development of the mineral sector including the mining and 
metallurgy of all non ferrous metals both in private and public sectors but excluding Natural Gas , Petroleum 
coal and Atomic minerals. Mmeral resources are national assets. Conservation and planned exploitation of 
minerals are therefore, of prime importance to the national economy. Besides providing the basic inputs to 
domestic industry the mineral sector accounts for sizeable exports and foreign exchange earni ngs. Having 
regard to the extent and variety of mineral resources in the country there is great potential for rapid growth 
of this sector. It is the onus of the. Ministry of the Mines to develop this sector with utmost care and caution 
to enable this sector to compete with the contemporary globalisation in the internatio nal area. But the 
Committee finds that the entire mines and minerals sector is in doldrums. Large number of mines have either 
closed or at the brink of closure. The situation is very alarming particularl y in the States of Bihar , Andhra 
Pradesh , Rajasthan, Goa, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh etc. where a good number of Mines have closed dov·m. 
There is no provision in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the revival of closed Mines in the 
country. The Committee has not been told of any kind of package prepared by the Ministry for the reopening 
of closed mines in the country and make them viable. Rather the Committee has been told that the minerals 
belong to the State Governments. The onus of re-opening of closed mines is therefore the responsibility of 
the States and Ministry has washed its hands off by pointing out the responsibihty on the States ignoring 
the loss being caused to the nation due to the closure of mines throughout the country. The States faced with 
acute resource constraints and are unable to divert their attention towards the closed· mines. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government must also pay attention towards the closed/ 
closing mines throughout the country and prepare a comprehensive package for their revival in 
consultation with the State Governments concerned. There must be a perfect co-ordi nation between 

2 
the Governme nt and the Gove rnm ent of the States in thi s •·egard . The Governm ent should constitut e 
a tea m of experts to find out the causes of closure of mines and suggest the ways for their revival within 
a t ime frame. 
6.02 The Committee finds that there is lack of coordination between the Government and the Government 
of the States as far as regulating of mining is concerned. Responding to a query about the foreign investment 
in the mineral sector after the enactment of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) 
Amendment Act, 1994 the Secretary of Ministry of Mines states that the minerals belong to the State 
Governmen ts. All applicat ions have to be submitted by entrepreneurs to the concerned State Governments 
and it is they who have to give the prospecting licence or the mining lease as the case may be. The 
Government did not have precise information whether any State Government had received any formal 
proposa l and whether any foreign party has applied for any prospecting licence. The Committee finds it not 
convincing. After opening the mineral sector of the country for foreign investment and participation in order 
to accelerating i nflow of domestic and foreign capita l into the mineral sector the Governme nt has left the 
matter entirely to the State Governments. On such a vital issue there should have been a perfect 
understanding and coordination between the Central and State Governments. The Committ ee, ther efor e,

sector and advi se the c once rn ed State Government to make best u se of such a propo sal with out

basic geologic~ I information essential for the successful implementation of practically are the developmen­
tal programmes of the count!). The investigation carried out by GSI contribute directly to the discovery and 
evaluation of mineral resources ensuring thereby the continued and steady supply of vital ra\\ materials to 
the core industrial sector . The results of investigation aid in the better understanding of the cmstal 
framework and the geological process with bearing on development in other as vital sectors such as 
agriculture, land use management, irrigation and power development. utilisation of water resources. 
development of transport and communication, educat ion and scientific management of environment. Thus 
survey and mapping and mineral exploration are the most important functions ofGSI for Mineral sector 
and geological process having bearing on other important sectors oft he country but the committee finds that

INTRODUCTION
I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee  on Industry,  having   been  
authorised  by the  Committee, hereby present this 100 th Report of  Sub-Committee-I for  Ministry of Steel and Mines (
of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry)  on  Performance Review  of  National Mineral
Development Corporation Limited (NMDC) which is under the administrative control of  Ministry of Steel .
2.The Committee on Industry constituted Sub-Committee-I for Ministry of Steel and Mines .  The Sub-Committee took
up the issue of Performance Review of National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC)). The Sub-
Committee visited Hyderabad  from 28th and 29th June , 2002 and interacted with the  management of National Mineral
Development Corporation Limited (NMDC). 
3.            The Report has been prepared on  the basis of   on the spot  study and  interaction with the    Secretary ,
Ministry of Steel and officials  of National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC). 
4          The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 17th  December, 2002  considered and adopted  the  Report. 
5.         The Committee at its meeting held on 17th December,  2002 considered and adopted the Report.         
 
NEW DELH
December   17, 2002   
                                      
 DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman
Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
REPORT
 
National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC) , a Government of India Enterprise and  a “Mini
Ratna Category-I” Company was established  in the year 1958, in pursuance of Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 to
promote and undertake development of minerals (other than coal, oil and atomic minerals) in Public Sector. NMDC is
the largest producer and exporter of iron ore in this Country. Its exports are around 7 million tonnes of iron ore per
annum (through Minerals & Metals Trading Corporation Ltd - canalising agency). It has also exported about 1.7 MT of

100th Report of Committee on Industry

iron ore directly to China in 2001-02. NMDC has earned approximately Rs.750 Crores during the year 2001-02 by way
of foreign exchange. NMDC has been consistently achieving the rating of “ Excellent” from the very first year of
signing the MoU viz 1991-92.  It was placed in the fourth rank amongst the MOU signing PSEs for the year 1991-92,
from which it moved to third rank in the year 1992-93.  For the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96, for NMDC’s
performance of excellence and the achievement of composite score of 1.00 in each of these years under the MOU
performance evaluation, NMDC has been placed as the ‘ Joint Top Rank PSE’ in the country. This unique achievement,
as the Joint Top Rank,   has been achieved continuously for three years in succession.  Again, in 1996-97, 1997-98,
1999-2000, 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 NMDC was adjudged “Excellent”, barring 1998-99 during which period there
was general recession. 
 
1.2.      The Secretary, the Ministry of Steel, during  the course of interaction, held on  4
th April, 02,  on Demands for
Grants (2002-03) informed  the Committee that  the performance of NMDC is of higher order.  NMDC has reported
profit of Rs.160.00 crore for 1999-2000 and upto Rs.234.00 crore for the year (2000-01)  and  in the current year   the
company might improve over the figure  of last year. 
 
1.3       In the same meeting CMD  of NMDC   Shri  P.R. Tripathi  added :-
 
“The Corporation was set up in 1958  with the sole objective of development of minerals resources of the country other
than coal, oil, natural gas and atomic minerals  and  chemicals.  Now, the NMDC’s activities are concentrated on mining
of  Iron Ore, limestone and diamonds.  Due to a very good team spirit, we have an excellent system of management in
the company.  We have been consistently making profits since 1990.   NMDC had been  paying a dividend of 20 per
cent, then it has been increased to 25 per cent on the capital of Rs,132 cores.  We have returned the whole amount that 
has been given to us by the Government.  The profit of the company is the highest in the Steel Ministry.  Last year we
had Rs.314 crores.  This year our profit is very good and in spite of very poor and difficult situation in the steel industry,
we have a very good turnover.  This is mainly because we are very well diversified.  45 per cent of our  products are 
very well  diversified.  45 per cent of our products are being exported and 55 per cent is being consumed by the
domestic market.   ISPAT, ESSAR, VIKRAM are  depending on our product.  VSP is our major customer.  We
maintain very cordial relations with all so  that we can flourish in our business.”
 
1.4       The Committee notes that NMDC had been setting new records of performance in the areas of production,
despatches of iron ore, production and sales of diamonds,  increased supplies to domestic consumers.  Thus, NMDC has
been consistently scaling new heights of achievements from year to year both in physical and financial terms including
foreign exchange earnings to the country.
 
2.0       MISSION
 
2.1
              The Sub-Committee was informed that NMDC has the following Mission :-
 
“To emerge as global mining organization with international standards of excellence, rendering optimum
satisfaction to all its stake holders.”
 
2.2       The Committee notes the NMDC’s Mission to become a world leader in Mining and providing optimum
satisfaction to all its state  holders. The Committee appreciates the vision and professionalism embodied in NMDC’s
Mission. The Committee  extends  its best wishes of NMDC for realization of mission.
 
3.         OBJECTIVES OF NMDC
 
            The NMDC management informed the Sub-Committee that NMDC has chalked out macro and micro objectives
in order to translate its mission into actual performance.
 
3.1       Macro Objectives:
a.
                   Achieve sales turnover of Rs.2000 crores by year 2005.
b.                  Achieve international standards in per capita productivity, value addition and      cost      effectiveness.

Marketing.
 
3.2       Micro Objectives: Achieve growth by
                        (i)      Expansion of existing mines
                      (ii)      Operating new mines fully owned by NMDC or in joint venture.
                     (iii)      Produce High Tech value added products from Blue dust.
                    (iv)      Give thrust to exploration and exploitation of diamonds, gold and other high value minerals.
                      (v)      Maintain high level of technical excellence in the field of open cast mining and mineral processing from
investigation to production of value added items.
                    (vi)      Provide consultancy and technical know-how too other organizations.
                   (vii)      Achieve safe working conditions and work towards zero accidents.
                 (viii)      Develop human resources within the organization for achieving optimum output to match the requirements
of work in future years.
                    (ix)      Achieve high level of eco-friendly environment.
                      (x)      Achieve high level of customer satisfaction.
                    (xi)      Improve and develop R&D, for optimum use of waste, by-products and co-products, both for improving
environment and generating additional value.
 
3.3       In order to translate the Mission of the company into actual performance NMDC  has chalked out elaborate
macro and micro objectives. It is but natural that to be global player one has to outperform the others and for doing so
laying of clear-cut objective is the first and foremost requirement. So has done the NMDC.  NMDC has set the
objectives of increasing its turnover (to the tune of Rs.2000.00 crore by the year 2005), productivity, cost effectiveness
in the areas of Mining. NMDC has set the objectives  of obtaining growth by expanding the existing mines in self-
enterprise or joint venture, exploration of high value minerals and production of value added items, extending
consultancy services and impetus to HRD and adherence to safety norms. While noting  the macro and micro objectives
of NMDC, the Committee hopes that NMDC would have a resilient strategy and feasible plan and course of action to
achieve the set objectives.
 
4.0       MANAGEMENT BY OBJECTIVES (MBO)
 
4.1       Pertaining the sub-committee’s query as  to what extent NMDC management is guided by the principle of
Management by Objectives (MBO) and to what extent the efforts undertaken by the management helped in realizing the
Mission of the company, NMDC management stated that          NMDC is not functioning or guided by terminology of
Management By Objectives but follows a strategy for achieving it’s mission and objectives.  Since mission and
objectives are clear to most of the employees, all efforts are guided to achieve the mission through set objectives.  This
approach is definitely helping the Corporation which can be seen by constant increase of turn over. NMDC had a turn
over of Rs.281.98 crore in 1991-92 which has gone up to Rs.1272.39 crore in 2001-02. This was possible only due to
increase in iron ore production and its sale and also in the production and sale of diamonds.
 
4.2       The Committee is pleased to note that NMDC  follows a strategy for achieving its mission and objectives. By
application of the principle of Management by objective (MBO) the Committee meant  as to what extent the efforts of
management and  workers are  guided to achieve the mission through set objectives. However, the Committee expresses
its satisfaction that NMDC, for all its practical purposes, is guided by ‘management by objective’  (MBO) and not
`management by activities. (MBA).

10.0     COST COMPONENTS OF PRODUCTS PRODUCEDBY NMDC .
 
10.1     The main components of the cost of production are  Fixed Cost and  Variable Cost.
The fixed cost consists of salaries and wages, depreciation and office/ selling expenses. The fixed cost is being reduced
by introduction of multi-skilling concepts and by adoption of CCTV at OCSL Plants. The variable cost consists of
explosives, drill bits, tyre & tubes, spares and consumables. It also consists cost incurred towards royalty and
electricity. 
 
10.2     The cost of production at pit head is comparable with the International Mining Operations. NMDC has to incur
additional Railway freight and Port handling charges  before product reaches the consumer. The port charges and
Railway freight charges are not under the control of NMDC. It may be worth mentioning that the cost incurred in
Railway freight and port charges amounts to 60% of the cost and balance 40% cost is in the control of NMDC. This
situation creates difficulty for NMDC to compete in the  international market for iron ore. Unless efforts are made to
reduce the railway freight and port charges, it will be difficult for NMDC to sustain the progress of the Corporation.

12.0     MOU RATING OF NMDC 
 
12.1     NMDC is one of the Public Sector Enterprises which has been signing Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)
with the Government of India since 1991. At the beginning of each financial year, an agreement is reached to achieve
certain parameters such as production, sales, gross margin, ratio of net profit to capital employed, energy conservation,
R & D efforts, human resource development, project implementation etc. based on the past performance into account,
the growth need and the potential to achieve such levels of performance.  These achievements at the year end are
evaluated for the said parameters and the company gets ranked based on the evaluation score. NMDC has been
consistently achieving the rating of “ EXCELLENT” from the very first year of signing the MoU viz 1991-92.  It was
placed in the fourth rank amongst the MOU signing PSEs for the year 1991-92, from which it moved to third rank in the
year 1992-93.  For the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96, for NMDC’s performance of excellence and the
achievement of composite score of 1.00 in each of these years under the MOU performance evaluation, NMDC has
been placed as the ‘ Joint Top Rank PSE’ in the country. This has been a unique achievement as the Joint Top Rank  
has been achieved continuously for three years in succession.  Again, in 1996-97, 1997-98, 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and
2001-2002 NMDC was adjudged “EXCELLENT”, barring 1998-99 during which period there was general recession. 
NMDC had been setting new records of performance in the areas of production, despatches of iron ore, production and
sales of diamonds, profits, increased supplies to domestic consumers.  Thus, NMDC has been consistently scaling new
heights of achievements from year to year both in physical and financial terms including foreign exchange earnings to
the country.   For the year 2001-2002, the company has surpassed the MOU target of dispatches of 180 lakh tonnes of
iron ore by achieving 182.04 lakh tonnes. The company has achieved an ever highest profit before tax of Rs.320.15
crores during 2001-2002.

19.0     LEGAL FRAMEWORK  FOR GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT OF MINING         OPERATION.
 
19.1     To what extent the existing legal framework is conducive to the growth and development of mining operation.
Any suggestion on the part of NMDC management for legal reform in this regard is as follow:-
 
“Mineral industry is governed by certain statutory act and rules such  as  Mines and Mineral Development and
Regulation Act, Mineral Conservation and Development Rules,  Mineral Concession Rule, , Mines Act etc.  With the 
economic liberalization, a new National  Mineral Policy  was announced in 1993 in which 13  major minerals were
dereserved and also foreign investment in the mineral industry was encouraged.  With the existing change in the legal
frame work, State Governments have been empowered to grant and renew mining lease as  minerals are considered to
be property of  the  concerned States.  However, it is observed that State Govts. are imposing their own conditions in
granting of mining lease and this is causing hindrance in the systematic development of mineral industry.  State
Governments should be advised to  form uniform policy and grant mining/prospecting lease on first come first basis,
rather than tendering, asking  for  additional royalty etc.
 
19.2     Ministry of Mines in consultation with GSI & IBM identify mineral zones, which should be developed to meet
the country’s need and such mineral zones, which should be developed to meet the country’s need and such mineral
zones should be taken out from the purview of Forest Conservation Act. “
 
19.3     The Committee is anguished  to  note the  submission of NMDC management  that  State Govts. are imposing
their own conditions in granting of mining lease and this is causing hindrance in the systematic development of mineral
industry and asking  for sweet equity, additional royalty etc.
 
 
 
19.4     The Committee is of the view that  procedural hurdles and bureaucratic rest-redtapism  should not  come onto
the way of systematic development of mineral industry.
 
19.5     The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Steel should   approach the Department of Mines for
organizing  across the  table interaction of representatives of   mineral enterprises and  officials of state  Government  to
form uniform mineral policy as per the canons of National Mineral Policy 1993 and  sort out problems relating  to
granting of  mining/prospecting lease etc.    The Committee  feels that the Department of Mines should  issue direction 
to GSI and IBM for identification of `Exclusive Mineral Zones’ for systematic exploration and exploitation of  Mineral
resources.  Having been give due weightage  to environmental aspects, `exclusive Mineral zones may be taken out from
the  purview of forest   conservation Act.

21.0     'Pricing policy' of NMDC
 
21.1     NMDC is supplying iron ore in the domestic market as well as for export purposes.  The iron ore, which is
surplus to the domestic demand, is exported to countries like Japan, China and South Korea.  The main export of
NMDC’s ore is through MMTC as per the existing EXIM policy.  However, NMDC is also exporting small quantities of
iron ore directly based on the specific export license issued by the Ministry of Commerce / DGFT.
 
21.2     Export Prices ; The prices for export of iron ore are basically determined by the global demand and supply
position on year-to-year basis. The percentage increase/decrease in prices over the previous year is usually finalized
between the major exporters of iron ore like Australia and Brazil and major importers like Japan and European
countries.  The same percentage increase/decrease in prices is made applicable to the exports from India.  Consequently
the prices of NMDC iron ore is also decided on the same basis. 
           
21.3     Domestic Prices: The despatches to domestic market accounts for about 53% of the total dispatches of NMDC’s
iron ore.  The dispatches to domestic market are regulated in terms of long-term agreement signed by various domestic
customers.  The duration of the agreement is for a maximum period of 5 years.  Iron ore market has remained basically a
buyers market due to frequent and prolonged recessionary trends in the steel industry.  Therefore the fixed escalation in
prices is not the acceptable norm in the industry.  In terms of the long-term agreement the prices of iron ore are to be
settled each year by mutual discussions.  The mutual discussions to finalise the prices instills a sense of confidence
among the buyers that NMDC is sensitive to the customer’s needs.
 
21.4     The Board of Directors of NMDC delegated the powers for deciding the pricing through an internal committee
consisting of CMD, Director (Prdn), Director (Fin) and ED (Comml.) and authorizing CMD to take up action as deemed
necessary in this regard.
21.,5    In terms of the above decision of the Board, negotiations are held by NMDC with the parties concerned in the
beginning of the each financial year.  The negotiation are primarily based upon the “what the market can bear” criteria,
and the ground realities of steel sector.  The negotiation also to some extent take into consideration the global
demand/supply position and trends of iron ore prices in the international market. 
 
21.6     The prices so negotiated and finalized with the parties are put up for the information of the Board and adopted
for supplies during the relevant year.

 21.11.0           NEED OF   AUTONOMY FOR  NMDC IN EXPORT PROMOTION I.E.                               
DIRECT EXPORT BY NMDC
 
 
 21.11.1 The export of iron ore produced by NMDC is canalized through MMTC Ltd. in terms of the existing EXIM
policy.  The iron ore which is surplus to the demand of domestic industry is offered for export.  The major chunk of
export is canalised through MMTC and balance uncommitted quantity is permitted for exports directly by NMDC
through special export license.  The inherent drawback of the system are as follows:
 
                        (i)      The licenses issued to NMDC for exports by DGFT do not permit export to major importers of Iron Ore
like Japan and South Korea which together accounts for about 40 - 45% of sea-borne trade.
 
                      (ii)      The licenses are for limited quantity with a validity period of two/three years.  Therefore it is not possible
for NMDC to enter into an agreement/MOU on long-term basis with foreign buyers.
 
                     (iii)      NMDC has to ensure the parity of foreign exchange realization on exports on product-to-product basis with
MMTC.  Thus NMDC is deprived the freedom to adjust the prices etc. depending upon the available
inventory levels vis-à-vis the demand pattern.
 
                    (iv)      The import license imposes the restriction on NMDC to export to Japan and South Korea but for other
countries both MMTC and NMDC will be trading the same product and the brand image of the NMDC
product will never be established.
 
                      (v)      Since NMDC gets permission for Direct Export on piece-meal basis, the foreign steel mills operators have
reservations to consider NMDC as a long-term reliable supplier of iron ore.
 
                    (vi)      Since the Export Licenses are for limited quantities, NMDC cannot offer the whole product mix comprising
of both lump ore and fine ore as required by end users.
 
21.11.2            Therefore in the best interest of exports, NMDC should have complete autonomy and be permitted to
export its iron ore without any restriction of quantity, quality or geographical location.  This will enable NMDC to
operate more like any commercial organization and take business decision, which are in its best interest
 
21.11.3            NMDC is meeting the domestic demand of iron ore to an extent of 55% and the remaining 45% only is
being sold out to international market.  As per the policy of the government iron ore is to be exported through canalising
agency i.e. MMTC. MMTC finds out market to iron ore with 65% Fe content and above, whereas NMDC has got more
quantity of iron ore lying at pit head with less than 65% Fe content for which international market is available, but not
explored by NMDC.   To take care of this product NMDC is requesting Commerce Ministry to allow NMDC to direct
export to the countries other than the purchasers from MMTC i.e. Japan, Pakistan and South Korea. NMDC has already
exported directly to its foreign buyers 1.27 lakh tonnes in 1999-00, 9.65 lakh tonnes in 2000-01and  17.12 lakh tonnes in

recovery.  This trend of recovery has been further confirmed by the demand surge both from domestic buyers and
international prospective buyers during the last two months.  The increase in demand of iron ore as a consequence of
recovery in steel industry will definitely improve the financial performance of iron ore producers.

steel, it is  but natural , the existence  of inter-dependence  of steel production  and the quality of Iron –Ore  traded .  The

23.1     Keeping pace with the national policy on workers’ participation in industry, NMDC has made a remarkable

25.0     "KEY CONCERN AREAS OF MINING INDUSTRY" IN GENERAL AND    PROBLEMS BEING
FACED BY     NMDC IN PARTICULAR AND  HELP     REQUIRED FROM THE GOVERNMENT.
 
25.1  Inflated mileage on Kirandul-Kottavalasa line.
 
25.1.1.Railways have been charging freight on Kirandul-Kottavalasa line (SE Railway) by inflating the distance by 30%
NMDC has been representing for the removal of the same in view of the increased traffic handled on the line. The
inflation in distance on K-K line had been continuing since 1967. Initially it was 65.2% but with the traffic volume
increasing, this was reduced to 30% in 1981. This percentage of inflation has been continuing since then. In the last
eighteen years there has been significant increase in the traffic handled on K-K line originating iron ore movement has
gone up from 56.36 lakh tonnes in 1987-88 to 145 lakh tonnes in 2000-01. In addition, the line has been handling other
traffic particularly on account of the NALCO's alumina plant near Koraput. In addition to the budgetary increase in the
freight charges over the years since 1981, Railways had been revising the classification of iron ore upwards resulting in
further increasing in the freight charges. The classification of iron ore which was 110 in 1989-90 had increased to 120 in
1994-95 and 125 in 1999-2000. For the year 2001-02, the Railway freight in respect of iron ore has been further
increased by 3% over that of the previous year with the classification remaining unchanged at 120.
 
25.1.2  The reduction in inflated mileage would help both NMDC and other domestic customers like VSP, Essar Steel,
Ispat Industries Ltd and Vikram Ispat to improve their economy in the operations.
 
25.1.3  The Sub-Committee was informed  that the Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. is linked to  Balladilla Mines of NMDC
for sourcing its iron  ore  requirements.  The  Kothavalasa-Kirandul section (  KK Line) under  Waltair Division of S.E.
Railway measures a distance of 475 kms.  Out of this distance, 118 k.m. is  on the Eastern Ghat Section and the balance
distance is in the plains  or  plateau.  This was constructed at a  cost of Rs159 Crore. and  was  opened for traffic in 
November, 1968.  In the initial stages,  Railways levied freight charges by  inflating the distance by 65.2 percent  with
stipulation  that the freight should be levied  on discontinuous  mileage basis (i.e.)  out of  475 k.m., only 35 km (i.e.)
from Kothavalala to VSP  will be charged normal freight.  Upon a further review in  1981, the percentage of  inflation
on the total distance was reduced to 30 percent  with effect from 1.6.1981. VSP is opereating from 1989 and since then
the inflated freight charge is being levied.  VSP has  transported 463.91 lakh tonnes upto March, 2002 and paid a freight
of Rs.1634.34 crore .Had VSP paid normal freight  (i.e.)  Rs.1284 crore  paid upto 2001-02 , VSP would have saved

25.1.4  Railways claim that they use additional locos to the extent of two or  three to move iron ore as well as high
maintenance cost  due to steep gradients  which accounts only for about  1/4th  of the total distance i.e., 118 kms.   But 
the traffic of 6 MT was reached in 1988-89 and it has already  reached 14.5 MT in the year 2000-01  which is almost
two and half times more than what was originally envisaged to have a break-even.
 
25.1.5  Initially the KK line was being used for export of iron ore from, Bailadilla sector only.  However, with domestic
iron and steel   producers  like RINL, Essar  Steel & Ispat Industries started using  the same line and the  haulage of iron
ore on KK line increased rapidly.  It is expected that by  end of the  year 2002, it would be 16.3 million tonnes. 
 
25.1.6  During the last 10 years, VSP has been requesting in various coordination meetings held by Ministry of Steel or
by Ministry of Railways for the withdrawal of  these inflated freight charges.  Since 1995-96, withdrawal of this extra
freight  charge formed a part of the chapter on " assistance from the Government" in MOUs  signed with RINL.
 
25.1.7  In the meeting of  the Sub-Committee  held on 12
th September, 2001 on the subject of "Key Concern Areas of
Steel Industries and promotion of steel consumption in various sectors of economy ", the issue of inflated freight charge 
was  discussed in detailed.  Participating in discussion  Shri R.N. Malhotra, Chairman, Railway Board  expressed his
views :-
 
" On the questions of concessions, I would like to say that we are prepared to consider any request from any
manufacturer for certain concessions which will help them and which in turn would help the Railways.  But Sir, by
reducing our revenue, we cannot help anyone.  If they are prepared to give us  an undertaking that  if we  reduce the
freight on the KK Line by a certain percentage, they will be able to give us so much  of extra  traffic, we can consider
it."
 
25.1.8  Interjecting in the discussion, the Secretary, Ministry of Steel expressed   his opinion in following words:-
 
" The question that has been raised with regard to the KK Line related to movement of iron ore from Bailadilla,
which is used by the Vizag Steel Plant.  It has a very long history.    It is not really a question of incremental traffic.  The
operative issue here is that 65 per cent additional freight charge was put at a certain  point  of time because that line was
specifically created for the movement of iron ore from point A to point  B,  with an understanding that if the level of
freight crossed six million tonnes, this additionality would   be removed.  The  situation today is that, as against the 65
per cent  enhanced rate that was being charged, the  current enhanced rate is 30 per cent, and the traffic  generated on
that line, today,  12 tonnes. We can not have a persistent kind of an incremental situation going on.  We understand that
at a point of time, the line was constructed for captive use, and additional charges were levied in order to make it viable
for the Railways.  Once a certain threshold of traffic generation has been achieved, the incremental rate should not
apply.  That was the original understanding.  One cannot have a situation wherein because  there is an incremental rate,
in order to reduce it, you must have incremental traffic.  The fact  that rate was brought down from 65 per cent  to 35 per
cent and now to 30 per cent is, itself, a recognition of the  understanding on which this 65 per cent  was  charged.  Now,
as per that understanding, that additionally factor should now go.  This  is the issue that has to be examined.
 
25.1.9  Responding to the arguments of Secretary, the Chairman, Railway Board, added :-
 
            " The Additionally which was charged earlier was for several reasons.  The first reason was that because it was a
hilly area, with sharp edges and curves, the construction cost of rails was very high.  The second reason was that we had
put surcharge on  movement of any traffic on that line because of the fact that in place of one locomotive, which is
normally required on a  plain terrain, we had to put three locomotive in place .  So, the cost of operation also was very
high.   Also, the  electricity  bill for the  operational  of  this line is five times higher than what it would cost in the case
of   a line on the plain.  Now, how do we recover that cost ?  We cannot go on reducing our revenue, unless there is a
commitment on the part of the steel plants that they will be able to sell so much of extra steel and thus give us that much
of extra traffic.".

RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee noted that many of the Central PSEs are making losses due to their inability to face the competition, because of their obsolete
R&D, high cost of production, shortage of work orders, etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should
infuse capital, state of the art technology and entrepreneurship into potentially viable PSEs so as to make these ‘Modern Temples’ capable to face the
private sector MNCs in the consumer economy.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The strategies for strengthening and improving the potentially viable PSEs include:---
           1.    Revival of PSEs through BIFR.
           2.    Financial restructuring wherever appropriate.
           3.    Joint Venture formation to have continuous access to technology, finance and marketing.
           4.    Manpower rationalization.
        Out of 26 BIFR referred PSUs under the Department of Heavy Industry revival plans have been sanctioned by BIFR in case of 12 PSUs. These
involve cash infusion of Rs.654 crore by the Government besides financial restructuring of Rs.2106 crores. Apart from BIFR sanctioned revival
plans, Government has on its own, approved the financial restructuring in case of 7 other sick/loss making PSUs involving fresh infusion of funds to
the extent of Rs.531 crores and financial restructuring of Rs.1443 crores.
        In order to rationalize the manpower, Government have provided an amount of about Rs.1700 crores under Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)
for retiring about 70,000 employees of PSUs.

Ltd. have already been converted into joint venture companies. Also in case of 30 PSUs of Department of Heavy Industry, the process of JV
formation/disinvestments has been initiated.

execution of projects financed by the United Nations/World Bank or any other International Organisation. This amended custom duty structure has

Para 10.7, 10.9, 10.11
HINDUSTAN PAPER CORPORATION LTD. (HPC)
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee recommends that while rationalizing the duty structure compatible with WTO guidelines, the Government should protect the
interests of the domestic paper industries.
        The Committee views the Government’s Policy of reducing customs duty from 35% to 30% as against the WTO bound rate of 40% as a major
threat for the domestic paper industries. The Committee conceives that the reduction in customs duty would definitely encourage import, which in
turn, would adversely affect the paper industries. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should review its decision and revise
the custom duty to 35% or 40%.
        The Committee recommends that the Government should stop the ‘Disguised Import’ of newsprint in order to save the domestic paper
industries. The Committee also recommends that the BHI should take up this subject with the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) for
reversing the custom duty on newsprint from the present 5% to 20% which is still lower to the WTO bond rate of 25%.
        The excise duty on writing & printing paper may also be reduced from 16% to 8% 
ad-valorem.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The matter has been taken up with Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.

domestic market share. Capital goods sector has witnessed a decline of 2.7% in April-Sept.2000 as compared to a growth of 5% in 1999-2000 and
11% in 1998-99.
2.     Some of the factors responsible for deceleration are slow down in investment, reduction in the custom duty on capital goods/project imports
from a high of 85% to 0-5%. Domestic manufacturers continue to suffer cost disadvantages such as sales tax, octroi, high cost of finance and

manufacturers are not able to avail the price preference of 15% for projects funded by such agencies.

1.1       The commitments and mutual responsibilities of the Government and the PSUs are clearly defined in the MoU

2.1       MFL was incorporated in December, 1966 as a public sector undertaking with authorised share capital of Rs. 14

shareholding in MFL.

CAPTIVE  FERTILIZER  BERTH  AT  ENNORE  PORT  TERMINAL  (EPT)
2.4       MFL is planning to shift its port operations to the newly developed Ennore Port Terminal from Chennai Port,
considering the long-term benefits for the company and to overcome the present problems of port congestion and port-
to-plant logistics.
2.5       In this backdrop, MFL is planning to set up a Captive Fertilizer Berth as a joint venture project to handle 2
million TPA of Dry bulk and Liquid cargo, made up of 1.5 million MT is dry bulk cargo comprising of Urea, MOP,
DAP and finished grades of fertilizer and 0.5 MT liquid cargo comprising of Phosphoric acid and Liquid ammonia.
Modern handling facilities like Unloading Systems, Bagging Systems and Transit Storage form part of the project.
2.6       MFL is in the process of engaging a consultant to select a suitable Joint Venture Partner, among 12 parties who
have evinced interest to participate in this Captive Fertilizer Berth Project.
CAPTIVE  POWER
2.7       MFL consumes around 130 million unit of electrical power per year drawn from TNEB grid and also from
captive generation. 8 Diesel Generators and 2 Gas Turbines generate 32.7 million units (25%) per year as captive power.
2.8       To tide over frequent power failure, under-frequency and voltage fluctuations of TNEB grid, MFL is seeking
alternate power capacity from outside supply sources other than TNEB.
2.9       MFL had preliminary discussion with Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) for participation in their
proposed Rs. 2837 crore Independent Power Plant (IPP) Project of 500 MW capacity.
2.10     In the meantime, MFL is holding negotiation with CPCL for wheeling 4 to 5 MW of surplus power from their
existing captive Power Plant facility.
2.11     The company did not pay dividend to its shareholders after 1992-93. It is running in losses. The loss was
contributed by shortfall in production of urea and NPK, reduction in contribution for NPK, higher specific consumption
of raw materials, steep exchange rate variation, monsoon failure resulting in lower sales, higher rebates and discounts
and higher interest cost.
2.12     The company's operations continue to be unprofitable. During April and May 2001, Ammonia plant load had to
be restricted due to high Ammonia inventory levels caused by poor off-take by downstream urea/NPL plants. Similarly,
urea plant was also operated at low levels as off-take of NPK for sale has been poor. The annual turnaround was taken
up on May 28, 2001 with a schedule to complete it on June 22, 2001. However, due to the unexpected developments,
the turnaround was extended and the company could come back to production stream in respect of NH
3 only on August
3, 2001. Keeping in view the advice given by urea reactor manufacturers, the company decided to get the urea reactor
inspected which was not envisaged in the original schedule. The inspection of reactor was a difficult job involving
erection of structure above the reactor with hoisting facility. Though an attempt was made to erect the structure while
the plant was in operation, enough progress could not be made due to unfavourable environmental conditions. After the
shut down of the plants, erection work was taken up and hoists were provided at the top level of about 60 mtrs. height to
life the reactor bundles, each weighing 36 T. Reactor B was inspected on July 18 and after attending to some minor
repairs was boxed up.
2.13     In contrast, the inspection of reactor 'A' revealed extensive damages. A quick assessment was made and
necessary action was initiated by the company to rectify the bundles. Notwithstanding all these constraints, the company
decided to start and run the Ammonia and Urea plants at around 50% load. The quality of Urea being produced now is
relatively better with temperature of the Prill hovering around 50
o Celsius, which are the main objectives of Urea Prill
Tower modifications, aimed and achieved by the company. The repair works to Reactor 'A' involve procurement of
imported materials, extensive welding and other specialized jobs, which has been entrusted on a turnkey basis to the
manufacturer M/s Nooter Fabricators Inc. USA to secure Guarantee Test Run of urea plant.

2.14     The acute water scarcity situation affected the Chennai City subsequent to failure of monsoon. The water supply
to the company has been restricted to 0.33 million gallon per day (MGD) as against the requirement of 2.5 MGD. There
is an apprehension that the present supply could be cut down further. This problem is being tackled by the company by
purchasing water at a lighter rate from Metro Water with a view to sustain production at a maximum possible level.
Thus even if there was no problem in Urea Reactor, Urea production had to be curtailed to 45% due to cut in raw water
supply. On the sales front also, the company had been affected due to adverse agro climatic conditions prevailing in the
entire marketing territory of the company viz. Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. In Andhra Pradesh and
Karnataka, drought like situation is prevailing and posing threat to company's marketing efforts. In these states, rainfall
has been only 73% of normal and sowing has been only 40%.
FINANCIAL  ASSISTANCE  CUM  CAPITAL  RESTRUCTURING  (FACR)
2.15     MFL has submitted original FACR proposal to Government of India during January 1999. Whereas the proposal
relating to FIs have been approved and implemented by them during April 1999, the proposal submitted to Government
of India has undergone several revisions till date. In view of the losses incurred during 2000-01 and continuing during
the current year 2001-02 MFL has requested for a revised FACR packages from Government of India and other
institutions, which have extended long term/short term assistance. In respect of FIs, the revised proposal inter-alia
included downward revision of interest rate with moratorium on principal and interest payment for 2 years. With regard
to Government of India loans, the proposal provides for waiver of interest amounting to Rs. 71 crores and downward
reduction of interest rate. Similarly, the revised FACR envisages lower interest on the working capital assistance
received from commercial banks. With a view to avoid company becoming sick, the FIs and Government of India are
working out a comprehensive package.
2.16     The Company has been taking up with various policy-making bodies about disadvantageous position in which
the company has been operating with costly feedstock like Naphtha on one hand and high capital-related charged on the
other hand (consequent to implementation of Revamp Project at the cost of around Rs. 601 crores). Accordingly, in
order to reduce the yawning gap between cost of production and realization, company has represented to Tariff
Commission to reckon industry related/MFL specific problems in the areas of :-
                  –  Assessment of capacity utilization and normative capacity utilization
                  –  Consumption norms
                  –  Interest on working capital
                  –  Selling and distribution expenses
                  –  Return on capital employed
                  –  PCS based on cost of bought (imported) urea and Naptha-based captive Ammonia used in NPK production
                  –  Compensation to cover cost of 90 days forward cover for exchange rate variation.
            The above, if considered favourable by the Government, will help the company in recovering certain costs
substantially.

senior management of the public sector, the officers of the Department of Fertilizers, etc. The Committee noted that
criteria for giving weightage under MoU system was as under :

                  –  An overriding emphasis was found to have been laid on the financial performance in the MoU structure.
Nearly 60% weight was assigned to this factor.
                  –  Dynamic parameters like safety were assigned a very low weightage of 2 for frequency and 2 points for
severity whereas the impact of these on the socio-economic environment of operation would be extremely
catastrophic.
                  –  The energy efficiency parameter should be high in view of the energy intensity of the manufacturing
process. Presently, it is said to be built in to the financial parameters whereas separate weight to be given
to this as it forms a statutory requirement under the balance sheet.
                  –  Environmental aspect did not find any weight in the MoU structure.
                  –  Bio-fertilizers had a very low weight. These apart, new products for enhancing the life expectancy of soil
also did not find any weight.
                  –  R&D has very low weight in the MOU structure. R&D should also be split into process development,
product development and system improvements.
                  –  Extension services should become an integral part of MoU structure under the weightage for farmer's
education.
                  –  HRD weight should also include separate weightage to public health, sanitation, social Security, etc. in

3.       The Committee thereafter, took up Auto Policy for discussion. The Chairman apprised the Members that the
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry had recommended in its 59th Report that the Government should
formulate an Auto Policy in view of the ongoing liberalization of the economy and W.T.O. obligations. In response to
the Committee's recommendations the Department of Heavy Industries in its Action Taken Note has informed the
Committee that Government of India has brought out an Auto Policy on 7th March, 2002.
3.1     The Chairman stated that the Committee on Industry took up the Auto Policy for detailed discussion as the policy
laid down certain recommendations for the growth of the Industry. Since most of these recommendations required
actions by the Ministries other than the Department of Heavy Industries and so far these recommendations had not been
translated into real Government Policy.
3.2.    The Chairman apprised the Members that the Committee had already taken up the matter for discussion and in
this regard the Committee had held two meetings on 24th June and 16th July, 2002. Based on the discussion held on
24th June, 2002 a questionnaire was prepared and replies thereon was obtained from Department of Heavy Industries. In
the meeting held on 16th July, 2002 the Committee had interacted with Automotive Research Association of India
(ARAI); Society of India Automobiles Manufacturers (SIAM); Automotive Tyre Manufacturers Association (ATMA)
and Automotive Component Manufacturers Association (ACMA); Prozon Inc. (manufacture of fuel saver). Apprising
the Members the details of discussion held in these two meetings, the Chairman spelt out the scope for discussion in

Commission pay scales as an interim measure.  The clearance of balance dues of retired and separated employees would
however be dependent on approval of further financial assistance by the Ministry of Finance.

Recommendation (Para 5.6 )
 
Failure of financial and  revival package
           
            The Committee is of the view that since the Government is giving impetus to the construction sector and because
HSCL is engaged in the construction works, therefore, its should not be difficult for the HSCL management to procure
work order.  Moreover, the Steel Industry is up swinging, it is being  hoped that HSCL would be able to meet its target
for 2002-2003 to procure the work order to the tune of Rs. 300 crore.  The Committee further recommends that
optimum utilization of manpower resources at the disposal of the Company is the responsibility of HSCL management.

That  since most of  the employees in HSCL  are in the age of group  of 52 and above  as such  the scope of

added  managerial  skill  as how to   re-orient    its  workforce  for making the same efficient and effective.   The 
Committee hopes that   the strategic plan  and restructuring plan where   a consultant has been engaged, would take care 
of all these  practical aspects.
 
Recommendation ( Para 7.3)
 
System of Sub-Contracting Business Pattern
           
            The Committee feels that  entrusting  HSCL merely the supervisory role  and continuing  with   the system of
Sub-contracting would not be  a  sustainable proposition  for the Company.   There is no need   for making a mini
Ministry   with in the  Ministry  of Steel .  The Ministry of Steel is already playing the  supervisory role  over the steel
PSUs,   therefore,   Steel PSUs should  do the actual  work, the Committee feels .  The Committee,  therefore,  
reiterates   that   direct undertaking of work by HSCL staff would give  larger  margin to HSCL and thus opening  scope
for profitability of HSCL, therefore, it would be better that the system of sub-contracting is  replaced  by direct
involvement of HSCL employees, sooner than later.

            The Committee feels that,  since  HSCL  is a  steel PSUs so it is  but natural  that the proportion of  work order

HSCL  when in deep trouble, by  continuing   to award  work order on priority basis.

enhancement of  its good will and  thus enriched  goodwill  would be  off immense help in procurement of  further work

handicapped persons, Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribes are retrenched at the end.  The Committee hopes that the new
management would ensure the implementation of the provision inwards and deeds.
 
4.            Efficiency Vs Human Relation Approach
 
            The Committee is of the view that the new management would take every care for optimum utilization of
manpower by adopting the principle of placing a right man at right place in right time in such a way that company
affairs are managed in the efficient and effective manners and keeping in view endowment of human values and ethics.
 
5.            Keeping track with changing economic scenario
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that the new management should keep an eye to the changing economic
scenario at the national and International market and reorient its mission and objectives so as to improve its physical and
financial performance.  In demand driven economy it is essential that adequate attention is being given to market
research and reorient its production plan as per the demand of the market.   New management should keep on analyzing
the strength, weaknesses, opportunities and threats     of the company and chalked out future course of action as per the
requirement. 
 
 
6.         New management initiative for employee participation
 
            The Committee hopes that the joint consultative Committee (JCC) consist of nominees of workmen and
management would be functional in real terms and all efforts would be made for achieving organizational goals of
productivity, quality, cost management and good employee relation.
 
7.            Initiative in Inventory Management, Sales, Marketing and Finance
 
            The Committee notes that the initiative taken by the new management in the field of inventory management,
sales, marketing and finance and hopes that such initiative would lead to quick disposal of inventories, increment in
turnover and  sales and market share of HZL products and attainment of favorable financial ratios.
 
8.         Welfare amenities
 
            The Committee is happy to note that the welfare amenities which were available to nearby population of the
Units prior to disinvestment continue to be availed by them. The Committee hopes that   the new management will   
initiate renewed course of action for peripheral developments.  
 
9.            Environmental awareness and  sustainable development
 
              The Committee, while appreciating the initiative taken by the new management    for implementation of
environmental awareness  and sustainable development objectives recommends that the new management would
continue with  its concerted efforts.
 
10.            Disinvestment proceeds  for  spending  on social sector
 
            The Committee is of the considered view that   the Government should create a special fund to keep the  this
disinvestment proceed of  the company for spending on social sectors scheme with high appeal.

INTRODUCTION 
         I, the Chairman of  the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having 
been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred-Sixth Report on the Globalisation 
and capital goods industry pertaining to the Department of Public En terprises, Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises. 
2.      The Committee, in this context, held m eetings with various Minist ries and representatives o f
Industry Organisations on 16 th April, 8 th May, 25 th June, 12 th August and 27 th November, 2002 
respectively. 
3.      The Committee in its meeting held on 17th December, 2002 considered and adopted the Report.
 
  
CHAPTER – I 
INTRODUCTION 
         A new trend of global integration began to emerge all over the world in 1980s. This was facilitated
by the gradual integration of the world economics, which ensured free flow of capital and goods from
one country to another country. Foreign capital is now freely available to finance the large infrastructure
projects. Acceptance of WTO regime  by most of the countries has si nce led to a gradual abolition o f
quantitative restrictions and reduction duties and removal of restrictions on inter-country trade. 
1.1    In our context, the Industr ial Policy of 1991 starte d the process of de-lic ensing and except 18 
industries, licensing was withdrawn. The process of de-regul ation was aimed at en larging competition 
and allowing new firms to enter the market s. The market was opened up to domestic
entrepreneurs/industrialists, which as reserved for public sector unde rtakings, and foreign capital was
provided free entry up to 51% equity in high technol ogy areas. With the adve nt of globalization, when
World Bank-aided projects started to come to country, the lifting of import control and drastic reduction 
of import duties, competition from overseas posed a proble m to the domestic capital goods industry. It
has become difficult to stay in the race for this industry in the fa ce of stiff competition from the
multinational giants. 
1.2    Despite the tremendous odds even on date, there are examples of various domestic Indian
companies in sectors like automobi les, steel, engineering, etc. in both public and private sectors that
have successfully with stood the changes brought about by the liberalization of Indian economy; fo r
example Maruti cars are being exported and Tata have similar plans. TISCO has been recognized as one
of the least cost steel producers in the world and companies like IRCON, BHEL and L&T have been
successfully executing contracts abroad. These com panies have mana ged to meet the stiff com petition

1.3    The Committee deliberated upon the matter and in its 36th Report observed as under:
 
         “One such company (BHEL) which has successfully withstood the changes brought about by 
the liberalization of Indian econom y. The impressive track record of  it calls for a special mention 
of its achievements. As a matter of fact, BHEL is a role model for other PSUs of Ministry of Heavy 
Industry. For, it has managed to stay in the race  despite the odds faced by  it as a result of stif f 
competition unleashed by the multina tional giants operating in its fi eld of specialization namely, 
manufacture of power plants. T hough BHEL has managed to sustain it s viability yet it is facing 
some unfair challenges. The abse nce of a level playing field vis-à-vis its multinational competitors 
has been posing stiff challenges to the company. This  is leading to an eve r-increasing pressure on 
its profitability. Despite this, the company has been constantly  upgrading its technology and has 
also been successful in acquiring state of the art technology used in HVDC  power projects. This 
reflects the commitments of the company as a whole to serve th e nation even when the odds are 
stacked against it. Therefor e, what this company requires is a li ttle help from th e Government in 
the form of suitable policy measures. In this re gard, the sub-committee draw s the attention of the 
Government to the issues of pr ice and purchase preference to BHEL, and import duty concessions 
to the foreign companies. Through  in some cases price and purchas e preference is granted to the 
PSUs, the positive results of this measure are negated by the import duty concessions extended to 
the foreign companies by the Government. These concessions and exempti ons are precisely the 
reasons for the playing field not be ing level for domestic companies or  for that matter PSUs as the 
bids offered by foreign players are much lower in comparison to the ones offered by PSUs. In other 
words, the competition is killed well before it begins. The Committee believes that the need of the 
hour is not to go back to the days of protectionism rather to provide  a level playing field to all the 
players for the sake of healthy competition.

domestic companies especially the PSUs. It is the considered view  of the committee that foreign
companies should not be shown favour at the expense of domestic companies.”

CHAPTER – III 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
3.        The amendment of Customs Notification N o. 85/99 dated 6.7.1999 was issued amending the 
earlier Notification No. 84/99 permitting imports at zero duty for projects funded by international
Organizations. With th e notification, the preference polic y under World Ba nk guideline has
automatically reduced to zero and adversely affected the domestic industry. The Committee consistently
followed up the matter and recommende d for corrective measures in its 36 th, 45th and 59th Reports and 
had five meetings with several mi nistries and public and private sect or domestic industry to resolve the
matter. The World Bank issue is not only applicable  to Public Sector Undert akings but also to capital
goods industry in general. The Committee’s objective was to utilize it for the development of the
country. 
3.1      The Committee recalls that in the meetings held on 16 th April, 8th May and 25th June, 2002, The 
Ministries/Departments had expresse d their own reservations and concer ns but ultimately they realized
that if only they put their heads together they could resolve the i ssue. The Committee appreciates the
ministries and departments for their coordinated approach. 
3.2      Since globalization, the country is facing ma ny problems but at the sa me time the country cannot
go back. We have to see how to safeguard the country’s interest – both public and private sectors. 
3.3      Now, in view of the clarificatory notification issued by the Department of  Economic Affairs,
there is no need to rescind the Notification No. 85/99 and the Comm ittee hopes that the capital goods
industry of the country would be ab le to compete with the foreign bi dders in the projects funded by
international organizations. The Committee, however, urges upon the i ndustry to keep vigil and watch
with regard to any deviation of the World Bank gui deline by any international agency by not including
the price preference clause in the NIT (Notice I nviting Tender) and thereby depriving the domestic
industry to bid for the project and the industry should also immediately bring any instance to the notice
of Department of Economic Affairs in case such price preference is not extended to domestic industry
by any multinational organizations. 
3.4      The Committee understands more internati onal funded projects would come to the country in
future and the domestic industry w ould be able to reap the benefi t and contribute to the country’s 
development.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
CHAPTER–I
LIQUIDATED DAMAGES – THE CONCEPT
            In a supply contract if there is a delay beyond the contractual delivery period in execution of supply, services,
erection and commissioning, the consignee may end up suffering actual or potential losses. Direct losses arising out of
the delay actual in nature that can be directly quantified like debt servicing etc. Potential losses are indirect losses like
opportunity costs, cost overrun of the project, time overrun of the project leading to inflation of project cost etc. The
losses tantamount to the damages suffered by the consignee and quantified unit of these damages are known as
Liquidated Damages.
2.         As per the standard terms of conditions of contracts internationally acclaimed the amount of liquidated damages
is generally ½% of the total value of the contract for every week of delay in supplies or other performance of the
contract plus any cost escalation that has taken place on account of any increase in taxes or imposition of fresh taxes, or
cost escalation of any raw material on account of this during the period of delay, cost escalation of labour due to any
new wage agreement, or imposition of any statutory conditions. However, the supplier will be entitled to any decrease in
cost on the above account of remission of taxes or withdrawal of taxes during the said period between stipulated
delivery period and the actual date of delivery.
3.         As per standard terms of conditions of supply contract generally also provide for force majeure clause meaning
unforeseen circumstances like legal injunctions, natural calamities, industrial action by workers etc. are reasons
attributable to the delay in supply or performance, the same is exempt from imposition of liquidated damages.
4.         The Sub-Committee-III for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises of Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry came to know about the effect of Liquidated Damages on the supplier
when it visited Bharat Heavy Plates and Vessels at Visakhapatnam (a subsidiary of BYNL) on 11th July, 2000. The
workers union as well as management of BHPV informed the Committee that due to delay in deliveries, Rs. 41 crores
had been held up with different units of the company which had created cash flow problems. Later on, after visiting

account LDs imposed on them by their client companies. The matter came up before the Sub-Committee at its meeting
held on 9th November, 2000. The Convenor, after hearing the Secretaries, Department of Heavy Industry, and Ministry
of Petroleum and Natural Gas, about the present status of the outstanding issues of amounts of BYNL group of
companies withheld by various oil sector PSUS on account of LD and other disputed matters, directed the Secretary,
Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises to suitably take up the issue with the Ministry of Petroleum and
Natural Gas for advising the Oil PSUs to consider these cases favourably. The Committee also directed to follow it up
by personal visits by representatives of BYNL and their respective subsidiaries to the concerned Oil PSUs.
5.         Thereafter,  the Committee on Industry in its 44th Report present/laid on 21st December, 2000 recommended as
follows :
5.1       The Committee also came to know during its interaction with the workers and management of some PSUs that
due to non-delivery of final goods in schedule time, penalties have been imposed on them in the form of Liquidity
Damages (LD) which are proving a death knell for some of them.
5.2       The Department of Heavy Industry should take up the matter with the client PSUs for release of outstanding
amount locked-up on account of Liquidity Damages (LD) to such a possible extent, which can be released by the client
PSUs. This will be a helpful gesture to the PSUs who are having working capitalproblem.
5.3       The Ministry of Heavy Industry and Public Enterprise in their Action Taken Note informed that Government had
been taking up the matter with the concerned Ministries/Departments for release of withheld amount on account of LDs.
6.         This was reported to the House vide Committee's 60th report presented/laid on the 19th December, 2001. Since
the persuasive efforts of Department of Heavy Industry could not bear much fruit, 
Sub-Committee-III observed that these issues needed to be approached through a coordinated effort. The Committee
also felt that there was a lack of appreciation of concerns expressed by DHI in respect of the said issue by the other
Ministry. The Committee, therefore, decided to hear both the Department of Heavy Industry and the Ministry of
Petroleum and Natural Gas to find out a probable solution.
CHAPTER–II
MEETINGS HELD WITH THE MINISTRIES AND PSUS THEREUNDER
7.         The Committee held meetings on 17th April, 13th August and 4th December, 2002 on the issue. The
deliberations of the Committee are given below :
Meeting held on 17th April, 2002
7.1       At the outset, the Convenor welcomed the Secretaries of the Ministries of Heavy Industries and Public
Enterprises and Petroleum and Natural Gas, and representatives of various Central PSUs. The Convenor apprised the
Committee that the Committee had been pursuing the case of liquidated damages, which had been imposed by the client
PSUs on the supplier PSUs for non-adherence to the delivery schedule. There had been some problems among the
PSUs. These Liduidated Damages were imposed due to delay and as a result the money had been held up and the
supplier PSUs, specially the BYNL group of companies, had been facing working capital problem.
7.2       Secretary,  Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, informed the Committee that the engineering
industries were facing some problems as there had been no fresh investment in the economy. One of the main problems
had been the lack of working capital because the working capital limits had become irregular. The banks were not
willing to give further advance and the Government was also reluctant to issue fresh funds for the working capital. The
BYNL group of companies had a large measure of support from oil sector and the oil sector was one sector in the
economy where there had been some investment. About 50% of the turnover of these companies came from the oil
PSUs and generally oil sector PSUs also gave benefit of purchase preference to these companies. There had been delay
in execution of projects but in the recent past, these companies had assured that things had improved and some of those
delays or level of delays or the extent of delays that took place earlier, were not taking place now. The process of
disinvestments in all these companies was under way and in order to optimise the return to the Government, the

Ministry was trying to do everything that would add value to these companies and if these companies were running well
